### 2.6.2 The instruction descriptor

PTX ISA 9.4, 9.7.18.4.2, Table 51 defines the 32-bit instruction descriptor for `.kind::f16`. CuTe's `InstrDescriptor` (`cute/arch/mma_sm100_desc.hpp:416-443`) mirrors it with the field names this lecture and the kernel's own comment use (explicit.cu:173: `c_format F32 (bit 4), n_dim 128 >> 3 = 16 at [17,23), m_dim 256 >> 4 = 16 at [24,29)`). The kernel's constant `kInstrDesc = 0x10200010` is F32 accumulate (bit 4), F16 inputs (zeros), K-major both (zeros), `n_dim = 128 >> 3 = 16`, `m_dim = 256 >> 4 = 16`; measured D7 `idesc = 0x10200010` in every K3 record. It is a run-time `"r"` operand of W29 but constant for the whole kernel, because the instruction shape never changes. The full bit map with the kernel's values is Chapter 5, Section 5.8.2.

---

## 2.7 TMA: tensor maps, boxes, swizzles, multicast, bulk groups, the async proxy

### 2.7.1 Tensor maps

A tensor map is a 128-byte opaque descriptor: the driver API's `CUtensorMap`, an array of 16 opaque 64-bit words. It is 64-byte aligned in the CUDA 12 headers and 128-byte aligned in the CUDA 13 headers (explicit.hpp:66 comment and note G.3). CuTe's `using TmaDescriptor = CUtensorMap;` is cute/arch/copy_sm90_desc.hpp:292; its fallback definition three lines down, `struct alignas(64) { char bytes[128]; }` (:295), spells the size out, and explicit.hpp:67 pins it with `static_assert(sizeof(CUtensorMap) == 128, ...)`. The host encodes it with `cuTensorMapEncodeTiled` and passes it to the kernel by value as `const __grid_constant__` (explicit.cu:1096: `explicit_blackwell_fp16_gemm_kernel(const __grid_constant__ ExplicitGemmParams params)`), so the device uses its parameter-space address. The driver-API rules (CUDA driver API, `cuTensorMapEncodeTiled`): `globalAddress` "must be 16 byte aligned"; `globalDim` "must be non-zero and less than or equal to 2^32"; `globalStrides` "must be a multiple of 16 and less than 2^40"; `boxDim` "must be non-zero and less than or equal to 256"; `boxDim[0] * elementSizeInBytes` "must be a multiple of 16 bytes"; for swizzled maps "the bounding box inner dimension (computed as boxDim[0] multiplied by element size derived from tensorDataType) must be less than or equal to the swizzle size" (32/64/128 bytes). All of these hold here trivially: `cudaMalloc` pointers are aligned to at least 256 bytes (CUDA Programming Guide, "Device Memory Accesses"), the extents are 8192, the strides 16384 and 32768 B.

The six maps of this run (A, B, C, D, plus CUTLASS's two fallback copies of A and B, byte-identical to them and never passed to the explicit kernel; note 5.3, measured D3; all rank 3 with a batch mode of extent 1 and stride 0):

| Map | dtype | dims (inner first) | strides (bytes) | box | swizzle | inner box bytes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | FLOAT16 | (K, M, L) = (8192, 8192, 1) | (16384, 0) | (64, 64, 1) | `CU_TENSOR_MAP_SWIZZLE_128B` | 64 x 2 = 128 = the swizzle span |
| B | FLOAT16 | (K, N, L) | (16384, 0) | (64, 64, 1) | `SWIZZLE_128B` | 128 |
| C, D | FLOAT32 | (M, N, L) | (32768, 0) | (32, 16, 1) | `CU_TENSOR_MAP_SWIZZLE_128B_ATOM_32B` | 32 x 4 = 128 |

Common: `INTERLEAVE_NONE`, `L2_PROMOTION_L2_128B`, `OOB_FILL_NONE`. The inner box is 128 bytes in every map because the 128-byte swizzle rule caps it there: a 64 x 64 fp16 box is 8192 B, a 32 x 16 fp32 box is 2048 B. This is why one A/B stage is two boxes per CTA (one A half, one B half: Section 2.7.4) and why one 128 x 16 fp32 epilogue subtile is four D boxes (note 13 item 14; `kStoreBoxBytes = 32 * 16 * 4 = 2048`, explicit.cu:120).

`prefetch.tensormap` (W20, explicit.cu:440-447) "brings the cache line containing the specified address in the .const or .param memory state space for subsequent use by the cp.async.bulk.tensor instruction" (PTX ISA 9.4, 9.7.10.16). The kernel prefetches all four maps once per CTA in the prologue (explicit.cu:1114-1119; measured SASS `UTMACCTL.PF` x 4).

### 2.7.2 Boxes, coordinates and out-of-bounds fill

PTX ISA 9.4, 5.5.3.1: "A tensor can be accessed in chunks known as Bounding Box ... Size of each bounding Box must be a multiple of 16 bytes. The address of the bounding Box must also be aligned to 16 bytes ... The tensor-coordinates, specified in the PTX tensor instructions, specify the starting offset of the bounding box." Coordinates are element indices, innermost first: `(k, row, 0)` for A/B and `(m, n, 0)` for C/D (explicit.cu:134-135 comment; measured K4a/K4b). 5.5.3.3: "Zero fill mode: Elements in the Bounding Box which fall outside of the tensor boundary are set to 0. OOB-NaN fill mode: ... set to a special NaN called OOB-NaN." `CU_TENSOR_MAP_FLOAT_OOB_FILL_NONE` is the zero-fill mode (driver API). In this run no box ever crosses a boundary (8192 is a multiple of 64, 32 and 16), so OOB fill is configured but never exercised; a general kernel gets residue handling for free from it (Chapter 13).

### 2.7.3 Swizzle modes: `SWIZZLE_128B` and `SWIZZLE_128B_ATOM_32B`

Why swizzle at all. For the MMA operands the reason is shared-memory bank conflicts. A K-major core matrix is 8 rows x one 16-byte chunk at the same column position; without swizzling those eight chunks sit 128 B apart in the same four of the 32 x 4-byte banks, and XOR-ing the chunk index with the row index mod 8 spreads them over all eight positions of the 128-byte line (analysis of the layout; the hardware's actual access grouping is not documented; Chapter 8, Section 8.8.2). For the epilogue stage the reason is different. Its mode is dictated by the D tensor map (`CU_TENSOR_MAP_SWIZZLE_128B_ATOM_32B`, chosen by CUTLASS's epilogue builder through `Layout_MN_SW128_32B_Atom<float>`, note 13 item 10), and the generic-proxy writer must produce exactly the byte pattern the TMA store will read back. For this kernel's stores it is *not* a bank-conflict fix: each warp-wide `st.shared.b32` covers one 128-byte line, all 32 banks once, with or without the XOR (derived from explicit.cu:1013; Chapter 10, Section 10.5.5):

```
    st_off[c] = OFF_SMEM_CD + 2048u * w + 4u * (l & 7u) + 128u * c + 32u * (((l >> 3) & 3u) ^ c);
```

In both modes the TMA unit permutes 16-byte (or 32-byte) chunks inside each 128-byte line on the way in, and the consumer applies the same permutation on the way out: the MMA through its descriptor (Section 2.6.1), the TMA store through its map.

**`SWIZZLE_128B` with 16-byte atomicity** (PTX ISA 9.4, 5.5.7 "128 byte swizzle mode ... 16-byte atomicity sub-mode: In this sub-mode, the 16-byte of data is kept intact while swizzling"; the pattern table is given for a 1024-byte-aligned start). Chunk `c` (0..7) of line `r` is stored at chunk position `c ^ (r % 8)`:

```
  16-byte chunk position inside the 128-byte line:   0  1  2  3  4  5  6  7
  line r = 0  holds chunks                           0  1  2  3  4  5  6  7
  line r = 1                                         1  0  3  2  5  4  7  6
  line r = 2                                         2  3  0  1  6  7  4  5
  line r = 3                                         3  2  1  0  7  6  5  4
  line r = 4                                         4  5  6  7  0  1  2  3
  line r = 5                                         5  4  7  6  1  0  3  2
  line r = 6                                         6  7  4  5  2  3  0  1
  line r = 7                                         7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0
  ... pattern repeats every 8 lines = 1024 bytes
```

In address terms: byte-address bits [4,7), the chunk index, are XOR-ed with bits [7,10), the line index mod 8. That is CuTe's `Swizzle<3,4,3>` (explicit.cu:204 asserts `yyy_msk = 0x380`, `num_shft = 3`; the comment at explicit.cu:127: "the 16-byte chunk inside a 128-byte row is XOR-ed with (row % 8)"). The pattern repeats every 1024 B, so a stage must start on a 1024-byte boundary for the TMA write and the descriptor read (base offset 0) to agree (explicit.cu:162; Chapter 8, Sections 8.8.1 and 8.8.3). The TMA table (5.5.7) says "The value of swizzle base offset is 0 when the dstMem shared memory address is located at the following boundary: 128-Byte swizzle: 1024-Byte boundary", and the descriptor's Table 50 (Section 2.6.1) says the same for the reader.

**`SWIZZLE_128B_ATOM_32B`** keeps 32-byte units intact ("This sub-mode requires 32 byte alignment at shared memory", 5.5.7). CuTe writes it as `Swizzle<2,5,2>` on byte offsets: bits [5,7) XOR-ed with bits [7,9), period 512 B. explicit.cu cross-checks its own formula against CuTe at compile time (explicit.cu:197; `static_assert`s at :199-202):

```
__host__ __device__ constexpr uint32_t epi_swz(uint32_t o) { return o ^ ((o & 0x180u) >> 2); }
```

Example (explicit.cu:196 comment): offset `0x1E4` becomes `0x1E4 ^ ((0x1E4 & 0x180) >> 2) = 0x1E4 ^ 0x60 = 0x184`. The period 512 B is why the C/D stages are 512-aligned (explicit.cu:163); the UMMA descriptor enum lists this mode as its own layout type, `SWIZZLE_128B_BASE32B = 1` (PTX ISA 9.4 Table 49: "128-Byte with 32B atomic swizzling"; the epilogue never builds a descriptor, so only the TMA side uses this mode here). Chapter 10 derives the epilogue's byte formula from this swizzle; Chapter 5 shows the `static_assert`s.

### 2.7.4 Loads: `complete_tx`, `cta_group::2`, multicast

The load string is W21 (explicit.cu:450-460, quoted in Section 6.6.3).

Qualifier by qualifier (PTX ISA 9.4, 9.7.10.28.5.3):

- `cp.async.bulk.tensor` "is a non-blocking instruction which initiates an asynchronous copy operation of tensor data from the location in .src state space to the location in the .dst state space." `.3d`: three coordinates. `.shared::cluster.global`: destination may be any CTA of the cluster, source is global memory through the tensor map.
- `.mbarrier::complete_tx::bytes`: "Upon the completion of the asynchronous copy operation, the complete-tx operation, with completeCount argument equal to amount of data copied in bytes, will be performed on the mbarrier object specified by the operand mbar." And: "When the mbarrier object mbar resides in the shared memory of a different CTA within the cluster (a remote barrier), .dst must be specified as .shared::cluster".
- `.cta_group::2`: "The modifier .cta_group is used to signal either the odd numbered CTA or the even numbered CTA among the CTA-Pair ... When .cta_group::2 is specified, the mbarrier object mbar can be in shared memory of either the same CTA as the shared memory destination dstMem or in its peer-CTA." This is what lets the peer's B load (W22, no multicast) name the **leader's** `full[s]` (Colfax, cluster tutorial: "Setting this to `cta_group::2` allows the TMA copy to arrive at the mbarrier of either the executing CTA or its peer CTA").
- `.multicast::cluster`: "Operand ctaMask specifies the destination CTAs in the cluster such that each bit position in the 16-bit ... ctaMask operand corresponds to the %cluster_ctarank of the destination CTA ... The source data is multicast to the same offset as dstMem in the shared memory of each destination CTA." With `.cta_group::2`: "the mbarrier signal is multicast either to all the odd-numbered CTAs or even-numbered CTAs for each possible CTA-Pair within a cluster. In particular, for each destination CTA specified in the ctaMask, the mbarrier signal is sent either to the destination CTA or its peer-CTA based on the %cluster_ctarank parity of the shared memory where the mbarrier object mbar resides." The kernel passes an **even** barrier address (bit 24 cleared, Section 2.9.3), so every destination's signal goes to the even CTA of that destination's pair.
- `.L2::cache_hint`: "The 64-bit operand cache_policy specifies the cache eviction policy that may be used during the memory access ... treated as a performance hint only". The value `0x1000000000000000` is CUTLASS's `CacheHintSm100::EVICT_NORMAL` (`cute/arch/copy_sm90_desc.hpp:193-194`, = `Sm100MemDescDefault`, copy_sm100_tma.hpp:46; explicit.cu:188); the encoding of the policy word is opaque in the ISA and I have not found a public breakdown of its bits (unverified beyond the CUTLASS constant).

Per stage `s` every CTA issues one A box (8192 B, its 64-row half, rows `128 tm + 64 y .. + 64` in its own tile coordinates, explicit.cu:777, multicast to ranks `x` and `x + 2`) and one B box (8192 B, not multicast).

Measured K4a (D8): every coordinate and destination of all four ranks matched the per-rank rows and columns and the address formulas (Chapter 8, Sections 8.5.1 and 8.7) for 128 records (Chapter 8, Section 8.7.2). That the *issued* operand is the leader's masked address is shown by the SASS (`sass_gemm.txt` `0x1b90`/`0x1e80`: the baseline's per-k-tile `ULOP3 ..., 0xfefffff8` on the barrier register, whose PTX form D.2 lists as `and.b32 %r, %r, -16777224`; G.3: the explicit kernel's mask folded onto the hoisted base as `& 0xfefffff0`; Section 2.9.3) and by every run completing value-equal (G.1), where an unmasked operand would deadlock at `q = 0` (Chapter 8, Section 8.5.3).

### 2.7.5 Stores: bulk groups

The store (W23, explicit.cu:476-484, quoted in Section 6.6.5) uses the other completion mechanism.

`.bulk_group`: "cp.async.bulk.commit_group instruction creates a new per-thread bulk async-group and batches all prior cp{.reduce}.async.bulk{.prefetch}{.tensor} ... instructions ... initiated by the executing thread but not committed to any bulk async-group" (9.7.10.28.6.1). "cp.async.bulk.wait_group instruction will cause the executing thread to wait until only N or fewer of the most recent bulk async-groups are pending and all the prior bulk async-groups committed by the executing threads are complete ... The optional .read modifier indicates that the waiting has to be done until all the bulk async operations in the specified bulk async-group have completed: reading from the tensormap, the reading from their source locations" (9.7.10.28.6.2).

Hence the kernel's per-subtile triple (explicit.cu:1066-1069): four `tma_store_3d` from stage `e % 4`, one `cp.async.bulk.commit_group` (W24), one `cp.async.bulk.wait_group.read 1` (W25); quoted in Section 10.10.

Why `.read` and why `1` in `wait_group.read 1`. The epilogue only needs the smem stage back, not the global write to be visible, so `.read` is the cheaper wait. Allowing one group to stay pending lets the store of subtile `e` overlap the arithmetic of subtile `e + 1`, while still guaranteeing that the group which read stage `e % 4` four subtiles earlier has finished when subtile `e + 4` reuses it (note 13 item 16; Chapter 10, Section 10.10.4 walks the ring). Per-thread groups are why the warp that issues the stores is the warp that waits: a group belongs to the issuing thread. That a single warp, warp 4, issues the stores mirrors CUTLASS ("one warp issues TMA store", `sm100_epilogue_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:739-740`; `issue_tma_store = (w == 0u)`, explicit.cu:1018), and all 32 lanes of warp 4 issue with uniform operands (measured K4b: 32 active lanes, one `UTMASTG.3D` per box).

### 2.7.6 The async proxy and `fence.proxy.async`

PTX ISA 9.4, 8.6 ("Proxies"): "A memory proxy, or a proxy is an abstract label applied to a method of memory access. When two memory operations use distinct methods of memory access, they are said to be different proxies. A proxy fence is required to synchronize memory operations across different proxies." Operations not in the generic proxy include "async-proxy and tensormap-proxy accesses by .async.bulk operations" and, as quoted in Section 2.4.2, the smem reads of `tcgen05.mma`. The CLC response is also written "using weak async-proxy writes" (9.7.15.18). 9.7.15.4: "Value .async of the .proxykind qualifier specifies that the memory ordering is established between the async proxy and the generic proxy. The memory ordering is limited only to operations performed on objects in the state space specified."

Where generic and async proxies touch the same bytes in this kernel, and the fence that orders them (W15, explicit.cu:418-425, quoted in Section 6.4.2):

1. Epilogue: 16 generic `st.shared.b32` per thread into stage `e % 4`, then the TMA store reads the stage through the async proxy. Every thread fences, then `bar.sync 1, 128` makes all 128 threads' fenced writes precede warp 4's store issue (explicit.cu:1050-1051, quoted in Section 10.10).

2. CLC: the generic `ld.shared.b128` of the response slot must be ordered before the **next** async-proxy write of the same slot (the next `try_cancel` two queries later). The fence after the decode at explicit.cu:683 stands where the ISA example places its "before next iteration async-proxy write to handle" fence; the example spells that fence as the uni-directional `fence.proxy.async::generic.release.sync_restrict::shared::cta.cluster` (paired with an `.acquire` fence after its cluster barrier), whereas CUTLASS and explicit.cu use the bi-directional `fence.proxy.async.shared::cta`.

What does **not** need a *proxy* fence: TMA load -> MMA (both async proxy, ordered through the mbarrier's release/acquire); MMA -> `tcgen05.ld` (ordered by `tcgen05.commit` -> mbarrier; the `tcgen05.fence::after_thread_sync` of the ISA's canonical pattern for this hand-off, and the `tcgen05.fence::before_thread_sync` of the reverse `tcgen05.ld` -> MMA hand-off, both of which CUTLASS and explicit.cu omit, are *tcgen05* fences, not proxy fences, Section 2.4.4); `mbarrier.init` -> remote use (that is `fence.mbarrier_init.release.cluster`, Section 2.10.1, an operation fence, not a proxy fence). Measured (D.2): `fence.proxy.async.shared::cta` lowers to `MEMBAR.ALL.CTA; FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S`; 12 sites in the explicit kernel's PTX (8 epilogue subtiles + 4 CLC decodes), G.3.

### 2.7.7 L2 promotion and cache hints

`CUtensorMapL2promotion` specifies "the byte granularity at which L2 requests are filled from DRAM" (driver API); the maps use `L2_128B`, so a TMA request that misses L2 fills 128-byte lines. The per-instruction `.L2::cache_hint` policy (`EVICT_NORMAL` here) is a hint about eviction priority. CUTLASS's defaults were kept because the measured kernel already runs at the baseline's speed (G.2); a different hint would be an optimisation experiment, not a semantic requirement (analysis).

---

## 2.8 `mbarrier` in depth

### 2.8.1 The object

PTX ISA 9.4, 9.7.15.16.1: an mbarrier is a `.b64` with 8-byte alignment in `.shared`. 9.7.15.16.3 ("Contents of the mbarrier object"): "irrespective of the layout", it "keeps track of the following information: Current primary and conditional phases of the mbarrier object; Count of pending arrivals for the current phase of the mbarrier object; Count of expected arrivals for the next phase of the mbarrier object; Count of pending asynchronous memory operations (or transactions) tracked by the current phase of the mbarrier object. This is also referred to as tx-count." Ranges (Table 43, `.layout::v0`): expected arrival count 1 .. 2^20 - 1, pending arrival count 0 .. 2^20 - 1, **tx-count -(2^20 - 1) .. 2^20 - 1** (signed).

Initialisation (9.7.15.16.12, `mbarrier.init`): "The primary and conditional phases are initialized to zero. The expected arrival and pending arrival counts are initialized to count. The initial transaction count tx-count is initialized to zero." W5 (explicit.cu:286-294) is that instruction; the kernel initialises 33 barriers in the prologue (explicit.cu:1128-1166).

### 2.8.2 The operations

- **arrive-on** (9.7.15.16.9): "the pending arrival count is decremented by count. If the count argument is not specified, then it defaults to 1", then "If the current phase has been completed then the mbarrier transitions to the next phase." W9 local, W10 remote (`mapa` + `.shared::cluster`), W11 remote through the masked address. For a `.shared::cluster` barrier "Sink symbol '_' is mandatory for the destination operand" (9.7.15.16.16), hence the `_` in W10/W11.
- **expect-tx** (9.7.15.16.6.1): "increases the tx-count of an mbarrier object by the value specified by expectCount". `mbarrier.arrive.expect_tx` does "an expect-tx operation ... prior to the arrive-on operation ... the count argument of the arrive-on operation is assumed to be 1" (9.7.15.16.16). W12 is the local form (the 49152-byte arming); W13 is the remote, predicated form (lanes 0..3 of CTA 0's scheduler warp arm all four CTAs' `clc_full[idx]` with 16 bytes, explicit.cu:842; Section 2.12.2 explains why every CTA's barrier is armed). The family has a third member the kernel does not use: a bare `mbarrier.expect_tx` (expect-tx without the arrive-on), which CUTLASS's beta != 0 C-load producer issues *after* its loads, all 32 lanes then arriving separately (note 7.2 and note 13 item 15). With beta = 0 that path does not exist in explicit.cu, so W12/W13 are the kernel's whole expect-tx vocabulary, both in the `arrive.expect_tx` form.
- **complete-tx** (9.7.15.16.6.2): "tx-count is decremented by completeCount", then the phase may complete. Performed by the hardware for every TMA load box (`.mbarrier::complete_tx::bytes`) and every CLC response (16 bytes).
- **phase completion** (9.7.15.16.8): the phase completes "when all of the following conditions are met: The count of the pending arrivals has reached zero. The tx-count has reached zero." Then atomically "The mbarrier object transitions to the next primary and conditional phases. The pending arrival count is reinitialized to the expected arrival count."

The signed tx-count is load-bearing (analysis of the rules above). A TMA box may land, and drive the tx-count below zero, **before** the leader's `arrive.expect_tx` adds 49152. That is legal, and the phase still cannot complete early, because the pending-arrival count stays 1 until the leader's arrive. The CLC barrier works the same way: its remote `arrive.expect_tx(16)` and the hardware's `complete_tx(16)` complete the phase exactly once in either order (Chapter 4, Sections 4.2.2, 4.4.1 and 4.4.4).

### 2.8.3 Phases, parity and a worked state machine

9.7.15.16.19 (`test_wait`/`try_wait`): "The .parity variant of the instructions test for the completion of the phase indicated by the integer parity of the operand phaseParity, which denotes either the current phase or the immediately preceding phase of the mbarrier object. An even phase has integer parity 0 and an odd phase has integer parity of 1 ... The test_wait and try_wait operations are valid only for: the current incomplete phase, for which waitComplete returns False. the immediately preceding phase, for which waitComplete returns True." And: "the use of the .parity variants of the instructions requires tracking the phase of an mbarrier object throughout its lifetime." The operand description in the same section: "Indicated by the 32-bit unsigned integer operand phaseParity, whose integer parity denotes either the current phase or the immediately preceding phase of the mbarrier object ... An even phase has integer parity 0 and an odd phase has integer parity of 1".

Worked example: mainloop `full[3]` of rank 0 (count 1, 49152 tx bytes), used by k-tiles `q = 3, 11, 19, ...` of tile 0 (stage `s = q % 8`). One possible interleaving for the first use:

```
 event                                              phase | pending | expected | tx-count | consumer try_wait.parity(0)
 ---------------------------------------------------+------+---------+----------+----------+----------------------------
 mbarrier.init [full[3]], 1                          |  0   |    1    |    1     |     0    | false (phase 0 current, incomplete)
 rank 2's A half lands in rank 0 (complete_tx 8192)  |  0   |    1    |    1     |  -8192   | false   (tx-count may go negative)
 rank 0 leader lane: arrive.expect_tx 49152          |  0   |    0    |    1     |  40960   | false   (pending 0 but tx != 0)
 rank 0's A half, rank 0's B half land (2 x 8192)    |  0   |    0    |    1     |  24576   | false
 rank 1's A, rank 3's A, rank 1's B land in rank 1   |  0   |    0    |    1     |  0       | -> phase completes:
   (all three credit rank 0's full[3])               |  1   |    1    |    1     |  0       | true    (phase 0 is now "immediately preceding")
 MMA warp issues 4 MMAs on stage 3, commits empty[3] |  1   |    1    |    1     |  0       |
 second use (q = 11): consumer waits parity 1 ...     |  1   |    1    |    1     |  0       | try_wait.parity(1) false until the second 49152 land
 ... completes                                       |  2   |    1    |    1     |  0       | try_wait.parity(1) true; next use waits parity 0
```

Row 2 is the A multicast from rank 2, rank 0's `x`-partner in the other pair, not its peer. The peer's boxes, the three that land in rank 1 (its own A and B halves and rank 3's A half, multicast to ranks 1 and 3), are those of row 5; all three credit rank 0's barrier through the masked operand.

Chapter 4, Section 4.3 derives the stage and parity formula for the n-th use of a ring; Section 4.7 draws the per-tile timeline for all five pipelines (the five rings of Section 4.1).

### 2.8.4 `try_wait`, the suspend-time hint, `test_wait`

9.7.15.16.19: "mbarrier.test_wait is a non-blocking instruction which tests for the completion of the phase. mbarrier.try_wait is a potentially blocking instruction which tests for the completion of the phase. If the phase is not complete, the executing thread may be suspended. Suspended thread resumes execution when the specified phase completes OR before the phase completes following a system-dependent time limit. The optional 32-bit unsigned integer operand timeHint specifies the time limit, in nanoseconds, that may be used for the time limit instead of the system-dependent limit."

The blocking wait (W6, explicit.cu:297-311) is CUTLASS's `ClusterBarrier::wait` (barrier.h:410-430), its asm text verbatim (quoted in Section 6.3.3).

`kWaitTicks = 0x989680 = 10,000,000` ns = 10 ms is the `timeHint` operand, named `suspendTimeHint` in earlier ISA versions (explicit.cu:189; CUTLASS comment, `include/cutlass/arch/barrier.h:414`: "Arbitrarily large timer value after which try-wait expires and re-tries"). Why that large: the thread should stay suspended until the phase completes, not spin and steal issue slots from the MMA/TMA warps on the same SM; the time limit (10 ms if the hint is honoured) only guarantees that the loop re-polls eventually (how the wake on phase completion is realised: Chapter 12, Section 12.2.2). Measured lowering (D.2): `SYNCS.PHASECHK.TRANS64.TRYWAIT P, [addr], R` with the parity in bit 31 of `R`, and the retry loop `@!P NANOSLEEP.SYNCS 0x989680; @!P SYNCS.PHASECHK.TRANS64; @!P BRA` placed out of line.

Three wait shapes appear in the kernel: the blocking W6; the one-shot **peek** W7 (`try_wait.parity` without a hint, returns a token) used to skip the blocking wait when a stage is already free (`producer_try_acquire`/`consumer_try_wait`, explicit.cu:732, :739, :916, :927, :1030); and W8 `test_wait.parity` (non-blocking, never suspends), used only in the CLC producer tail (explicit.cu:860). All three are `.shared::cta`: a wait is always on the CTA's own barrier; only arrivals cross CTAs.

**Default `.sem` and `.scope`.** All three forms are written without `.sem`/`.scope`. 9.7.15.16.19: "If the .sem qualifier is absent, .acquire is assumed by default" and "If the .scope qualifier is not specified then it defaults to .cta. In contrast, the .shared::<scope> indicates the state space where the mbarrier resides." So the kernel's waits are `.acquire`-at-`.cta`-scope waits on `.shared::cta` barriers, CUTLASS's `ClusterBarrier::wait` form (cutlass/arch/barrier.h:410-430). The releasing side reaches across CTAs: TMA `complete_tx` "has .release semantics at the .cluster scope", the `tcgen05.commit` arrive is at "cluster scope", and the W10/W11/W13 arrives are made on `shared::cluster` addresses, mostly from other CTAs; written without `.sem`/`.scope`, those arrives themselves carry the `mbarrier.arrive` defaults, `.release` at `.cta` scope (9.7.15.16.16: "If the .sem qualifier is absent, .release is assumed by default" and "If the .scope qualifier is not specified then it defaults to .cta"). What the acquire wait guarantees when it returns true is spelled out in the same section: "All cp.async.bulk asynchronous operations using the same mbarrier object requested prior, in program order, to mbarrier.arrive having release semantics during the completed phase by the participating threads of the CTA are performed and made visible to the executing thread" (and the analogous clause for generic accesses). The ISA does not state why a `.cta`-scope acquire suffices here. The reason I can offer (analysis, unverified) is that everything the waiter reads after the wait (the A/B stage, the CLC response slot, the TMEM stage, the freed smem) lives in the waiting CTA's own SM, and the remote arrivals carry no data of their own. CUTLASS's headers offer no other wait form (at cb424739 all four `mbarrier.try_wait`/`test_wait` asm strings under `include/` are `.shared::cta` without `.sem`/`.scope`), so every Hopper and Blackwell kernel built on them uses exactly this form, and the ISA's own examples show `.relaxed.cluster` waits paired with explicit fences instead (the tcgen05 patterns of Section 2.4.4, and the 9.7.15.4 `membar`/`fence` example `mbarrier.try_wait.relaxed.cluster.shared::cta.b64 complete, [addr], parity; fence.acquire.sync_restrict::shared::cluster.cluster;`, from the example block whose `fence.mbarrier_init` snippet Section 2.10.1 quotes). A from-scratch writer who prefers the ISA letter to the CUTLASS precedent can write `mbarrier.try_wait.parity.acquire.cluster.shared::cta.b64`, a form the ISA lists among its examples (`mbarrier.try_wait.parity.acquire.cluster.shared::cta.b64 complete, [shMem], 0;`).

---

## 2.9 Addresses: `shared::cta`, `shared::cluster`, `mapa`, and bit 24

### 2.9.1 Two windows, one address space

PTX ISA 9.4, 5.1.7: "Additional sub-qualifiers ::cta or ::cluster can be specified on instructions with .shared state space to indicate whether the address belongs to the shared memory window of the executing CTA or of any CTA in the cluster respectively. The addresses in the .shared::cta window also fall within the .shared::cluster window ... Instruction mapa gives the .shared::cluster address of the corresponding variable in another CTA in the cluster." 9.7.10.26 (`mapa`): "Get address in the CTA specified by operand b which corresponds to the address specified by operand a ... b is a 32-bit integer operand representing the rank of the target CTA."

So a CTA's own 32-bit `shared::cta` address is already a valid `shared::cluster` address of that CTA, and `mapa` turns it into the same offset in another CTA. That address is what `__cvta_generic_to_shared` returns; `smem_u32` (explicit.cu:258) mirrors `cute::cast_smem_ptr_to_uint` (cute/arch/util.hpp:93-108). W10 (explicit.cu:357-367) is quoted in Section 6.3.6.

**Distributed shared memory (DSMEM).** The CUDA Programming Guide ("Distributed Shared Memory") makes the whole cluster's shared memory addressable: generic `ld`/`st`/`atom` to a `shared::cluster` address obtained through `mapa` (or `cluster.map_shared_rank()` in cooperative groups) are legal. This kernel never performs a generic DSMEM load or store. It touches remote shared memory only through hardware units or barrier operations: `mbarrier.arrive{.expect_tx}.shared::cluster` on another CTA's barrier (W10, W11, W13), the `cta_group::2` TMA loads (the multicast writes of A, W21, and both loads' `complete_tx` on the pair leader's `full[s]`, W21/W22, explicit.cu:770), the `tcgen05.mma` reads of the peer's halves of the A/B stages (W29), the `tcgen05.commit` multicast arrives on the barriers of the CTAs in its mask (W30), and the CLC `::all` multicast response (W33). The exit rule of Section 2.9.4 applies to all of them.

### 2.9.2 What this machine does (measured)

The ISA does not say how the rank is encoded in a `shared::cluster` address. The measurements (D5, D.2, G.3) say, for this compiler and hardware:

- rank `r`'s dynamic smem base is `0x400 + (r << 24)`: `0x00000400`, `0x01000400`, `0x02000400`, `0x03000400`;
- `mapa(base_r, t) == base_t` for every pair of ranks tested;
- ptxas materialises the base as `0x400 | (SR_CgaCtaId << 24)` (`S2UR UR6, SR_CgaCtaId; UMOV UR29, 0x400; ULEA UR29, UR6, UR29, 0x18`, quoted in note D.1 D5 from the baseline's `sass_gemm.txt` at `0x440`/`0x470`/`0x4c0`; the explicit kernel has the same lowering with two `S2UR SR_CgaCtaId`, note G.3) and lowers `mapa` to a byte-3 insert of the rank (`PRMT ..., 0x654, ...`), so the convention is compiler-visible: **the rank occupies address bits [24,32)**, and for a 4-CTA cluster only bits 24-25 are ever set. How wide the field is for larger clusters is not established by the note: its D5 prediction was [24,28), and note 6.2 writes "rank in bits [24,26)" from the four measured bases.

Consequence: the low 24 bits of every address are identical across the four CTAs, all `OFF_*` offsets are relative to each CTA's own base, and the base is **not** the same number in the four CTAs, which is why the kernel computes `smem_base` at run time and never hard-codes `0x400` (Section 2.2).

### 2.9.3 The peer bit

Bit 24 is rank bit 0, i.e. the pair parity `x`. Clearing it on any address of an odd CTA yields the same offset in the even CTA of its pair: the pair leader, usable as a `shared::cluster` address (note B.6). CUTLASS's constant and comment (`cute/arch/copy_sm100_tma.hpp:45` and :61-62): `Sm100MmaPeerBitMask = 0xFEFFFFFF`; "Executed by both CTAs. Set peer bit to 0 so that the transaction bytes will update CTA0's barrier." Colfax states the rule the same way: "a CTA can find the address of its leader CTA's mbarrier by taking its own mbarrier address and setting the 24th bit to 0". explicit.cu:187:

```
constexpr uint32_t kPeerBitMask      = 0xFEFFFFFFu;                  // cute::Sm100MmaPeerBitMask (copy_sm100_tma.hpp:45); nvcc folds it to 0xFEFFFFF8
```

Two users:

1. The producer's barrier operand for both TMA loads (explicit.cu:770): `full_masked_base = smem_base & kPeerBitMask`, so `full_masked_base + 8 s` is the leader's `full[s]` whichever CTA issues (Section 2.7.4).
2. The accumulator release (W11, explicit.cu:370-379; cutlass/arch/barrier.h:905-921 `umma_arrive_2x1SM_sm0`; quoted in Section 6.3.7).

Worked examples. Rank 3's `full[5]`: `0x03000400 + 8 x 5 = 0x03000428`; masked: `0x03000428 & 0xFEFFFFFF = 0x02000428` = rank 2's `full[5]`. Rank 2's `acc_full[1]` (explicit.cu:138 comment): `0x02000400 + 240 + 8 = 0x020004F8`. The compiler does not emit the mask as written, and the fold differs per site (measured, note D.6 item 2 and G.3). At the epilogue release (W11) the PTX constant is `-16777224` = `0xFEFFFFF8`: nvcc folded the three known-zero alignment bits of an 8-byte-aligned barrier address into the constant (SASS `0x44c0`). At the producer site (explicit.cu:770) it applied the mask to the hoisted, 1024-byte-aligned `smem_base` and folded one bit further to `0xFEFFFFF0` (PTX `-16777232`, SASS `ULOP3 ... & 0xfefffff0` at `0x0c00`); a `ULEA` adds `8 s` afterwards, so the baseline's per-k-tile `ULOP3 ..., 0xfefffff8` has no counterpart in the explicit kernel, whose SASS carries the literal `0xfefffff8` exactly once, at the epilogue release (measured, G.3). All three masks have the same effect as `0xFEFFFFFF` on every barrier address of this kernel, because the extra low bits they clear are already zero: the barriers are 8-byte aligned, `smem_base = 0x400 + (r << 24)` has bits 0..9 zero, and the producer's fold is applied to `smem_base` before the `ULEA` adds `8 s`, so the `8 s` term (at most 56) is never masked. The baseline CUTLASS kernel applies `0xFEFFFFF8` at all three of its PTX sites, per k-tile at the two producer sites and once per tile at the epilogue release (D.2: `and.b32 %r, %r, -16777224` at ptx.txt:898, :1004, :4190). In the baseline's SASS the release is `SYNCS.ARRIVE.TRANS64.RED.A1T0 RZ, [R62+URZ], RZ` with `R62 = (base + 0x110 + 8 st) & 0xFEFFFFF8` (note D.2, the baseline's dictionary; `0x110 = 272`). The explicit kernel emits the same opcode on `[UR24]` at `0x44f0`, three instructions after the `ULOP3 ... 0xfefffff8` at `0x44c0`, with subtile 7's `LDTM.x16` and a `NOP` between them (measured, `sass_explicit.txt`; the W11 row of Chapter 12, Section 12.2). The source comment at explicit.cu:187 names only the first value; a reader checking the PTX or SASS should expect both constants.

Why this is safe rather than a hack (analysis): the TMA's `cta_group::2` rule needs only the **parity** of the barrier's CTA ("based on the %cluster_ctarank parity of the shared memory where the mbarrier object mbar resides"), and the pair definition is "differs by the last bit only". Whatever the encoding of the rank in the address, the leader's barrier is the one at the same offset in the CTA with bit 0 of the rank cleared; this implementation happens to place rank bit 0 at address bit 24. A kernel written against another toolchain should re-measure this (Chapter 13, end of Section 13.3, lists it among the assumptions to re-verify).

### 2.9.4 Consequences for descriptors and for exit

- Descriptors drop the rank (Section 2.6.1): `((smem_base + OFF) >> 4) & 0x3FFF` sees address bits [4,18) only; the assert at explicit.cu:165 checks that the base and size stay under 2^18 so the field cannot wrap.
- DSMEM exit rule: CUDA Programming Guide ("Writing SIMT Kernels", "Distributed Shared Memory"): "The user also needs to ensure that all distributed shared memory operations happen before the exit of a thread block." And for `.multicast::cluster::all` CLC: "The behavior of instruction with .multicast::cluster::all qualifier is undefined if any CTA in the cluster is exited" (9.7.15.18). Remote mbarrier arrivals onto a CTA that has exited are DSMEM operations after exit. This is the hardware reason for the four tails of note 7.10: every CTA's warp 2 absorbs the last multicast commits into its `empty[]` (8 waits), CTA 0's warp 1 absorbs the last 800-arrival releases (2 test/wait pairs), the leader's warp 0 absorbs the last 256-arrival releases (4 waits), and the pair handshake orders the deallocation. Chapters 8, 7 and 9 place them (Sections 8.6.8, 7.6.8, 9.6.3 and 9.6.4).

---

## 2.10 Cluster barriers, named barriers, `elect.sync`, and convergence

### 2.10.1 `barrier.cluster` and `fence.mbarrier_init`

The forms are `barrier.cluster.arrive{.sem}{.aligned}` with `.sem = {.release, .relaxed}` (default `.release`) and `barrier.cluster.wait{.acquire}{.aligned}` (default `.acquire`). PTX ISA 9.4, 9.7.15.3: "barrier.cluster.arrive instruction marks warps' arrival at barrier without causing executing thread to wait for threads of other participating warps. barrier.cluster.wait instruction causes the executing thread to wait for all non-exited threads of the cluster to perform barrier.cluster.arrive ... The barrier.cluster.wait instruction guarantees that when it completes the execution, memory accesses (except asynchronous operations) requested, in program order, prior to the preceding barrier.cluster.arrive by all threads in the cluster are complete and visible to the executing thread ... The optional .relaxed qualifier on barrier.cluster.arrive specifies that there are no memory ordering and visibility guarantees provided for the memory accesses performed prior to barrier.cluster.arrive." Completion: "When all non-exited threads in the cluster have executed `barrier.cluster.arrive`, the barrier completes and is automatically reinitialized". `.aligned`: "all threads in the warp must execute the same barrier.cluster instruction."

explicit.cu uses the relaxed arrive and the default (acquire) wait (same section: "If the optional .acquire qualifier is absent for barrier.cluster.wait, .acquire is assumed by default") (W16/W17, explicit.cu:428-429, quoted in Section 6.5.1).

Relaxed is enough because the only thing that must be visible cluster-wide before the wait returns is the set of 33 `mbarrier.init`s, and a dedicated operation fence publishes those: `fence.mbarrier_init.release.cluster` (W14, explicit.cu:408-415), whose semantics are (9.7.15.4) "When .op_restrict is .mbarrier_init, the synchronizing effect of the fence only applies to the prior mbarrier.init operations executed by the same thread on mbarrier objects in .shared::cta state space." The ISA's own example (9.7.15.4) contains the kernel's release half, the same three operations (the ISA's `mbarrier.init [bar]` omits `.shared::cta.b64` and the count operand, and its arrive omits `.aligned`): `// Release local barrier state via generic proxy. mbarrier.init [bar]; fence.mbarrier_init.release.cluster; barrier.cluster.arrive.relaxed;`. The matching `barrier.cluster.wait.acquire;` appears in a separate preceding snippet of the same example (`// Acquire remote barrier state via async proxy.`, followed by a `fence.proxy.async::generic.acquire.sync_restrict::shared::cluster.cluster`); the two snippets together illustrate the pattern the prologue uses. The ISA's `barrier.cluster` example, captioned "use memory fence prior to arrive for relaxed barrier", gives the general form of the same pattern, `fence.cluster.acq_rel; barrier.cluster.arrive.relaxed.aligned; ... barrier.cluster.wait.aligned;`: publish with a fence, then arrive relaxed. The split arrive/wait lets the prologue compute `%cluster_ctaid` and the initial tile between the two (explicit.cu:1170-1179), and "no remote barrier operation before this point" (explicit.cu:1178 comment) is the invariant the wait establishes. Measured (D.2): the fence emits no SASS instruction (a bare `FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S` precedes each init group; that those belong to the init lowering rather than to the fence is inferred), the arrive is `UCGABAR_ARV`, the wait `UCGABAR_WAIT; CCTL.IVALL`.

Two more rules of 9.7.15.3 matter for the exits: "Each thread must arrive at the barrier only once before the barrier completes", and "barrier.cluster instructions cause the executing thread to wait for all non-exited threads from its warp". The prologue's rendezvous is the kernel's only cluster barrier: every thread arrives once and waits once. Warp 1 of ranks 1-3 and warp 3 of every CTA then exit (G.3: the `EXIT` at `0x1f00`) with no further cluster barrier; the "non-exited threads" wording makes that harmless, and no later `barrier.cluster` exists that could wait for them.

### 2.10.2 Named barriers

9.7.15.1: "Each CTA instance has sixteen barriers numbered 0..15 ... Operand b specifies the number of threads participating in the barrier ... the value must be a multiple of the warp size ... barrier{.cta}.arrive does not cause executing thread to wait for threads of other participating warps ... When a barrier completes, the waiting threads are restarted without delay, and the barrier is reinitialized so that it can be immediately reused." `bar.sync` = `barrier.sync.aligned`, `bar.arrive` = `barrier.arrive.aligned`.

CUTLASS reserves ids (cutlass/arch/barrier.h:169-178): `EpilogueBarrier = 1`, `TransposeBarrier = 2`, `TransformBarrier = 3`, `StreamkBarrier0/1 = 4/5`, `TmemAllocBarrier = 6`, `Sm120MainloopBarrier = 7`, and warns (barrier.h:163-164) "ID 0 should not be used for safety, as other driver APIs (i.e. __syncthreads) may use it". The rule behind the warning: the compiler typically lowers `__syncthreads()` to a CTA barrier, commonly barrier 0, so treat barrier 0 as compiler-owned and do not mix hand-written `bar.sync 0` protocols with `__syncthreads()` in the same region (NVIDIA internal). explicit.cu uses two (explicit.cu:190-191): `kBarEpilogue = 1` with 128 threads (warps 4-7, twice per subtile: explicit.cu:1051 and :1071) and `kBarTmemAlloc = 6` with 160 threads = warp 0's 32 `bar.arrive` (explicit.cu:887) + warps 4-7's 128 `bar.sync` (explicit.cu:997). The producer/consumer form the ISA describes ("The producer threads execute barrier{.cta}.arrive to announce their arrival at the barrier and continue execution without delay") is exactly the TMEM-address hand-off: warp 0 publishes the allocation result and goes on to its MMAs, and the epilogue warps wait for it once.

W18/W19 (explicit.cu:432-437) are quoted in Section 6.5.2.

### 2.10.3 `elect.sync` and warp convergence

9.7.15.15: "elect.sync elects one predicated active leader thread from among a set of threads specified by membermask. laneid of the elected thread is returned in the 32-bit destination operand d ... The predicate destination p is set to True for the leader thread, and False for all other threads ... The behavior is undefined if the executing thread is not in membermask. Election of a leader thread happens deterministically, i.e. the same leader thread is elected for the same membermask every time. The mandatory .sync qualifier indicates that elect causes the executing thread to wait until all threads in the membermask execute the elect instruction before resuming execution."

W2 (explicit.cu:264-278), CUTLASS's `elect_one_sync` (cute/arch/cluster_sm90.hpp:180-197), is quoted in Section 6.2.2.

With `membermask = 0xFFFFFFFF` every call must be made by a fully converged warp, which is how explicit.cu calls it: `if (elect_one_sync())` guards appear only at points all 32 lanes of the role warp reach (explicit.cu:740, :843, :932, :942, :944, :1125, :1136, :1146, :1156, and the prologue's `lane_pred` at :1103 computed once by every warp). Determinism is what lets the MMA-issuing lane and the commit-issuing lane be the same thread (Section 2.4.3) even though the kernel calls `elect_one_sync()` afresh for each.

Every `.sync.aligned` instruction the kernel uses demands the same convergence discipline: `tcgen05.alloc/dealloc/relinquish_alloc_permit`, `tcgen05.ld`, `tcgen05.wait::ld`, `barrier.cluster.*.aligned`, `bar.sync` (= `barrier.sync.aligned`). For the tcgen05 family the ISA says (9.7.18.7.1): "all threads in the warp must execute the same instruction. In conditionally executed code, the instruction should only be used if it is known that all threads in the warp evaluate the condition identically". For `barrier{.cta}` the `.aligned` rule is stated at CTA level (9.7.15.1): "all threads in CTA will execute the same barrier{.cta} instruction. In conditionally executed code, an aligned barrier{.cta} instruction should only be used if it is known that all threads in CTA evaluate the condition identically, otherwise behavior is undefined". The kernel meets it because whole warps, selected by the warp-uniform role index, execute the named barriers, with thread counts (128, 160) that are multiples of 32. Hence two rules of the kernel's structure: the kernel dispatches roles on a **warp-uniform** index (`warp_idx_sync()`, W1, explicit.cu:261: `__shfl_sync(0xffffffff, static_cast<int>(threadIdx.x / 32), 0)` makes the compiler see the value as uniform), and no role function splits its warp on lane-dependent control flow *around these instructions*.

Lane-dependent C++ branches as such are not forbidden. What is forbidden is a `.sync.aligned` or `elect.sync` instruction inside one, or a branch that has not reconverged before the next collective. explicit.cu has several such branches, all containing only non-collective work and all reconverging immediately. `if (is_leader_lane) { mbar_arrive_expect_tx_local(...); }` (explicit.cu:736; `is_leader_lane` is `lane_pred != 0u && is_leader` at the call :1192, with `lane_pred = elect_one_sync()` computed once at :1103) precedes the `if (elect_one_sync())` at :740 (three non-collective statements, :737-739, lie between them). Every `if (elect_one_sync())` body at the nine sites listed above is itself a lane-dependent branch run by one lane. `if (warp_idx == 1 && lane_pred)` / `if (warp_idx == 3 && lane_pred)` (:1113, :1117) guard the tensormap prefetches and `if (warp_idx == 0 && lane_pred)` (:1165) guards the `tmem_dealloc` barrier init. The CLC arming's `lane < 4u` (explicit.cu:842) sits inside an `asm` `setp`/`@p` pair (W13) not because convergence requires it but because that is CUTLASS's `ClusterTransactionBarrier::arrive_and_expect_tx(smem_ptr, bytes, cta_id, pred)` API (cutlass/arch/barrier.h:605-621), copied verbatim; a C++ `if (lane < 4)` around a W10-style arrive would be equally legal.

---

## 2.11 The uniform datapath and why warp-uniform issue matters

Since Turing the SM has a scalar *uniform datapath* (integer-only on Turing; Blackwell's also has FP32 arithmetic) beside the vector datapath, with 64 uniform registers per warp on Turing (`UR0`-`UR62` plus `URZ` in SASS notation), and 80 x 32-bit addressable uniform registers `UR0`-`UR79` per warp on Blackwell, `URZ` being a separate constant-zero register outside that count where the Turing figure includes it (NVIDIA internal; the baseline's Blackwell SASS, `trace_out_v2/sass_gemm.txt`, uses uniform registers up to `UR77`, consistent with that), on which an instruction executes once per warp on warp-uniform operands (paraphrase of Jia, Maggioni, Smith, Scarpazza, *Dissecting the NVidia Turing T4 GPU via Microbenchmarking*, arXiv:1903.07486, Section 3.5.2 "Uniform Registers"; quoted in Section 12.3.1).

Measured on Blackwell (note D.2 and G.3), the TMA, MMA, commit and CLC instructions are **uniform-datapath instructions**, `UTMALDG.3D.MULTICAST.2CTA`, `UTMALDG.3D.2CTA`, `UTMASTG.3D`, `UTCHMMA.2CTA`, `UTCBAR.2CTA.MULTICAST`, `UGETNEXTWORKID.BROADCAST`, `UTMACCTL.PF`, with `UR` operands, issued once per warp "regardless of how many lanes reach it". ptxas therefore folded away every `elect.sync` in the producer, MMA and scheduler loops, and the 32-lane TMA store of warp 4 costs one `UTMASTG` per box (Chapter 12, Section 12.3).

Three design consequences follow, each visible in explicit.cu:

1. **Keep issue operands warp-uniform.** Descriptor bases, barrier addresses, masks, coordinates and loop state are the same in every lane of the producer/MMA/scheduler warps, so they live in uniform registers and the per-k-tile loops stay short: 37 instructions in the explicit kernel's producer loop (33 on the fast path) and 47 in its MMA loop, against the baseline's 31 and 44 (G.3), all issued while the tensor core is busy with the previous k-tile's MMAs (the issue model of Chapter 12, Section 12.5.5, labelled [H] there).
2. **The uniform register file, not the vector file, is the scarce resource** in these warps (note D.7, inferred from the baseline's uniform-to-vector spills; Chapter 12, Section 12.3.2). explicit.cu keeps loop invariants few: its hot loops have no such moves, and the kernel uses 26 vector registers (G.3).
3. **Election is still written in PTX.** The `elect.sync` is the ISA-level contract (one issuing lane for `tcgen05.mma`, the instruction the ISA gives "single thread semantics"); that ptxas removes it on this architecture is an optimisation you observe, not one you rely on (analysis, note D.6 item 6).

---

## 2.12 Cluster Launch Control (CLC)

### 2.12.1 Semantics

PTX ISA 9.4, 9.7.15.18: "The clusterlaunchcontrol.try_cancel instruction requests atomically cancelling the launch of a cluster that has not started running yet. It asynchronously writes an opaque response to shared memory indicating whether the operation succeeded or failed. The completion of the asynchronous operation is tracked using the mbarrier completion mechanism at .cluster scope ... On success, the opaque response contains the ctaid of the first CTA of the canceled cluster; no other successful response from other clusterlaunchcontrol.try_cancel operations from the same grid will contain that id." The response "will be 16-byte opaque value"; with `.mbarrier::complete_tx::bytes`, "complete-tx operation, with completeCount argument equal to amount of data stored in bytes, will be performed on the mbarrier" (hence `kClcTxBytes = 16`, explicit.cu:181). `.multicast::cluster::all`: "the response is asynchronously written using weak async-proxy writes to the corresponding local shared memory addr of each CTA in the requesting cluster. The completion of the writes to addr of a particular CTA is signaled via a complete-tx operation to the mbarrier object on the shared memory of that CTA." The undefined-behaviour rules: "If the executing CTA has already observed the completion of a clusterlaunchcontrol.try_cancel instruction as failed, then the behavior of issuing a subsequent clusterlaunchcontrol.try_cancel instruction is undefined", and (9.7.15.19) "If the request fails the behavior of clusterlaunchcontrol.query_cancel.get_first_ctaid is undefined." The CUDA Programming Guide ("Work Stealing with Cluster Launch Control") says the same in C++ terms: "Submitting another cancellation request after **observing** a previously failed request is _undefined behavior_" and "Retrieving the thread block index of a failed cancellation request is Undefined Behavior". It also dates the feature: "Cluster Launch Control is a feature introduced in the NVIDIA Blackwell GPU architecture (compute capability 10.0)."

The CUTLASS documentation ("Blackwell Cluster Launch Control") states the scheduling model: a `ClcID` is "a coordinate from the 3D grid launched on GPU"; "A ClcID will be launched as a Worker when there are available resources. A ClcID can be queried by an existing Worker via clusterlaunchcontrol.try_cancel instruction. Every ClcID is guaranteed to be processed by either (1) or (2)"; "The most common reason of a decline is that all ClcIDs have been processed"; "Cluster launch control works on the granularity of clusters. For example, a 2x2 persistent worker cluster's query will consume 2x2 ClcIDs at once."

### 2.12.2 The two instructions in the kernel

W33 (explicit.cu:568-575), the query, is issued by the elected lane of CTA 0's warp 1 once per tile (quoted in Section 6.8.2).

Both operands are CTA 0's own `shared::cta` addresses: `clc_response[idx]` at `OFF_CLC_RESPONSE + 16 idx`, 16-byte aligned as the ISA requires ("naturally aligned address of the 16-byte wide shared memory location"), and `clc_full[idx]` at `OFF_CLC_FULL + 8 idx`. The `::all` multicast delivers the response and the 16-byte `complete_tx` to the same offsets in all four CTAs. That is why CTA 0's scheduler must first arm **every** CTA's `clc_full[idx]` with `arrive.expect_tx(16)` (W13, explicit.cu:842: lanes 0..3, one per rank, through `mapa`), and why ranks 1-3 need no scheduler warp at all.

W34 (explicit.cu:579-595; the comment at :578 records the `x0/y0/z0` caveat), the decode, is executed by every consuming warp of every CTA (quoted in Section 6.8.3).

In W34, `get_first_ctaid` is predicated on `p1`, the `is_canceled` predicate, because of the UB rule. For a failed response its outputs are left unwritten (measured D.3: they held the previous response's ids in all 165 not-cancelled decodes), so `clc_consume` reads `x0/y0` only under `valid` (explicit.cu:691-694). The first-CTA id of a cancelled 2 x 2 cluster is cluster-aligned (both even, measured D.3) and maps to this CTA's tile by `tm = 2 (y0 >> 1) + (x0 & 1) + x`, `tn = 2 (x0 >> 1) + (y0 & 1) + y` (explicit.cu:692-693; Chapter 7 derives it from the AlongN raster). The response is opaque per the ISA, but the SASS shows how this compiler decodes it (D.2, inferred from the extraction code): `is_canceled` = bit 0 of 32-bit word 2 (`LOP3.LUT P, RZ, Rword2, 0x1`), `x0` = word 0, `y0` = word 1 & 0xffff, `z0` = word 1 >> 16; in the MMA warp only the valid bit survives (its `get_first_ctaid` is dead code there). That is useful for reading `launch0.csv`, never something a kernel may rely on.

### 2.12.3 How the loops respect the UB rules

The scheduler issues query `t` and then consumes response `t` in the same iteration (explicit.cu:847 then :853) and exits on the first invalid response. So a query is never issued after a failure has been *observed*; at most one is in flight when the failure *occurs*, which the ISA permits. Every other role consumes exactly one response per tile and ends on the same invalid response. The throttle pipeline (count 32/32) makes CTA 0's loader begin tile `t` before query `t` is issued, so at most one query is outstanding per cluster beyond the tile being loaded (measured D.3: 0 violations in 1024 queries, at most 25 outstanding GPU-wide; Chapter 7, Sections 7.3, 7.6.7 and 7.6.9).

The measured dynamics are in Chapter 12, Section 12.6.3: 33 native clusters, 991 cancelled responses with ids 33..1023 each exactly once plus 33 not cancelled, a hand-out in roughly increasing launch-linear order, median query-to-consume latency 1408 ns in the CUTLASS trace and 1024 ns in the explicit trace, hidden behind one tile (the per-tile times are there too), and 32/31/19 tiles per cluster in the trace builds. The kernel must not depend on any of them (D.7), only on the exactly-once guarantee.

---

## 2.13 Programmatic Dependent Launch: `griddepcontrol`

PTX ISA 9.4, 9.7.15.14: "The griddepcontrol instruction allows the dependent grids and prerequisite grids as defined by the runtime, to control execution in the following way: .launch_dependents modifier signals that specific dependents the runtime system designated to react to this instruction can be scheduled as soon as all other CTAs in the grid issue the same instruction or have completed. The dependent may launch before the completion of the current grid. There is no guarantee that the dependent will launch before the completion of the current grid. Repeated invocations of this instruction by threads in the current CTA will have no additional side effects past that of the first invocation ... .wait modifier causes the executing thread to wait until all prerequisite grids in flight have completed and all the memory operations from the prerequisite grids are performed and made visible to the current grid." The CUDA Programming Guide ("Programmatic Dependent Launch and Synchronization"): "when the secondary kernel is configured with _Programmatic Dependent Launch_, it must always use cudaGridDependencySynchronize or other means to verify that the result data from the primary is available." `cudaGridDependencySynchronize()` itself "will block until all primary kernels the secondary kernel is dependent on have completed and flushed results to global memory". The same guide says that `cudaGridDependencySynchronize` "block[s] until all primary kernels the secondary kernel is dependent on have completed and flushed results to global memory", and that "The CUDA driver can launch the secondary kernel when all primary thread blocks have launched and executed cudaTriggerProgrammaticLaunchCompletion".

W35/W36 (explicit.cu:599-600), CUTLASS's `wait_on_dependent_grids` / `launch_dependent_grids` (cutlass/arch/grid_dependency_control.h:95-98, 85-88), are quoted in Section 6.9.1.

Placement: `griddep_wait()` is the first statement of two roles, the producer (explicit.cu:764, before any TMA load of A/B, the kernel's only reads of global memory) and the scheduler (explicit.cu:821, which itself reads no global memory), exactly where CUTLASS places it (`sm100_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:618-620`: "Ensure that the prefetched kernel does not touch unflushed global memory prior to this instruction"). So a preceding kernel's writes to A and B are visible before the first TMA read, while the barrier initialisation, TMEM allocation and cluster rendezvous overlap the predecessor's tail. Warp 0 issues `griddep_launch_dependents()` after its last tile (explicit.cu:950), i.e. when this CTA has no more MMAs to issue, letting a successor kernel start its prologue while the epilogues drain (CUTLASS comments: "Launching a dependent kernel too early can compete with current kernels, while launching too late can lead to a long latency", and, at `sm100_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:778-780` in cb424739 numbering, "Hint on an early release of global memory resources. The timing of calling this function only influences performance, not functional correctness."). The build defines `CUTLASS_ENABLE_GDC_FOR_SM100=1` (note Section 0; B.3.1 step 10, measured D14), so both are emitted unconditionally. The host launch in explicit.cu:1299-1312 passes only the cluster attribute, no programmatic-stream-serialization attribute, so in the measured runs there was no prerequisite grid: `griddepcontrol.wait` returned immediately, and `launch_dependents` had no designated dependent to signal (analysis: with no prerequisite or dependent grid "as defined by the runtime" there is nothing to wait for or to release; the guide does not spell this out, unverified as a quotation). Even with PDL configured, `launch_dependents` is a hint, "There is no guarantee that the dependent will launch before the completion of the current grid", so a kernel may only ever gain from it, never depend on it. Measured lowering (D.2, G.3): `ACQBULK` 2, both on executed paths (warp 2 of every CTA and warp 1 of CTA 0), `PREEXIT` 1 (warp 0); the baseline's source places the wait in **three** warp roles, warp 2 (`sm100_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:620`), the scheduler (`:688`) and the epilogue-*load* warp 3 (`:810`, under `else if (is_participant.epi_load)`, before its TMA loads of C for `beta != 0`), so it had a third, never-executed `ACQBULK` in that warp-3 path (D.2), which is the 3-versus-2 delta.

# Chapter 3. The Design: From 8192^3 to 256x128x16, and the Speed of Light

This chapter is the top-down companion of the bottom-up Chapters 5-11. Chapter 2 introduces the machine facts it relies on (TMEM, tcgen05, TMA multicast, CLC).

---

## 3.1 The computation and its layouts

### 3.1.1 The math and the memory

The kernel computes, for the fixed run, `D(m, n) = alpha * sum_k A(m, k) * B(k, n) + beta * C(m, n)` with `M = N = K = 8192`, `L = 1`, `alpha = 1.0f`, `beta = 0.0f` read at run time from the parameter block (note, Section 0; Chapter 5 explains why they must stay run-time values). The harness declares the types at `70_blackwell_fp16_gemm.cu:103`, `:108`, `:113`:

```
using         LayoutA     = cutlass::layout::RowMajor;                      // Layout type for A matrix operand
using         LayoutB     = cutlass::layout::ColumnMajor;                   // Layout type for B matrix operand
using         LayoutC     = cutlass::layout::ColumnMajor;                   // Layout type for C and D matrix operands
```

In CuTe's vocabulary (note, Section 3, derived from `make_cute_packed_stride`):

| Tensor | Logical shape | Packed stride | Byte address of element | Contiguous ("major") mode |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | (M, K, L) | (K, 1, 0) | `2 * (m * K + k)` | K |
| B | (N, K, L) | (K, 1, 0) | `2 * (n * K + k)` | K |
| C, D | (M, N, L) | (1, M, 0) | `4 * (m + n * M)` | M |

"K-major" means the K index is the unit-stride index: a row of A (fixed m) and a column of B (fixed n) are each 8192 contiguous fp16 = 16384 bytes. D is M-major: a column of D (fixed n) is 8192 contiguous fp32 = 32768 bytes. This is the classic "TN" GEMM of BLAS (A row-major, B column-major, both with K innermost), and it is the layout pair Section 3.1.2 calls the natural UMMA operand layout: for swizzled K-major operands the descriptor's LBO field is "not used, assumed to be 1" (PTX ISA 9.4, Section 9.7.18.3.1.1).

### 3.1.2 Why K-major is the natural UMMA operand layout

A `tcgen05.mma` does not read A and B from registers. This kernel uses the `_SS` atom: both operands sit in shared memory, and the instruction reads them through two 64-bit *shared-memory descriptors* (Chapter 6, W29). Each descriptor names a start address, two strides (LBO and SBO) and a layout type (the swizzle). The ISA also allows A to come from tensor memory (the `_TS` form): "the A matrix has shape MxK, in either Tensor Memory or Shared Memory; the B matrix has shape KxN, in Shared Memory of the current CTA and optionally in peer CTA; the D matrix is of the shape MxN, in Tensor Memory" (PTX ISA 9.4, Section 9.7.18.10). The kernel does not use the TMEM-A form, so everything below concerns the `_SS` descriptor path. In CUTLASS's own notation (`cute/arch/mma_sm100_desc.hpp:720-732`, comment block), the hardware's canonical K-major layout for the 128-byte swizzle is:

```
LayoutType::B128       : Swizzle<3,4,3> o smem_ptr o ((8,m),(T,2)):((8T,SBO),(1, T ))
```

Read it with `T = 8` fp16 elements per 16-byte unit. Eight consecutive rows (M or N index) of 128 bytes each form a 1024-byte swizzle atom; `m` such atoms are `SBO` apart; within a row the 16-byte chunks are contiguous. The kernel's 128 x 64 fp16 A stage is exactly 16 such atoms stacked along M with `SBO = 1024` B, and the 64 x 64 B half-stage is 8 of them. Four facts follow (derived from source):

- the TMA box of A and B is (64 k, 64 rows, 1) with `CU_TENSOR_MAP_SWIZZLE_128B` (note, Section 5.3). The box's inner dimension is 64 fp16 = 128 bytes, the maximum the 128-byte swizzle allows ("the bounding box inner dimension to be <= 128", `cuTensorMapEncodeTiled` documentation); 64 rows = 8 atoms; one box is 8192 bytes;
- the descriptor's constant high word is `0x40004040` (`explicit.cu:171`): `SBO = 64` sixteen-byte units = 1024 B, `version = 1`, `layout_type = 2 = SWIZZLE_128B`; the low word carries `LBO = 1` (unused for swizzled K-major; `mma_sm100_desc.hpp:831-832` sets it to the canonical `stride_10 = 1`) and the 14-bit start address;
- advancing one k-block (16 k values = 32 bytes) inside a row is a `+2` on the low word, and advancing one stage is `+1024` (A, 16384 B) or `+512` (B, 8192 B), `explicit.cu:928-929` and `:933-934` (quoted in Section 9.5);

- the instruction descriptor `0x10200010` (`explicit.cu:173`) has `a_major = 0` and `b_major = 0` at bits 15 and 16 (note, Section 7.6), which is what `Major::K` encodes.

The CollectiveBuilder resolves the majors from the layout tags, `sm100_umma_builder.inl:201-202` (`tag_to_umma_major_A<RowMajor>` is K, `tag_to_umma_major_B<ColumnMajor>` is K), and the smem atom from the K-major branch of `sm100_smem_selector` (`sm100_common.inl:115-118`: `Layout_K_SW128_Atom` when the k-tile is a multiple of the atom's 64 elements).

**What would change for an MN-major operand** (derived from the source comment block `mma_sm100_desc.hpp:697-717` and the MN branch `:767-798`; the kernel does not implement this, so treat the list as a design note, not as verified code):

| Item | K-major (this kernel) | MN-major (e.g. a ColumnMajor A) |
|---|---|---|
| Canonical descriptor layout (SW128) | `((8,m),(T,2)):((8T,SBO),(1,T))`: 8 rows of 128 B along M/N, K contiguous inside a row | `((T,8,m),(8,k)):((1,T,LBO),(8T,SBO))`: 64 M/N elements (128 B) contiguous, 8 k-rows per atom |
| Live stride fields | SBO = 1024 B (8-row group); LBO fixed at 1 | LBO = stride between 64-element MN chunks, SBO = stride between 8-k groups (`:797-798` swap the roles relative to `SWIZZLE_NONE`) |
| k-block advance | `+32 B` inside the 128-byte row (`+2` on the low word) | a multiple of SBO, the stride between 8-k-row groups: two groups per 16-k block. SBO depends on the order in which the 1024-byte atoms are tiled, not on the MN extent alone. CUTLASS's SM100 collective tiles MN-major operands K-first (`sm100_mma_warpspecialized.hpp:178-184`: "Tile along K mode first before tiling over MN", `Step<_2,_1,_3>` when `is_mn_major<StrideA>()`), so consecutive 8-k groups stay 1024 B apart for any MN extent: SBO = 1024 B, a k-block step is 2 x 1024 = 2048 B, and the 64-element MN chunks (8 x 1024 = 8192 B apart for a 64-wide k-tile) go into LBO. Only if a 128-row A tile were tiled MN-first (two atoms along M before the k groups) would SBO be 2 x 1024 = 2048 B and a k-block step 4096 B. (`mma_sm100_desc.hpp:704`: in `((T,8,m),(8,k)):((1,T,LBO),(8T,SBO))` the m-mode has stride LBO and the k-mode stride SBO; `:797-798` assign `stride_11`, the k-group stride, to SBO for swizzled MN layouts.) |
| TMA box | (64 k, 64 rows): inner dim = K | (64 m, 64 k) or (64 n, 64 k): inner dim = M/N, still 128 B |
| Smem atom chosen by the builder | `Layout_K_SW128_Atom` (`sm100_common.inl:115-118`) | `Layout_MN_SW128_Atom` (MN branch of the same selector, `:89-114`) |
| Instruction descriptor | bits 15/16 = 0 | bit 15 (A) or 16 (B) = 1 |
| `SWIZZLE_128B_BASE32B` | invalid for Major-K (`:811` static_assert) | accepted by `make_umma_desc<Major::MN>` (`:705`, `:775`), but for MN-major operands the hardware allows it only for 32-bit types (PTX ISA 9.4, Section 9.7.18.10.3, Table 65: 16-bit MN-major is "All except 128B swizzling with 32B atomicity", 32-bit "Only 128B swizzling with 32B atomicity") and the builder selects `Layout_MN_SW128_32B_Atom` only when `sizeof(ElementType) == 4` (`sm100_common.inl:91-93`), so an fp16 ColumnMajor A would not use it. The epilogue's fp32 M-major D stage (Section 3.6) uses the same `Swizzle<2,5,2>` atom, but as the TMA mode `CU_TENSOR_MAP_SWIZZLE_128B_ATOM_32B`; it never builds a UMMA descriptor (Section 2.7.3) |

The point to remember: with K-major operands every k-block of a k-tile is a constant 32-byte offset inside one swizzle row, so the four MMAs of a k-tile differ only by `+2` in a 32-bit descriptor word. That is what keeps the MMA warp's hot loop at 47 instructions, 37 of them uniform-datapath (note G.3; Chapter 12 explains uniform registers, the uniform datapath and the SASS mnemonics quoted in this chapter). The hardware supports MN-major, but it costs a different descriptor walk and a different TMA map.

---

## 3.2 The tile hierarchy

### 3.2.1 From the problem to the instruction

Two names used in the diagram: `CX = blockIdx.x >> 1` is the cluster column (it indexes N) and `CY = blockIdx.y >> 1` the cluster row (it indexes M), so `blockIdx = (2 CX + x, 2 CY + y)` and, from `explicit.cu:1175-1176` (quoted in Section 11.6), `tm = 2 CY + x`, `tn = 2 CX + y`.

```
  8192 x 8192 (M x N) output, K = 8192
  |
  |  32 x 32 = 1024 cluster tiles of 256 x 256     (one per CLC work item; note 7.4)
  v
  +----------------- 256 columns (N) -----------------+
  |  rank 0 (x=0,y=0)       |  rank 2 (x=0,y=1)       |   128 rows: tm even   = 2*CY
  |  CTA tile (tm, tn)      |  CTA tile (tm, tn+1)    |
  |-------------------------+-------------------------|
  |  rank 1 (x=1,y=0)       |  rank 3 (x=1,y=1)       |   128 rows: tm odd    = 2*CY + 1
  |  CTA tile (tm+1, tn)    |  CTA tile (tm+1, tn+1)  |
  +---------------------------------------------------+
        128 columns: tn even        128 columns: tn odd
        = 2*CX                      = 2*CX + 1

  x = %cluster_ctaid.x selects the M half (tm % 2 == x), y = %cluster_ctaid.y selects the N half.
  MMA pairs: {0,1} (y = 0) and {2,3} (y = 1): a pair shares tn and covers 256 rows x 128 columns.
  A-sharing: ranks x and x+2 share tm, i.e. the same 128 rows of A -> A is multicast across y.
  |
  |  128 k-tiles of 64 (q = 0..127), one smem stage s = q % 8 each
  v
  per k-tile per pair: 4 x tcgen05.mma.cta_group::2  256 (M) x 128 (N) x 16 (K), kb = 0..3
                       FLOP per MMA = 2 * 256 * 128 * 16 = 1048576
```

Numbers (derived): 1024 cluster tiles x 128 k-tiles x 4 MMAs x 2 pairs = 1048576 MMAs, each 2^20 FLOP, total 2^40 = 2 x 8192^3 FLOP, the ledger row of note Section 9.

The constants that encode this hierarchy are in `util.hpp:29-35`:

```
constexpr int      kFixedM = 8192, kFixedN = 8192, kFixedK = 8192, kFixedL = 1;   // Section 0 shape
constexpr int      kCtaTileM = 128, kCtaTileN = 128, kTileK = 64;                  // Section 4 CTA tile / k-tile
constexpr int      kClusterX = 2, kClusterY = 2, kClusterZ = 1;                    // Section 2 cluster (2,2,1)
constexpr unsigned kGridX = kFixedN / kCtaTileN, kGridY = kFixedM / kCtaTileM, kGridZ = 1;   // (64,64,1) after the AlongN transpose (Section 7.4, B.1.2 step 2)
constexpr unsigned kBlockThreads = 256;                                             // Section 4
constexpr unsigned kSmemBytes = 230400;                                             // Section 6.2 SharedStorageSize
constexpr unsigned kProblemTilesM = kFixedM / 256, kProblemTilesN = kFixedN / 256, kProblemTilesL = 1;   // 32 x 32 cluster tiles (B.1.1 step 11)
```

and `explicit.cu:105-106` (`kMmaM = 256, kMmaN = 128, kMmaK = 16` and `kKBlocks = kTileK / kMmaK`; quoted in Section 5.5).

The harness asks for `MmaTileShape_MNK = Shape<_256,_128,_64>` and `ClusterShape_MNK = Shape<_2,_2,_1>` (`70_blackwell_fp16_gemm.cu:123`, `:125`). The builder turns the MMA tile into the CTA tile by dividing by `AtomThrShapeMNK = (2,1,1)` (`sm100_umma_builder.inl:229-230`): the 2SM atom spans two CTAs along M, so each CTA owns 128 x 128 x 64 (note, Section 4 table).

**Why K = 16 per instruction.** The UMMA K extent is fixed at 256 bits of the operand type (`mma_traits_sm100.hpp:1174-1175`: "Size of instructions's K extent is always 256bits"), i.e. 16 fp16, so a k-tile of 64 is 4 instructions. The authoritative statement is PTX ISA 9.4, Table 48 "Various combinations of .kind and shapes" (Section 9.7.18.2.1). For `.kind::f16`, `cta_group::2`, dense, the legal shapes are 128xNxK and 256xNxK with N = {16, 32, ..., 256} in steps of 16 and K = 16 (K = 32 for sparse). For `cta_group::1` without `.ws` they are 64xNxK and 128xNxK with N = {8, 16, 24, ..., 256} in steps of 8 and K = 16. For `.kind::tf32` the same table gives K = 8: on sm_100a the K extent is 256 bits for every kind (Table 48 also lists wider dense K values, K = 64 for `.kind::f8f6f4` and `.kind::mxf8f6f4` and K = 96 and 128 for `.kind::mxf4` and `.kind::mxf4nvf4`, but its Target ISA Note, 9.7.18.2.1.1, confines them to sm_103a, sm_107a and sm_107f or higher), which is what the CuTe comment encodes for the f16 traits. The kernel's 256 x 128 x 16 is the largest M of the 2SM table with N = 8 x 16.

**Why a k-tile of 64 and not 16.** The TMA box inner dimension must be a multiple of 16 bytes, and the swizzle atom wants a full 128-byte row. 64 fp16 = 128 bytes fills the SW128 row exactly. That gives the largest box the swizzle allows and the fewest barrier round trips per byte: one `full`/`empty` cycle per 48 KiB of pair data instead of per 12 KiB.

### 3.2.2 Which bytes each UMMA reads

Fix a pair {2y, 2y+1}, stage `s`, k-block `kb`.

| Operand half | Source CTA | Shared-memory bytes read (pre-swizzle addresses, relative to that CTA's `smem_base`) | MMA rows / columns |
|---|---|---|---|
| A rows 0..127 | leader (rank 2y) | `OFF_SMEM_A + 16384 s + 128 m + 32 kb .. +32`, m = 0..127 (4096 B) | M 0..127 |
| A rows 128..255 | peer (rank 2y+1) | same offsets in the peer's smem (4096 B) | M 128..255 |
| B columns 0..63 | leader | `OFF_SMEM_B + 8192 s + 128 n + 32 kb .. +32`, n = 0..63 (2048 B) | N 0..63 |
| B columns 64..127 | peer | same offsets in the peer's smem (2048 B) | N 64..127 |

**Worked example.** Cluster at launch-linear coordinates `(CX, CY) = (4, 2)`: rank 0 computes CTA tile `(tm, tn) = (4, 8)`, rank 1 `(5, 8)`, rank 2 `(4, 9)`, rank 3 `(5, 9)` (from `explicit.cu:1175-1176` with blockIdx = (2 CX + x, 2 CY + y)). The pair {0,1} instruction covers rows 512..767 of D (tm 4 and 5) and columns 1024..1151 (tn 8); the pair {2,3} covers rows 512..767 and columns 1152..1279 (tn 9). A rows (`a_row` and the mask, explicit.cu:777 and :772): rank 0 (x = 0, y = 0) loads rows `128 * 4 + 0 = 512..575` into slot `+0` of ranks 0 and 2. Rank 2 (x = 0, y = 1) loads rows `576..639` into slot `+8192` of ranks 0 and 2. Rank 1 loads `640..703` into slot `+0` of ranks 1 and 3. Rank 3 loads `704..767` into slot `+8192` of ranks 1 and 3. B columns: rank 0 loads `128 * 8 + 0 = 1024..1087`, rank 1 `1088..1151`, rank 2 `1152..1215`, rank 3 `1216..1279` (explicit.cu:778). The {0,1} instruction then reads A 512..767 (leader 512..639, peer 640..767) and B 1024..1151 (leader 1024..1087, peer 1088..1151): exactly the 256 x 128 block it accumulates.

(`a_row` and `b_col`: `explicit.cu:777-778`, quoted in Section 8.6.) Chapter 8 walks through these loads instruction by instruction; here the point is the geometry. The TMEM side of the same instruction is Section 2.5.1; the TMEM map is Section 9.3.2.
