## 3.3 Data-reuse arithmetic: why (2,2,1)

### 3.3.1 Bytes per cluster per k-tile

Per k-tile every CTA needs, in its own shared memory, the full 128 x 64 fp16 A stage (16384 B) and the 64 x 64 B half-stage (8192 B) it supplies to the pair. The question is how many bytes have to be *requested from L2* to get them there. Four designs (derived; the kernel implements the last row):

| Design | A bytes requested from L2 per CTA | B bytes requested per CTA | L2 bytes per cluster (4 CTAs) per k-tile | FLOP per cluster per k-tile | FLOP per L2 byte | Smem bytes written + read per SM per k-tile (read: a lower bound, at least the bytes TMA delivered to that SM, Section 2.5.3) | FLOP per smem byte per SM (2097152 FLOP per CTA per k-tile; an upper bound where the read count is a bound) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1SM MMA 128x128, no multicast ("(1,1,1)") | 16384 | 16384 (full 128 x 64 B) | 131072 | 8388608 | 64 | 32768 + 32768 = 65536 | 2097152 / 65536 = 32 |
| 1SM MMA, A multicast across the 2 CTAs that share tm ("(1,2,1)") | 8192 | 16384 | 98304 | 8388608 | 85.3 | 65536 | 32 |
| 2SM MMA 256x128, no multicast ("(2,1,1)") | 16384 | 8192 | 98304 | 8388608 | 85.3 | 24576 + 24576 = 49152 | 2097152 / 49152 = 42.7 |
| 2SM MMA + A multicast across y (this kernel, (2,2,1)) | 8192 | 8192 | 65536 | 8388608 | 128 | 49152 | 42.7 |

How to read it:

- The **2SM MMA** halves the B bytes a CTA must hold: with N = 128 split 64/64 across the pair, each CTA stores only its 64 columns. This saves L2 requests *and* shared-memory writes: the operand bytes TMA delivers to each SM drop from 32 KiB to 24 KiB per k-tile. The read term in the table's smem column (and the 42.7) keeps the read-once model of Section 2.5.3, which `cta_group::2` does not imply for B, so it is a bound, not validated traffic (NVIDIA internal). Colfax states the same effect for the 256 x 256 shape: "the 256x256 MMA does the same number of FLOPs but transfers half the operand data" versus two 128 x 256 MMAs.
- **A multicast** halves the L2 requests for A: the two CTAs that share tm (ranks x and x + 2) each fetch one 64-row half from L2, and the TMA unit writes it into both CTAs' smem. It does not reduce smem traffic: both CTAs still receive 16 KiB of A per k-tile. Read the two FLOP-per-byte columns together. Multicast moves the FLOP-per-L2-byte column (64 -> 85.3 -> 128) and leaves the FLOP-per-smem-byte column alone (32 stays 32); the 2SM MMA is the only mechanism in this design space that improves shared-memory reuse (32 -> at most 42.7: the read count assumes the read-once model of Section 2.5.3, which `cta_group::2` does not imply, NVIDIA internal information). Section 3.9.3 explains why that second column is the one that matters for the 128 x 128 CTA tile.
- Together they reach 128 FLOP per L2 byte, twice the naive design. The mask that implements the multicast is `explicit.cu:772`:

```
  uint16_t const a_mcast_mask     = static_cast<uint16_t>(0x5u << x);            // ranks x and x + 2 (create_tma_multicast_mask<2>)
```

  `0x5 = 0b0101` selects ranks 0 and 2; shifted by x = 1 it becomes `0xA = 0b1010`, ranks 1 and 3. The builder chooses the multicast copy for A whenever the cluster's N extent is not 1 (`sm100_common.inl:203-214`) and the plain 2SM copy for B when the cluster's M extent is exactly 2 (`:239-250`): with only one pair along M there is no second pair with the same tn to share B with.

### 3.3.2 Why not the other cluster shapes (analysis)

- **(1,1,1)**: no pair, no multicast; 64 FLOP per L2 byte and 32 KiB of operand smem writes per k-tile per SM. Section 3.9 argues (hypotheses 3.9.3 and 3.9.4) that even the (2,2,1) design is close to the shared-memory and L2 bandwidth limits, so (1,1,1) would be bandwidth-bound by a wide margin.
- **(2,1,1)**: the pair exists but nothing is multicast. L2 bytes per FLOP are 1.5x those of (2,2,1). It also halves the cluster size, which marginally helps residency (Section 3.8), but the measured SM placement suggests that residency is limited by TPC pairing inside GPCs, not by cluster count. Terms: a TPC (texture processing cluster) is a pair of SMs `(2j, 2j+1)`; a GPC (graphics processing cluster) is a group of TPCs that forms one cluster-launch domain; a 2 x 2 cluster needs two whole TPCs in one GPC. The 2 SMs per TPC and the per-GPC TPC counts (the GPC skyline) are NVIDIA internal information, consistent with the pair placement and the 16 idle SMs in note D.3; Section 2.1.1 has the machine picture and the arithmetic.
- **(1,2,1)**: multicast without the pair. Same L2 bytes as (2,1,1) but the full 32 KiB of operand smem writes per k-tile per SM, and the 1SM MMA with M = 128 and N = 128 (the only M the 1SM F16 atom allows besides 64, `mma_sm100_umma.hpp:88`).
- **(4,1,1)**: two pairs stacked along M share tn, so B could be multicast instead of A. Each CTA would request A 16384 (its own 128 rows, no sharing) + B 4096 (one quarter of the 128 columns, multicast to the other pair) = 20480 B, worse than 16384, because A is the larger per-CTA operand in this tile shape and it is A that benefits from sharing. The builder's rule (`sm100_common.inl:239-250`) does switch B to multicast for cluster M = 4, so the design point is real; it is simply not the better one for 128 x 128 CTA tiles.
- **Larger clusters** ((2,4,1), (4,2,1)): more sharing, but 8 CTAs must be co-resident in one GPC. The measured placement (note D.3) shows that even 4-CTA clusters leave 16 of 148 SMs idle (the cause, given this B200's skyline, Section 2.1.1: each odd-sized GPC leaves one TPC unpaired; NVIDIA internal information); 8-CTA clusters would quantise worse. Hypothesis, not measured here.

### 3.3.3 What the CollectiveBuilder resolves (note, Section 4) and the rule behind each `Auto`

| Requested | Resolved | Rule (verified in source) |
|---|---|---|
| `KernelScheduleAuto` with static cluster | 2SM path, `SM100_MMA_F16BF16_2x1SM_SS<half_t, half_t, float, 256, 128, Major::K, Major::K>` | `is_2sm` is true when the schedule tag derives from `KernelSchedule2Sm`, or when it derives from neither `KernelSchedule1Sm` nor `KernelSchedule2Sm` and the cluster is static with cluster M even (`sm100_umma_builder.inl:208-212`). The harness's `KernelScheduleAuto` is the second case. Under `KernelScheduleAuto` the 2SM atom is taken when cluster M % 2 == 0 and tile M % 128 == 0 (`sm100_common.inl:455-464`) |
| UMMA majors | A: K, B: K | `tag_to_umma_major_A/B` on RowMajor / ColumnMajor (`sm100_umma_builder.inl:201-202`) |
| `AtomThrShapeMNK`, `CtaTileShape_MNK` | (2,1,1), (128, 128, 64) | first mode of the atom's thread layout; tile / atom shape (`:229-230`) |
| GmemTiledCopyA / B | `SM100_TMA_2SM_LOAD_MULTICAST` / `SM100_TMA_2SM_LOAD` | A: cluster N != 1 -> multicast (`sm100_common.inl:203-214`); B: cluster M == 2 -> no multicast (`:239-250`) |
| SmemLayoutAtomA / B | `Layout_K_SW128_Atom<half_t>` | K-major and BLK_K (64) divisible by the atom's 64 elements (`:115-118`) |
| AccumulatorPipelineStageCount | 4 | `min(4, 128 * 512 / (128 * 128)) = min(4, 4)` (`sm100_umma_builder.inl:260-267`; Section 3.4.2) |
| SchedulerPipelineStageCount | 2 | 2 for non-grouped GEMM (`:282`) |
| KernelSmemCarveout | 192 B | sum of the kernel-level barrier, CLC-response and TMEM-base-pointer storage (`sm100_pipeline_carveout.inl:45-83`; Section 3.4.1) |
| PipelineStages (`StageCountAutoCarveout`) | 8 | `floor((232448 - 192 - 33792) / 24592)` (`sm100_umma_builder.inl:84-98`, capacity `arch.h:44`) |
| `EpilogueScheduleAuto` | `TmaWarpSpecialized2Sm` | static even cluster M and MMA tile M in {128, 256} (`sm100_builder.inl:1697-1715`); for `OpClassBlockScaledTensorOp` only MMA tile M = 256 qualifies (`:1708-1710`), which matters when you move to FP8/FP4 block-scaled GEMMs |
| `EpilogueTileAuto` | (128, 16) | Section 3.6 (`sm100_builder.inl:1006-1046`) |
| EpiTiles, FragmentSize | 8, 16 | `(128 * 128) / (128 * 16)`, `(128 * 16) / 128` (`:1253-1255`) |
| Epilogue DispatchPolicy | `Sm100TmaWarpSpecialized<StagesC = 4, StagesD = 2, 16, ReuseSmemC = true, DelayTmaStore = false>` | `StagesD = min(EpiTiles, 2)`, `StagesC = max(min(EpiTiles, 4), StagesD + 1)` because C is wider than 8 bits (`:1107-1115`) |
| TileScheduler | `PersistentTileSchedulerSm100<Shape<_2,_2,_1>, 2>`, dynamic persistent | the `void` tag maps to the CLC scheduler on SM100 (note, Section 4) |

The explicit kernel hard-codes these results, most of them as the constants at `explicit.cu:104-120` (others elsewhere, for example the K-major SW128 layout in the descriptor constants `:171-173` and the multicast choice in the mask `:772`) and checks the ones that have arithmetic consequences with `static_assert` (`:158-166`, `:174-177`). The lesson for your own kernels is not the numbers but the *rules*: each `Auto` is a small function of the operand types, the tile and the cluster, and you should be able to evaluate it by hand before you trust the builder.

## 3.4 Budgets

### 3.4.1 Shared memory: 230400 bytes, and why 8 stages

The B200 offers 232448 bytes of opt-in dynamic shared memory per CTA (measured in note Section 0; `cutlass::arch::sm100_smem_capacity_bytes = 232448`, `arch.h:44`), with 1024 bytes of system-reserved shared memory below it (measured base `0x400`, note D.1 D5). The builder's carveout arithmetic (note, Section 6.1; `sm100_compute_stage_count_or_override`, `sm100_umma_builder.inl:84-98`, fed by `KernelSmemCarveout` at `:284-290`; `sm100_pipeline_carveout.inl:45-83`):

```
stage bytes      = 128*64*2 (A) + 64*64*2 (B) + 16 (one PipelineTmaUmmaAsync<1> barrier pair) = 24592
kernel carveout  = acc pipeline 64 + CLC pipeline 32 + load-order 16 + tmem-dealloc 8 + throttle 32
                   + CLC responses 2*16 + TMEM base pointers 2*4                            = 192
epilogue storage = TensorStorage 33280 + LoadPipeline 64 = 33344, rounded to 512-B alignment = 33792
stages           = floor((232448 - 192 - 33792) / 24592) = floor(198464 / 24592) = floor(8.07) = 8
```

The 16 is `sizeof(PipelineTmaUmmaAsync<1>::SharedStorage)`: one 8-byte `full` and one 8-byte `empty` barrier per stage. The `2*4` TMEM pointers are the builder's estimate; the real struct has one 4-byte `tmem_base_ptr`. The bound: 8 x 24592 = 196736 <= 198464 < 9 x 24592 = 221328.

The real layout (note, Section 6.2) is reproduced in `explicit.cu:139-155` (the `OFF_*` constants, quoted in Section 5.7); as a byte map:

```
  byte     0 .. 343   43 mbarrier slots (8 B each): 33 initialised; the 10 at bytes 128..207 (epi_load full/empty 4 + 4, load_order 2)
                      are reserved for the beta != 0 path and never initialised (explicit.cu:141-143; note E.10 item 6)
  byte   344 .. 351   padding (PipelineStorage is aligned_struct<16>)
  byte   352 .. 383   2 x 16 B CLC response slots
  byte   384 .. 387   TMEM base pointer, written by tcgen05.alloc
  byte   388 .. 511   padding to the epilogue's 512-B alignment                            [ 388 B used ]
  byte   512 .. 33279 4 epilogue C/D stages x 8192 B  (Swizzle<2,5,2>, needs 512-B alignment)
  byte 33280 .. 33791 FusionStorage (empty) padded to the next 512-B boundary
  byte 33792 .. 164863  8 A stages x 16384 B          (Swizzle<3,4,3>, needs 1024-B alignment)
  byte 164864 .. 230399 8 B stages x  8192 B          (idem)
  byte 230400           end; 232448 - 230400 = 2048 B unused
```

The `static_assert`s at `explicit.cu:158-163` (quoted in Section 5.7) pin the arithmetic and the alignments.

Why the alignments (derived): `Swizzle<3,4,3>` XORs address bits [4,7) with bits [7,10), so its pattern repeats every 1024 bytes. Both hardware units key the XOR on absolute address bits, and the kernel's UMMA descriptors leave the 3-bit `base_offset` field at 0 (`kSmemDescHi = 0x40004040`, `explicit.cu:171`), so a stage base must be 1024-byte aligned, or the TMA unit's write-side XOR and the UMMA unit's read-side XOR would not act on the same bits (Chapter 8, Section 8.8.3). `Swizzle<2,5,2>` XORs bits [5,7) with bits [7,9): period 512 bytes, hence 512-byte alignment for the epilogue stages. The offsets above satisfy both, but only because the dynamic base `0x400` is itself 1024-aligned. That is why the kernel must have no static `__shared__` data: its placement is not a source-level ABI contract (NVIDIA internal), so it could shift the dynamic base (note, Section 6.2; Chapter 11, Section 11.2.3). A further constraint is the 14-bit descriptor start-address field, which spans 2^18 = 256 KiB of shared::cta address space: `static_assert(kSmemBaseLow24 + kSmemBytes < (1u << 18), ...)` (`explicit.cu:165`; Chapter 9, Section 9.4.4).

**Why 230400 leaves exactly 2048 bytes** (derived). Put the builder's estimate and the real layout side by side:

```
                      builder estimate                              real SharedStorage
  non-stage bytes     192 (kernel carveout: barriers, CLC slots,     512 (bytes 0..511: 43 barrier slots, CLC slots,
                           TMEM pointers)                                 TMEM pointer, padding)
                    + 33792 (epilogue: 33344 rounded up to 512)    + 33280 (bytes 512..33791: 4 x 8192 D stages
                                                                          + FusionStorage pad to 512)
                    = 33984                                        = 33792
  stage bytes         8 x 24592 = 196736 (each stage carries         8 x 24576 = 196608 (the 8 full + 8 empty
                      16 B of PipelineTmaUmmaAsync<1> storage)        barriers live in the 512-B head instead)
  total               230720                                        230400
  capacity 232448     - 230720 = 1728 (floor remainder)             - 230400 = 2048
```

The 320-byte difference is 192 + 128. The 192 is the carveout, which the real head absorbs: 512 + 33280 equals the builder's 33792 epilogue estimate alone. The 128 is 8 x 16 B of per-stage barrier storage, counted inside the stage size but laid out in the head. 1728 + 320 = 2048. The slack is quantisation, not a design choice: a 9th stage would need 24576 more bytes.

**Why fill shared memory with stages at all?** The occupancy is 1 CTA per SM as soon as the footprint exceeds half of the SM's capacity, and this kernel's 230400 of 232448 bytes does, so leftover shared memory has no other consumer. Each additional stage adds 24 KiB of prefetch in flight for free (Section 3.5.1). This is the rule `StageCountAutoCarveout` encodes: take everything the epilogue and the barriers leave.

### 3.4.2 TMEM: 512 columns = 4 stages x 128 columns

Tensor memory is 128 lanes x 512 columns of 32 bits per SM (Section 2.3.1; `tmem_allocator_sm100.hpp:45-46`: "128 DP x 512 COL x uint32_t-addressing"; `Sm100TmemCapacityColumns = 512` at `:120`; the MLC chapter: "Each CTA has 128 lane rows and up to 512 32-bit columns"). The kernel allocates all of it (`explicit.cu:114`):

```
constexpr uint32_t kTmemColumns   = 512;             // tcgen05.alloc / dealloc column count
```

Derivation of the stage size: the CTA's accumulator tile is 128 rows x 128 columns of fp32. The MMA writes row m to TMEM lane m (lane = row, Section 2.5.1), so the 128 rows use the 128 lanes exactly, and each fp32 column occupies one 32-bit TMEM column: 128 columns per stage. 512 / 128 = 4 stages. The builder computes the same thing as `TotalTmem / (CtaTileM * CtaTileN) = 65536 / 16384 = 4` and then caps at 4 (`sm100_umma_builder.inl:260-267`). The result is the third parameter of the mainloop dispatch policy `MainloopSm100TmaUmmaWarpSpecialized<8,2,4,(2,2,1),Sm100>`: `int AccumulatorPipelineStageCount_,` at `include/cutlass/gemm/dispatch_policy.hpp:1025` (range `:1021-1035`; note D.1 D1). The kernel's address arithmetic is the same statement, `explicit.cu:1006` and `:1031`:

```
  uint32_t const tmem_lane_off = (32u * w) << 16;                                               // TMEM lanes [32 w, 32 w + 32): row 32 w + l of the CTA tile (0, 0x200000, 0x400000, 0x600000)
```

```
    uint32_t const taddr = T + tmem_lane_off + 128u * acc_stage;                                // warp-uniform TMEM address of this warp's 32 rows
```

What a 256 x 256 pair tile would cost: the CTA tile becomes 128 x 256, i.e. 256 fp32 columns per stage, and 512 / 256 = 2 accumulator stages. That is the TMEM price of the larger tile; Section 3.9.7 weighs it against its bandwidth benefit.

---

## 3.5 Pipeline depths and why

### 3.5.1 Eight mainloop stages: Little's law

The producer warp (Chapter 8) keeps TMA loads for up to 8 k-tiles in flight ahead of the MMA warp (Chapter 9). The first `load_ktiles` call covers `min(8, k_tiles)` k-tiles, the second the rest (`explicit.cu:788-791`, quoted in Section 8.6 and discussed in Section 8.6.5).

The depth needed follows from Little's law: *bytes in flight = ingest rate x latency*. Measured ingredients (note D.4, the CUTLASS baseline; the explicit kernel's own median gives 27.79 us, 0.14 % more, Section 3.9.2): at most 27.75 us per tile on a 32-tile critical path, i.e. 216.8 ns = 426 cycles per k-tile at 1965 MHz. Derived:

```
ingest rate per SM     = 24576 B per k-tile / 216.8 ns          = 113 GB/s
bytes in flight        = 7 stages ahead x 24576 B               = 172032 B   (8 stages: 196608 B)
latency tolerance      = 172032 B / 113 GB/s                    = 1.52 us    (8 stages: 8 x 216.8 ns = 1.73 us)
prefetch horizon       = 8 x 426 cycles                         = 3408 cycles = 1.73 us
```

At the ideal 256 cycles per k-tile (Section 3.9.2) the same 8 stages span 8 x 256 = 2048 cycles = 1.04 us.

The ring therefore hides any TMA round trip shorter than about 1.5 us: issue -> L2 or HBM -> smem landing -> `full[s]` completion, plus the `tcgen05.commit` -> `empty[s]` return path. Chips and Cheese measured about 150 ns to the directly attached L2 partition on B200 ("L2 latency to the directly attached L2 partition is similar to prior generations at about 150 ns"; a third-party measurement, not this machine). Cross-partition hits and HBM misses are longer: the article reports that latency "dramatically increases" when the footprint spills into the other partition, and HBM misses are of the order of a microsecond (an order-of-magnitude statement, unmeasured). So two stages (0.22-0.43 us, one or two k-tile times) would already cover a local L2 hit; 4 stages (0.65-0.87 us) would be borderline for far-partition and HBM traffic; the 8-stage ring (1.5-1.7 us) is sized for far-partition and HBM misses plus the commit -> `empty` -> producer -> TMA return path.

The ring absorbs a second thing besides memory latency: cross-CTA skew. The leader's `full[s]` is credited by six boxes from all four CTAs' producers (its own A half and B half, the sibling's multicast A half, and the peer's three boxes through the peer-bit-masked address; Section 3.11), so a stage is not full until the *slowest* of the four producers has issued it. The deep ring is what lets a *single* producer thread per CTA keep the tensor core fed.

How you would confirm: Nsight Compute's warp stall breakdown for warp 0. A `full[s]` wait that often fails shows up as stall samples on the `SYNCS.PHASECHK.TRANS64.TRYWAIT` / `NANOSLEEP.SYNCS` retry loop of the mainloop wait: the `NANOSLEEP` retries under the `sleeping` reason (the Profiling Guide names `NANOSLEEP` there); the `TRYWAIT` wait path under `long scoreboard` (NVIDIA internal: Nsight samples it there in an examined SM100 warp-specialised GEMM; a dependency/wait-path attribution, not proof that the `TRYWAIT` instruction itself is the root cause, since PC sampling can charge the following predicated or control instruction instead, here the `@!P0 NANOSLEEP.SYNCS` of the retry loop or the `@!P0 BRA` after the inline attempt, both in Section 12.2.2; Chapter 12 explains the SASS names). The TMA unit's "bytes in flight" is not directly exposed, so the practical test is to rebuild with `kStages = 4` and watch the per-k-tile time.

### 3.5.2 Four accumulator stages

The TMEM ring decouples the MMA warp from the epilogue warps. The MMA warp commits stage `st` with `tcgen05.commit` to `acc_full[st]` and immediately starts the next tile in stage `st + 1` if `acc_empty[st + 1]` is free; the epilogue drains stage `st` concurrently (Chapters 9 and 10; Chapter 4 for the barriers). Steady state needs the epilogue of tile t to finish before the mainloop of tile t + (stages - 1) finishes, i.e. `epilogue time per tile < (stages - 1) x mainloop time per tile`.

The mainloop takes about 27.75 us per tile (measured upper bound). The epilogue per tile per CTA moves 128 x 128 x 4 = 64 KiB from TMEM to smem by 128 threads (16 `st.shared.b32` per thread per subtile, 8 subtiles) and 64 KiB from smem to global by 32 TMA stores. At a nominal 128 B/clk shared-memory bandwidth that is at least 2 x 65536 / 128 = 1024 cycles = 0.52 us of pure data movement; with the eight `bar.sync 1, 128` pairs, fences and TMA issue it is plausibly a few microseconds. Chapter 10 (Section 10.12) bounds it at about 11-15 us under deliberately pessimistic assumptions. Both are estimates; no epilogue duration was measured in the note.

Even a 15 us epilogue is below one 27.75 us mainloop period, so **two** stages would already keep the MMA warp from waiting in steady state. Four is the TMEM-imposed maximum (Section 3.4.2) and the builder's cap ("4 accumulator stages works well to buffer the accumulators, while also preventing overhead in the epilogue tail on small tile sizes", `sm100_umma_builder.inl:266`). The extra two stages buy slack against jitter: a slow epilogue (an SM pair whose TMA stores contend in L2), a CLC response arriving late (1.4 us median, Section 3.5.3), or a tile whose A band misses L2. The TMEM has no other use in this kernel, so the slack is free.

How you would confirm: with the trace build, timestamp `acc_empty` waits in the MMA warp; in production, the number of `TRYWAIT` retries on `acc_empty` (the `NANOSLEEP.SYNCS` loop) is a proxy.

### 3.5.3 Two CLC stages and two throttle stages

The scheduler warp (Chapter 7) asks the hardware for the next cluster tile with `clusterlaunchcontrol.try_cancel` while the cluster computes the current tile. The response lands in a 16-byte slot and completes `clc_full[idx]` in all four CTAs. With two slots, one query can be outstanding while the cluster's 800 consuming threads are still reading the previous response. The throttle pipeline (count 32, 2 stages) ties the scheduler to rank 0's producer warp: the scheduler issues query i only after the loader has *started* tile i, so at most one query is outstanding beyond the tile the loader is on (note, Section 7.4).

Measured in the CUTLASS kernel's trace build (note D.3; full distribution in Chapter 12, Section 12.6.3): query-to-consume latency median 1408 ns, 31.9 us per tile, and 28.8-37.7 us per tile spent by the scheduler waiting on the throttle. The explicit kernel's trace build measured a median of 1024 ns, and 35.46 us per tile because of its extra diagnostics (note G.2). The Release per-tile figures are 27.75 us (CUTLASS, note D.4) and 27.79 us (explicit, note G.2). The latency is 5 % of a tile and entirely hidden. A deeper CLC ring would buy nothing; a shallower one (one slot) would serialise the consume of response t with the issue of query t + 1 by all 800 threads, which is exactly what the second slot avoids. The throttle exists because without it the scheduler would run ahead and cancel many unstarted clusters at once, hoarding tiles that other clusters could have taken (load imbalance) and holding responses in slots nobody is ready to consume.

### 3.5.4 Four epilogue smem stages of 8 KiB with `wait_group.read 1`

Warps 4-7 stage each 128 x 16 subtile in one 8192-byte smem buffer (stage `e % 4`); warp 4 then writes it to global memory with four TMA stores, commits them as one bulk group, and executes `explicit.cu:1069`:

```
        tma_store_wait_read<1>();                                                                // producer_acquire (always_wait): at most 1 group pending on its smem read
```

`cp.async.bulk.wait_group.read 1` returns when at most one committed group (the one just committed) may still be reading smem, so the group of subtile e - 1 has finished reading stage `(e - 1) % 4`. The next subtile writes stage `(e + 1) % 4`, whose last reader was the group of subtile e - 3, long complete. Two stages would suffice for this `read 1` discipline. The four come from the C-load side of the design: `StagesC = max(min(EpiTiles, 4), StagesD + 1) = 4` because `ReuseSmemC` is true for a 32-bit C (`sm100_builder.inl:1107-1115`), and D reuses C's buffers (`StorePipeline = PipelineTmaStore<StagesC, StagesD - 1>`, `sm100_epilogue_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:202-205`; `UnacquiredStages = 1` gives the `.read 1`, `sm90_pipeline.hpp:697-700`). For the beta = 0 run the two spare stages are unused slack: the `.read 1` discipline alone lets the epilogue warps run one subtile ahead of the TMA store's smem read, and whether that wait ever blocks does not depend on the stage count.

---

## 3.6 The epilogue tile (128, 16) and the (32, 16, 1) store box

The epilogue's unit of work is a 128 x 16 fp32 subtile; there are 8 per CTA tile (`kEpiSubtiles = 8`, `kEpiTileN = 16`: `explicit.cu:112-113`, quoted in Section 5.5).

Derivation (from `sm100_builder.inl:1006-1046`, verified; `:1047` is the `static_assert(CtaN >= N_min_C && CtaN >= N_min_D, "CTA tile too small")` that guards it):

1. **M = 128** from the TMEM load shape. `tcgen05.ld.sync.aligned.32x32b.x16.b32` is the "32 data path lanes, 32-bit pattern, repeated 16 times" operation (`copy_sm100.hpp:3575-3576`): each of the 32 lanes of a warp reads one TMEM lane (= one accumulator row), 16 consecutive 32-bit columns per lane. A warp may only address the 32 TMEM lanes of its own sub-partition, lanes `[32 (w % 4), +32)` (CuTe asserts this when `NDEBUG` is not defined, `copy_traits_sm100.hpp:400-402`; the epilogue checks "this tile's tmem subpartition is accessible by this warp", `sm100_epilogue_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:874`). Four warps x 32 lanes therefore cover 128 rows, and the builder's `M = min(CtaM, 32 * WarpM) = min(128, 128) = 128` (`sm100_builder.inl:1006-1007`, `DpFull = 32`).
2. **N = 16** from the performance table. With a residual C present (`DisableSource` false), 32-bit C/D, `CtaM > 64` and `CtaN <= 128`, `N_perf = 16` (`:1024-1025`). The minimum N for an M-major D is `8 * WarpN = 8` (`:1039-1044`). `N_tmp = min(CtaN, max(N_perf, N_min_C, N_min_D)) = min(128, max(16, 8, 8)) = 16` (`:1045`), and `N = CtaN % N_tmp == 0 ? N_tmp : CtaN` keeps it because 128 % 16 == 0 (`:1046`). The subtile is then 128 x 16 x 4 B = 8192 B, one smem stage, and `FragmentSize = 128 * 16 / 128 threads = 16` floats per thread (`:1255`), which is exactly the `.x16` of the load, `explicit.cu:1036`:

```
      tmem_ld_32x32b_x16(taddr + 16u * uint32_t(e), r);                                        // columns 16e..16e+15 of row 32 w + l (:881-883)
```

3. **The store box (32, 16, 1)** from the swizzle limit. D is M-major, so the TMA map's innermost dimension is M. The epilogue smem stage uses `Swizzle<2,5,2>` on a `(32, 4):(1, 32)` fp32 atom, encoded as `CU_TENSOR_MAP_SWIZZLE_128B_ATOM_32B`. The driver's rule reads, verbatim, "CU_TENSOR_MAP_SWIZZLE_128B* require the bounding box inner dimension to be <= 128". The asterisk stands for the `_ATOM_*` variants, so the `_ATOM_32B` used here has no separate limit; the rule applies only when the swizzle is not `CU_TENSOR_MAP_SWIZZLE_NONE`. The general constraints apply as well: "boxDim array ... must be non-zero and less than or equal to 256" and, for `CU_TENSOR_MAP_INTERLEAVE_NONE`, "{ boxDim[0] * elementSizeInBytes( tensorDataType ) } must be a multiple of 16 bytes". 128 bytes of fp32 is 32 elements. The box is therefore 32 (m) x 16 (n) = 2048 B, and a 128 x 16 subtile needs four of them (`explicit.cu:1055-1057`, quoted in Section 10.10).

Per CTA tile that is 8 subtiles x 4 boxes = 32 TMA stores of 2048 B = 64 KiB = 128 x 128 x 4 B, the ledger row "D TMA store instructions: 32 per CTA tile" (note, Section 9; correction 14 of note Section 13 fixed the draft's "eight 8192-byte D TMA stores per logical CTA work tile").

Why not a wider subtile (N = 32, 4 subtiles)? Each thread would carry 32 live accumulator registers instead of 16, and the epilogue smem would double: EpiTiles = 4, StagesD = min(4, 2) = 2, StagesC = max(min(4, 4), 3) = 4 (`sm100_builder.inl:1113-1115`), so 4 x 16384 + 512 (FusionStorage pad) + 64 (LoadPipeline) = 66112 bytes, rounded to 512 -> 66560. The carveout formula then gives floor((232448 - 192 - 66560) / 24592) = floor(165696 / 24592) = floor(6.74) = 6 mainloop stages instead of 8: the extra 32 KiB is 1.33 stage-sizes, but the floor rounds the loss up to two whole stages. Why not narrower (N = 8)? Twice as many barrier/fence/commit rounds per tile for the same bytes. The builder's `N_perf` table is NVIDIA's empirical answer; the explicit kernel inherits it.

---

## 3.7 Warp specialisation: 8 warps, 5 roles, 256 threads

```
 warp 0  MMA        both CTAs allocate TMEM; the pair LEADER's elected lane issues all 512 tcgen05.mma per tile
                    and the commits; the PEER's warp 0 only consumes CLC responses and advances state
 warp 1  scheduler  in every CTA its elected lane prefetches the A and B tensor maps in the prologue; on rank 0 it then
                    runs the CLC try_cancel + throttle loop, on ranks 1-3 it falls through the dispatch and exits
 warp 2  producer   one elected lane issues 2 TMA loads per k-tile (A multicast, B); on rank 0 also the throttle producer
 warp 3  idle       the CUTLASS kernel's beta != 0 C-load producer (no role function here); prefetches the C and D maps, initialises the throttle barriers, exits
 warps 4-7 epilogue 128 threads = 128 TMEM lanes = 128 rows; warp w owns rows [32 w, 32 w + 32); warp 4 issues the TMA stores
```

(`explicit.cu:104`; note, Section 7.1; the CUTLASS kernel's thread accounting is `sm100_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:136-147`.)

```
constexpr uint32_t kThreads       = kBlockThreads;   // 8 warps: 0 MMA, 1 Sched (rank 0), 2 MainloopLoad, 3 EpilogueLoad (exits), 4-7 Epilogue
```

Why each count is what it is (derived):

- **One producer warp.** A TMA load is issued by one thread; the TMA unit does the addressing, swizzling and multicast. Two instructions per k-tile from one lane (`explicit.cu:747`, `:754`) are the whole data path of a CTA. More producer threads would add nothing but contention on the `empty[s]` wait. The warp exists (rather than a single thread) because `elect.sync` and the warp-level `mbarrier` protocol want a converged warp.
- **One MMA warp, and only the leader's lane issues.** The peer's warp 0 therefore idles through the mainloop; it still has to exist for the pair-wide `tcgen05.alloc`/`dealloc`, which require one warp from each CTA of the pair (PTX ISA 9.7.18.5, Table 55; CUTLASS's allocator additionally requires the same logical warp ID in both, `tmem_allocator_sm100.hpp:132`, note B.6), and for the accumulator-state bookkeeping that keeps both CTAs' stage indices in step.
- **Four epilogue warps.** No other warp count can read a 128-row CTA tile; 8 epilogue warps would simply pair up on the same 32 lanes.
- **One scheduler warp, rank 0 only.** Warp 1 of every CTA (rank 0 included) prefetches the A and B tensor maps in the prologue (`explicit.cu:1113-1116`); on ranks 1-3 it then fails the dispatch test `warp_idx == 1 && is_cta0` (`explicit.cu:1194`) and falls through to exit, as the dispatch comment says (`explicit.cu:1190`: "warp 3 and warp 1 of ranks 1-3 fall through and exit"). Chapter 11 covers the prologue.
- **One idle warp.** Warp 3 is kept so that the warp numbering, the barrier initialisation order (it initialises the throttle barriers, `explicit.cu:1155-1163`) and the tensor-map prefetch of C and D stay identical to the CUTLASS kernel (Chapter 11).
- **256 threads, occupancy 1 CTA per SM.** Registers are not scarce: the explicit kernel uses 26 (measured, note G.3; the CUTLASS kernel 68). The design consequence matters for your own kernels: on this machine a GEMM CTA is the *single* resident unit on its SM, so every latency has to be hidden by asynchrony inside the CTA (TMA, UMMA, TMEM rings), not by switching to another CTA.

---

## 3.8 Persistent scheduling with CLC

### 3.8.1 Why dynamic hand-out

The launch grid is (64, 64, 1) = 4096 CTAs = 1024 clusters (`explicit.cu:1282-1284`, quoted in Section 11.8.3).

But only the clusters that fit the machine launch natively: measured 33 (note D.3, equal to `cudaOccupancyMaxActiveClusters`), on 132 SMs. 16 SMs stay idle (SM ids 64, 65, 122-129, 142-147) because a 2 x 2 cluster needs two whole TPCs in one GPC and each odd-sized GPC (NVIDIA internal) leaves one TPC unpaired (the pairing is inferred in the note; arithmetic and two cautions in Section 2.1.1; Section 3.3.2 defines TPC and GPC). Each resident cluster then *cancels* not-yet-launched clusters with `clusterlaunchcontrol.try_cancel` and takes over their work; 991 of the 1024 queries succeeded and 33 failed (one terminator per cluster).

The tail arithmetic (derived): 1024 tiles / 33 clusters = 31.03 tiles per cluster. Whatever the assignment, some cluster must do 32 tiles, so the makespan is 32 tile-times against an ideal of 31.03: a 3.0 % quantisation loss that no scheduler can remove at this shape and residency. What the dynamic scheme removes is the *variation*. The following counts come from the trace build of the CUTLASS kernel (note D.3); the Release distribution was not traced. 13 clusters did 32 tiles and 19 did 31; the probed cluster (0,0), 1.7x slower because of its per-instruction probes (inferred in the note), did 19. The 13 with 32 tiles were exactly the 13 with the shortest per-tile time. The per-tile times split into a fast group (31.1-31.8 us) and a slow group (32.0-32.7 us). The note *infers* (it does not measure) that the split follows the position inside the GPC rather than the cluster id, because fast and slow clusters recur at the same SM offsets in every SM-id group. A static assignment of 31 or 32 tiles per cluster would hand the slow clusters as many tiles as the fast ones and finish when the slowest finished; dynamic hand-out absorbs that roughly 3 % gap between the two groups (5 % from the fastest to the slowest unprobed cluster) automatically.

### 3.8.2 AlongN raster and L2 locality

The raster order is `AlongN` because the heuristic is `tiles_n > tiles_m ? AlongM : AlongN` and the counts are equal (`tile_scheduler_params.h:1810-1816`). The heuristic's general rule is to raster along the shorter tile axis (`tiles_n > tiles_m` -> `AlongM`): the wave of resident clusters then cycles through the panels of the smaller operand, which has the better chance of staying L2-resident as a whole, while a run of consecutive clusters reuses each panel of the larger operand. For a square problem both axes are equal and `AlongN` is the tie-break (my analysis). The CLC hardware hands out cluster ids in launch-linear order (measured: approximately increasing, 933 of 991 at their sorted position, ties within one 32 ns timer tick broken by ascending id; note D.3: "ascending except for a few local swaps"), so the *grid* is transposed on the host to make that order sweep N first: `possibly_transpose_grid` swaps x and y (`sm100_tile_scheduler.hpp:237-250`), and every tile id is transposed back on the device (`possibly_transpose_work_tile`, `:668-677`). That is where the two formulas of the kernel come from (`explicit.cu:1175-1176`, quoted in Section 11.6, and `:692-693`, quoted in Section 7.4).

Grid x indexes N (64 CTA columns), grid y indexes M; the low bit of each is the position inside the cluster. The hardware numbers clusters in grid-linear order over the transposed (64, 64) grid, so the launch-linear cluster id is `L = (blockIdx.x >> 1) + 32 (blockIdx.y >> 1) = CX + 32 CY`. (Note D.3 states the inverse: id L is the cluster tile `(m, n) = (L / 32, L % 32)`, i.e. `m = CY`, `n = CX`, and it records each cluster's successive ids as `(y0/2)*32 + x0/2`.) Since `tn = 2 CX + y` and `tm = 2 CY + x`, consecutive ids advance CX: they walk along N within one 256-row band of A. Measured consequence (note D.3): the 33 resident clusters hold about 33 consecutive ids, so they work on one full band plus one tile of the next, i.e. "two (834 of 991 hand-outs) or three (157) adjacent 256-row bands of A at any moment". For L2 this means: all 32 clusters of a band share its A band (256 rows x 8192 k x 2 B = 4 MiB), so HBM supplies it about once per band; exactly one cluster per band uses each B column block (also 4 MiB), and the next band touches it again. Section 3.9.5 turns this into bytes.

Swizzle is disabled (`max_swizzle_size = 0`, `swizzle_divisor = 0`, note Section 0 and the host guard `explicit.cu:1269`). CUTLASS's swizzle would group ids into blocks of a few columns so that the resident clusters share B blocks as well as A bands; it is a knob the harness leaves at its default, and the explicit kernel hard-codes the default. The design table in Section 3.10 lists it as the obvious alternative to try.

---

## 3.9 Speed-of-light analysis

### 3.9.1 Tensor-core peak

| Quantity | Value | Status and source |
|---|---|---|
| Dense FP16/BF16 tensor rate per SM per clock, Blackwell | 8192 FLOP/clk/SM | SemiAnalysis: "for FP16 we know the hardware can do 8192 MMA FLOPs per cycle per SM"; Chips and Cheese: "1024 16-bit MAC operations per cycle, per partition" x 4 partitions x 2 FLOP/MAC = 8192. Consistent with the datasheet below: 2.25e15 / 148 SMs / 8192 = 1.86 GHz, a plausible specification clock |
| Same, Hopper H100 | 4096 FLOP/clk/SM | the NVIDIA H100 product page lists "1,979 teraFLOPS" FP16 Tensor Core for H100 SXM with the footnote "With sparsity", i.e. 989.5 TFLOPS dense; it states no clock. At 132 SMs the dense figure *implies* 989.5e12 / (132 x 4096) = 1.83 GHz, below the commonly listed 1.98 GHz boost clock (that boost figure was not verified from a source opened here); the 4096 FLOP/clk/SM is half the Blackwell figure above and is the value this derivation assumes, not a datasheet number |
| B200 datasheet dense FP16/BF16 | 2.25 PFLOPS per GPU | HGX B200: "FP16/BF16 Tensor Core: 36 PFLOPS" for 8 GPUs, footnote "Specification in Sparse. Dense is 1/2 sparse spec shown": 36 / 8 / 2 = 2.25 |
| Peak at the measured 1965 MHz, 148 SMs | 148 x 8192 x 1.965e9 = **2.382 PFLOPS** | derived; above the datasheet figure because the datasheet assumes a lower sustained clock (hypothesis) |
| Peak at 1965 MHz, 132 busy SMs | 132 x 8192 x 1.965e9 = **2.125 PFLOPS** | derived |
| Per SM at 1965 MHz | 16.1 TFLOPS | derived |
| HBM3e bandwidth | 8 TB/s per GPU | DGX B200: "64 TB/s HBM3e bandwidth" for 8 GPUs, i.e. 64 / 8; the Lenovo HGX B200 product guide lists 7.7 TB/s per GPU (Section 2.2) |
| L2 | 126 MB total, two partitions; 21 TB/s local, 16.8 TB/s cross-partition (Chips and Cheese); read bandwidth 23.9 TB/s GPU-wide, about 12.0 TB/s per partition; write bandwidth 10.8 TB/s GPU-wide, about 5.4 TB/s per partition (NVIDIA internal) | Chips and Cheese measurements for the capacity and the local and cross-partition figures; NVIDIA internal information for the read and write bandwidths |
| Shared memory bandwidth per SM | 128 B/clk | SemiAnalysis: "the SMEM bandwidth is 128 B/cycle (per SM)", the primary source. The same figure is repeated by forum participants on the NVIDIA Developer Forums thread "About Shared-Memory Bandwidth Usage Of Tensor-Core In Blackwell Architecture" (neither is NVIDIA staff): user Curefab, "Each SM can do 128B/cycle of shared memory, which is shared between all 4 SM partitions", and user Nanodeoclus, "The SMEM pipeline shared between the four SM partitions can do either a load or a store per cycle, but not both" - who adds in the same post that this "doesn't necessarily mean that TMA writes to SMEM, or TC reads from SMEM, have the same limitation", and Curefab recalls that "the TC smem acceses are routed through the async engine, which is per lane". Whether tensor-core operand reads and TMA writes are charged to the same 128 B/clk is therefore **open in the thread itself** and **not confirmed** by any source opened here |

### 3.9.2 Where the kernel stands

Measured (note G.2): median `Avg runtime` 0.889354 ms, 2 x 8192^3 / 0.889354 ms = 1.236 PFLOPS (1.2363e15 FLOP/s; the harness prints 1.23498e6-1.23687e6 GFLOPS over the five explicit runs, and the 1.237e15 of note D.4 is the CUTLASS baseline). Derived fractions:

```
1.236 / 2.382 = 51.9 % of the 148-SM peak at 1965 MHz
1.236 / 2.125 = 58.2 % of the 132-SM peak (the SMs that actually run CTAs)
```

Against the 2.25 PFLOPS datasheet figure the kernel reaches 55 %; per *active* SM (132 of 148) it sustains 4770 FLOP per clock at 1965 MHz.

Per-k-tile budget (note D.4; a measured upper bound, because the timed interval also contains host work): 32 tiles on the critical path -> 27.75 us per tile -> 216.8 ns = 426 cycles per k-tile -> 106.5 cycles per 256 x 128 x 16 MMA. 27.75 us is note D.4's figure for the CUTLASS baseline, 0.888122 ms (0.888 ms) / 32. The explicit kernel's own median gives 0.889354 ms / 32 = 27.79 us = 217.1 ns = 427 cycles per k-tile (28.69 us for a 31-tile cluster), a 0.14 % difference that changes none of the conclusions, so 426 cycles is the working number throughout this chapter. The 1965 MHz is itself inferred, not measured inside the loops: the clock was sampled every 100 ms around the 9 ms timed loops (note D.4, G.2). At peak the pair's two SMs deliver 2 x 8192 FLOP/clk, so one such MMA (2^20 FLOP) takes 64 cycles and a k-tile 256 cycles = 130 ns. During the mainloop the kernel therefore runs the tensor cores at 64 / 106.5 = 60 % of their peak rate (derived; the 58 % whole-run figure adds the 3 % tail quantisation and the ramp).

So about 40 % of the tensor-core cycles are not used. The candidates below are listed with their arithmetic; the first is the leading hypothesis.

### 3.9.3 Candidate 1: shared-memory bandwidth (hypothesis, leading)

Per SM per k-tile, shared memory sees (derived from Sections 3.2-3.3):

```
TMA writes   : A stage 16384 B (own half by own load, other half by multicast) + B half 8192 B = 24576 B
UMMA reads   : A 128 rows x 16 k x 2 B x 4 k-blocks = 16384 B + B 64 cols x 16 k x 2 B x 4 = 8192 B = 24576 B  (a lower bound: at least the bytes delivered to this SM; cta_group::2 does not imply read-once B (NVIDIA internal); Section 2.5.3)
total        : 49152 B per k-tile per SM
at measured 426 cycles : 49152 / 426 = 115 B/clk  = 90 % of 128 B/clk
at peak     256 cycles : 49152 / 256 = 192 B/clk  > 128 B/clk
```

Suppose TMA writes and UMMA operand reads share one 128 B/clk shared-memory port (forum user Nanodeoclus's "either a load or a store per cycle, but not both" for the SMEM pipeline, quoted with its caveat in Section 3.9.1). The UMMA line is a lower bound on the reads (`cta_group::2` does not imply a read-once B, NVIDIA internal, Section 2.5.3); reads above it lower the cap. The TMA line (bytes landed in this SM's smem, copy traffic) and the UMMA line (what the tensor core consumes) are separate quantities: the leader issues the MMA while both CTAs receive smem data (NVIDIA internal). Then the 128 x 128 CTA tile *cannot* exceed 128 / 192 = 67 % of the tensor peak, i.e. 1.417 PFLOPS on 132 SMs. The measured 1.236 PFLOPS is 87 % of that cap. The remaining 13 % is attributed (not measured) to the 3 % tail quantisation, the first-tile ramp (the first interval of each cluster was 37.9 us against 31.9 us in the trace build, note D.3), the un-overlapped epilogue of the last tile, and the host work in the timed interval. The epilogue adds 2 % more smem traffic per tile (64 KiB of `st.shared` + 64 KiB of TMA-store reads = 128 KiB against 6 MiB of mainloop traffic per tile).

An anecdote in the same range, not a measurement of 60 %: the original poster of the forum thread (user tugrul_192bit) reports "a pipeline with 7 stages of 128x128x64 tile that has only 1100 tflops performance of bf16. But cublas does 1670 tflops" and later that "128 x128 tile size doesn't reach 60% of peak tensor core performance". 1100 TFLOPS is 49 % of the 2.25 PFLOPS dense datasheet figure and 66 % of that cuBLAS number. The cuBLAS figure is also the most useful *achievable* target in this chapter: 1670 TFLOPS is 74 % of the 2.25 PFLOPS datasheet peak and 70 % of the 148-SM peak at 1965 MHz (2.382 PFLOPS). That bounds how much of the 40 % gap is recoverable in practice (user measurement on an unspecified B200 and clock; treat as indicative).

The counter-hypothesis is in the same thread: if tensor-core operand reads are "routed through the async engine" rather than through the 128 B/clk LSU pipeline, the 192 B/clk sum above never competes for one port and Candidate 1 is wrong. One measurement of the port's total traffic would separate the two (no Nsight Compute counter directly exposes the tensor core's operand-read bytes, NVIDIA internal; see below). If operand reads *do* use the port, the mainloop's shared-memory throughput is at least 49152 B / 426 cycles = 115 B/clk = 90 % of 128, a lower bound because the UMMA read line above assumes read-once B, which `cta_group::2` does not imply (NVIDIA internal); if they do not, only the TMA writes count: 24576 B / 426 cycles = 57.7 B/clk = 45 % of 128.

How one would confirm with Nsight Compute, if a counter exposed it: measure the shared-memory port's total traffic during the mainloop, which is not the Memory Workload Analysis table's shared-memory throughput as a percentage of peak (the Profiling Guide's Shared Memory table shows Wavefronts and % Peak per access type; the shared-memory wavefront counters are `l1tex__data_pipe_lsu_wavefronts_mem_shared_op_{ld,st}.sum` (NVIDIA internal); the bank-conflict counters `l1tex__data_bank_conflicts_pipe_lsu_mem_shared_op_{ld,st}.sum` count shared load/store bank conflicts and should be normalised against those wavefront counts when comparing kernels, not divided by source-level load instructions (NVIDIA internal; the guide's Metrics Examples list the `l1tex__data_bank_conflicts_pipe_lsu.sum` family, not the `_mem_shared_op_*` names); these `pipe_lsu` counters cover the LSU/L1TEX path, not async-proxy traffic (NVIDIA internal): they see the epilogue's `st.shared` but neither the mainloop's TMA writes nor the tensor core's operand reads, both async-proxy operations (Section 2.7.6); the TMA side has its dedicated metrics, which cover only the write side (NVIDIA internal; request the `.sum` forms the installed Nsight Compute offers): `l1tex__m_xbar2l1tex_read_bytes_mem_global_op_tma_ld.sum` counts the bytes delivered into shared memory, expected CTAs x k-tiles x (A stage + B stage) = 4096 x 128 x 24576 B = 12 GiB for this run (the 24576 B landed per k-tile per SM is the 45 % derived above) and unchanged by multicast because every receiving CTA still gets a full tile (an internally measured 2-SM GEMM, not this run, showed exactly 1,073,741,824 B in both its multicast and its non-multicast arm); the `lts__t_bytes_equiv_l1sectormiss_pipe_lsu_mem_global_op_tma*` family is an L2 tag-stage request/sector metric (`lts__t` is the L2 slice tag stage per the Profiling Guide) whose expected value is the L2-side traffic, the 16384 unique bytes per SM per k-tile of Section 3.9.4, and is expected to fall with the unique request traffic under multicast (NVIDIA internal); no Nsight Compute counter is known to expose the tensor core's A/B shared-memory operand-read bytes directly, and UMMA reads them from shared memory through its descriptors, bypassing `ldmatrix` (NVIDIA internal), so that traffic has to be derived from the tile geometry and instruction counts, as the UMMA line above does) together with the tensor-pipe utilisation (`sm__pipe_tensor_cycles_active`, the UMMA math activity measure; `sm__pipe_tc_cycles_active` is the Profiling Guide's broader TC pipe, the MMA math plus `UTCCP`, `UTCBAR` and the TMEM allocation atomics, and the two are distinct; Section 12.7.5 lists both; `sm__pipe_tensor_op_hmma_cycles_active` is a tensor-pipe-active metric of the `sm__pipe_tensor_*` family, not by itself proof that `UTCHMMA` incremented it; all NVIDIA internal). A port total near 90 % with `sm__pipe_tensor_cycles_active` near 60 % would confirm the hypothesis and near 45 % (the TMA writes alone) refute it; but with no counter for the operand reads (above) that total cannot be read off Nsight Compute directly, and the 256 x 256 experiment of Section 3.9.7 remains the decisive test.

### 3.9.4 Candidate 2: L2 -> SM bandwidth (hypothesis, near-limit at peak)

Per SM per k-tile the TMA unit requests 8192 B of A (its own half; the other half arrives by multicast from the sibling's request) and 8192 B of B: 16384 unique bytes, the L2-side traffic the `lts__t` TMA metric of Section 3.9.3 is expected to report (NVIDIA internal). GPU-wide (derived):

```
measured rate : 132 SMs x 16384 B / 216.8 ns =  9.98 TB/s
at peak       : 132 SMs x 16384 B / 130.3 ns = 16.6  TB/s
without A multicast          (24576 B/SM) : 15.0 TB/s at the measured rate
without multicast and 2SM    (32768 B/SM) : 20.0 TB/s at the measured rate
```

against a measured L2 bandwidth of 21 TB/s within a partition and 16.8 TB/s across partitions (Chips and Cheese), and an L2 read bandwidth of 23.9 TB/s GPU-wide, about 12.0 TB/s per partition (NVIDIA internal). As built, the kernel uses 42 to 48 % of the L2 bandwidth at its measured speed (9.98 TB/s against 23.9 or 21 TB/s) and would need 69 to 99 % of it at tensor peak (16.6 TB/s against 23.9 TB/s, or against the 16.8 TB/s cross-partition figure). The two sharing mechanisms of Section 3.3 keep this candidate from being the first wall. Confirm with `lts__t_bytes.sum.per_second` and its percentage of peak: `lts` is an L2 cache slice and `lts__t` its tag stage (Profiling Guide, unit descriptions), and `lts__t_bytes.sum` is broad L2 tag-stage byte traffic, not DRAM bytes and not necessarily the payload bytes delivered to the consuming instruction, because hits, requests from several clients and request-side effects can contribute (NVIDIA internal), so read it against the table above as L2 traffic, not as a payload-byte count.

### 3.9.5 Candidate 3: HBM traffic implied by the raster (hypothesis, not the limiter)

Unique bytes: A 128 MiB, B 128 MiB, D 256 MiB = 512 MiB. With the AlongN sweep of Section 3.8.2, A is read from HBM about once (each band is shared by the 32 clusters working on it), D is written once, and B is re-read once per band unless it survives in L2 between bands. Bounds (derived):

```
best  (B read once)           : 128 + 128 + 256 MiB = 0.54 GB -> 0.54 GB / 0.889 ms = 0.60 TB/s =  8 % of 8 TB/s
worst (B re-streamed 32 times): 128 + 4096 + 256 MiB = 4.70 GB -> 5.28 TB/s                      = 66 % of 8 TB/s
```

Whether B survives: a B column block is reused one band later, i.e. after the whole 128 MiB of B has streamed through a 126 MB L2 split into two partitions (63 MB each if split equally; Chips and Cheese gives only the total), so with an LRU-like policy most of it is evicted (hypothesis). The truth lies between the bounds and is measurable with `dram__bytes_read.sum` and `dram__bytes_write.sum`. Even the worst case leaves a third of the HBM bandwidth free, so HBM is not the limiter at this shape. It would become one for a 128 x 128 CTA tile at tensor peak (5.28 TB/s x 426 / 256 = 8.8 TB/s); a tile swizzle (Section 3.8.2) is the standard remedy.

### 3.9.6 Candidate 4: barrier and issue overheads (derived, not the limiter)

The MMA warp's k-tile loop is 47 instructions, 37 of them on the uniform datapath (measured, note G.3), of which 4 are the MMAs and 1 the commit. At roughly one instruction per cycle it needs well under 100 of the 426 cycles, and it issues while the tensor core executes the previous k-tile's work. The producer's 37-instruction loop runs up to 8 stages ahead. The `full[s]` wait is normally a successful peek: the data arrived long ago (Section 3.5.1). The only per-k-tile synchronisation on the critical path is the completion of the `tcgen05.mma` -> `tcgen05.commit` -> `empty[s]` -> producer -> TMA -> `full[s]` cycle, and with 7 stages of slack it is off the path.

The commit is a deferred arrive: `tcgen05.commit` makes the mbarrier track the completion of all prior asynchronous tcgen05 operations of the issuing thread (PTX ISA 9.4, Section 9.7.18.12.1, quoted in Chapter 2, Section 2.4.3 and Chapter 4, Section 4.2.2). It therefore has to be issued by the same elected thread that issued the four MMAs. It cannot be replaced by a plain `mbarrier.arrive`, which would fire before the tensor core has finished reading the stage (note, Section 7.6). The empty-side release thus costs the MMA warp no wait at all: the hardware signals `empty[s]` when the four tracked MMAs have completed, which implies their reads of the stage are done (Section 2.4.3).

Overheads that *are* on the path occur once per tile: the `acc_empty` wait (hidden, Section 3.5.2), the CLC consume (1.4 us, hidden behind the throttle), and the first tile's cold start. None of these explains 40 %. Confirm with the warp-state sampling of warp 0 in Nsight Compute: if its dominant state during the mainloop is `selected` (the guide's "Warp was selected by the micro scheduler and issued an instruction") or waiting on the tensor pipe rather than `sleeping` in the `NANOSLEEP` retry loop that follows a failed `SYNCS` try-wait or `long scoreboard` on the try-wait path itself (Nsight Compute has no `SYNCS` state; the `long scoreboard` attribution and its caveat are NVIDIA internal information, Section 3.5.1), barriers are not the problem.

### 3.9.7 What the 256 x 256 pair tile would change (derived)

The 256 x 256 pair tile (128 x 256 per CTA) is the configuration this analysis predicts to be fastest for 8192^3. It was not profiled here, and no source opened for this chapter ranks CUTLASS configurations, so treat the prediction as a hypothesis.

The benefit: per 256 x 256 x 16 MMA each SM supplies A 128 x 16 (4 KiB) and B 128 x 16 (4 KiB) = 8 KiB, and the pair performs 2^21 FLOP = 128 cycles at peak. Per k-tile (4 MMAs, 512 cycles at peak) the SM writes 32 KiB by TMA and the tensor core reads at least 32 KiB, the read-once count of Section 3.9.3, now a lower bound since `cta_group::2` does not imply read-once B (NVIDIA internal; the actual count is unverified): 64 KiB / 512 cycles = **128 B/clk at peak** on that bound, exactly the nominal shared-memory bandwidth, against 192 B/clk for this kernel's tile. FLOP per smem byte, on the same bound, rises from 42.7 to 64; FLOP per L2 byte per SM from 128 to 171 (24 KiB requested for 4.19 MFLOP).

The costs: 256 TMEM columns per stage, so 2 accumulator stages instead of 4 (Section 3.4.2); a 32 KiB + 16 B stage and a larger epilogue buffer, so 5 mainloop stages instead of 8 by the carveout formula (derived by hand, not instantiated); and a 256 x 256 CTA-pair tile quantises a general problem worse.

The 5 comes out as follows. With CtaN = 256 the epilogue builder's `N_perf` becomes 32 (`sm100_builder.inl:1025`: `(CtaM > 64 && CtaN <= 128) ? 16 : 32`), so the epilogue tile is (128, 32) = 16 KiB per stage. EpiTiles = 128 x 256 / (128 x 32) = 8, StagesD = min(8, 2) = 2, StagesC = max(min(8, 4), 3) = 4 (`:1113-1115`), so the epilogue storage is the same 66560 B that Section 3.6 derives for the (128, 32) subtile (4 x 16384 + 512 + 64 = 66112, rounded to 512). Accumulator stages are 65536 / (128 x 256) = 2, so the accumulator pipeline's barrier storage halves from 64 to 32 B (`PipelineAsyncSharedStorage`: two `ClusterBarrier[Stages]` arrays, `sm90_pipeline.hpp:1005-1011`) and the kernel carveout is 192 - 32 = 160. Per-CTA stage bytes are A 128 x 64 x 2 = 16384 plus B 128 x 64 x 2 = 16384 (the 2SM atom's `BLayout` gives each CTA N/2 columns, `mma_traits_sm100.hpp:1181`, and the builder sizes B smem by that `BlockTileB_N`, `sm100_umma_builder.inl:241`, `:295`) plus 16 = 32784. Stages = floor((232448 - 160 - 66560) / 32784) = floor(165728 / 32784) = floor(5.05) = 5. For 8192^3 none of the costs bites, which is why this analysis predicts the larger tile to win there; the harness is a *teaching* example (its header: it "demonstrates minimal set of changes needed to transition from a Hopper CUTLASS 3.x GEMM kernel") and nowhere claims the 256 x 128 tile is the fastest one.

### 3.9.8 The 16 idle SMs

- **Idle SMs (measured, note D.3).** 132 of 148 SMs host CTAs: an 11 % loss relative to a perfect machine, independent of the kernel (on this B200's skyline, Section 2.1.1, it follows from the odd-sized GPCs and the (2,2,1) cluster shape; NVIDIA internal information). A cluster shape that pairs TPCs differently, or a 1SM kernel (cluster (1,1,1) or (1,2,1)) that can use the leftover TPCs, would recover part of it at the price of Section 3.3's reuse.

### 3.9.9 Summary of the SOL picture

```
                       tensor peak, 148 SMs, 1965 MHz                  2.382 PFLOPS   (100 %)
  16 idle SMs      ->  tensor peak, 132 SMs                             2.125 PFLOPS   ( 89 %)
  smem bandwidth   ->  x 128/192 (read-once bound) if reads share port  1.417 PFLOPS   ( 59 %)   [hypothesis]
  tail quantisation->  x 31.03 / 32                                     1.374 PFLOPS   ( 58 %)
  measured                                                              1.236 PFLOPS   ( 52 %)
```

Everything between 1.374 and 1.236 (10 %) is attributed, not measured, to ramp, last-tile epilogue, epilogue smem traffic and host overhead. That is where Nsight Compute, not arithmetic, has to take over. The decisive experiment is the 256 x 256 pair tile: if the shared-memory hypothesis is right, it lifts the cap from 59 % to 89 % of the 148-SM peak (1.417 -> 2.125 of 2.382 PFLOPS), i.e. from 67 % (128 / 192) to 100 % of the 132-SM peak of 2.125 PFLOPS, both on the read-once bound of Sections 3.9.3 and 3.9.7 (NVIDIA internal; the actual read traffic is unverified).

| Decision | Value | Why | Alternatives | Cost of the alternative |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Operand majors | A K-major, B K-major | canonical UMMA SW128 layout; 32-byte k-block step; TMA box 64 x 64 | MN-major A or B | different descriptor walk (LBO live, k-steps in multiples of SBO), different TMA map and smem atom (Section 3.1.2) |
| MMA shape | 256 x 128 x 16, `cta_group::2` | pair shares B (split 64/64, each CTA loads half, the instruction reads both) and stacks A along M (each CTA its own 128 rows); 4 MMAs per 64-wide k-tile | 1SM 128 x 128 x 16 | 32 KiB instead of 24 KiB operand smem per k-tile per SM; 1.5x L2 bytes in the (1,2,1) design of Section 3.3.1, 2x with no multicast |
| CTA tile | 128 x 128 x 64 | TMEM holds 4 stages; 8 smem stages fit | 128 x 256 (pair 256 x 256) | 2 TMEM stages, 5 smem stages (derived in Section 3.9.7), worse quantisation on small problems; but 128 B/clk smem at peak instead of 192, both at the read-once bound (NVIDIA internal) |
| Cluster | (2,2,1) | 2SM pair along M plus A multicast along N: 128 FLOP per L2 byte | (1,1,1) 64; (2,1,1) and (1,2,1) 85; (4,1,1) worse than (2,2,1) | more L2 traffic per FLOP, and for the 1SM shapes more TMA bytes written into each SM's smem too (Section 3.3) |
| k-tile | 64 | fills the 128-byte SW128 row; one barrier round per 48 KiB | 16 or 32 | 4x or 2x the barrier/TMA instruction rate for the same bytes; smaller TMA boxes |
| Mainloop stages | 8 | everything the carveout leaves: 1.5-1.7 us of prefetch | 4 | 0.65-0.87 us of latency tolerance (3-4 stages ahead x 24576 B / 113 GB/s); far-partition and HBM misses exposed (Section 3.5.1) |
| Accumulator stages | 4 | TMEM maximum for 128 columns per stage; 2 would suffice in steady state | 2 | less slack against epilogue or CLC jitter |
| CLC stages / throttle | 2 / 2 | one query outstanding, response consumed while the next is in flight; 1.4 us latency vs 27.75 us tile | 1 slot; no throttle | serialised consume/issue; hoarded tiles and load imbalance |
| Epilogue tile | (128, 16) | 32x32b.x16 load shape, 4 warps x 32 lanes, 16 registers per thread | (128, 32) | 32 live registers, 4 x 16 KiB stages, mainloop ring 8 -> 6 stages by the carveout floor (Section 3.6) |
| Store box | (32, 16, 1) | 128-byte inner-dimension limit of the 128B swizzle for an M-major fp32 D | unswizzled stage with a (128, 16, 1) box | legal: `SWIZZLE_NONE` has no 128-byte inner-box limit, boxDim[0] = 128 <= 256, and 128 x 4 B is a multiple of 16 B. The 16 `st.shared.b32` per thread are bank-conflict-free either way: for a fixed value index the 32 lanes write 32 distinct words inside one 128-byte span with the XOR of `explicit.cu:1013`, and 128 contiguous bytes without it. The real cost is leaving the CUTLASS builder's `Layout_MN_SW128_32B_Atom` choice (note, Section 4) and changing the ledger to 8 stores of 8 KiB per CTA tile. Any effect on the TMA store's smem-read side is unverified |
| Epilogue smem stages | 4 x 8 KiB, `wait_group.read 1` | inherited from `StagesC` with `ReuseSmemC`; 2 would suffice for beta = 0 | 2 stages | no slack; a slow TMA store read would stall the next subtile |
| Warps | 1 MMA + 1 sched + 1 producer + 1 idle + 4 epilogue = 8 | single-issuer units (TMA, UMMA, CLC); 128 TMEM lanes | 2 producer warps; 8 epilogue warps | nothing to issue; TMEM lane rule gives 32 lanes per warp regardless |
| Occupancy | 1 CTA/SM, `__launch_bounds__(256, 1)` | 230400 B of smem | 2 CTAs/SM with 3 stages each (4 each would need 2 x (33792 + 4 x 24576) = 264192 B > 228 KB per SM with this kernel's barrier and epilogue region; 3 each, 2 x 107520 B, fits) | 3/8 of the prefetch depth per CTA; two MMA issuers contending for one tensor core |
| Scheduling | dynamic CLC, persistent | absorbs the 3 % per-tile speed variation between cluster placements (SM position inside the GPC, inferred; trace build); tail 32 vs 31.03 | static persistent (tile = f(cluster id, iteration)) | slow clusters finish last; same quantisation |
| Raster | AlongN, swizzle 0 | heuristic on equal tile counts; resident clusters sweep one A band | swizzle 4-8 | fewer B re-reads from HBM (Section 3.9.5); the harness default is 0 |
| alpha, beta | run-time parameters | keep the FMUL + FFMA pair and bit-exact D (Chapter 5) | compile-time 1.0f / 0.0f | the 128 FMUL + 128 FFMA fold away and alpha, beta are frozen; D stays bit-identical, a -0.0 sign difference arising only from `alpha * acc` alone (Section 10.9) |
