(The loop ends with `} while (work_tile_info.is_valid()); clc_pipeline.producer_tail(clc_pipe_producer_state);` at :721-722 (:749-750 in this tree).)

`requires_clc_query` is always true for this scheduler (`fetch_next_work` returns `increment_pipe = true`, sm100_tile_scheduler.hpp:472 (:503 in this tree)), so the explicit kernel drops the flag.

Two names in the quoted code are not wrappers of this chapter: `elect_one_sync()` is W2 (explicit.cu:263, Section 6.2.2), and `lane` is the kernel's `threadIdx.x & 31u` (explicit.cu:1102), reused as the `cta_id` operand of W13 (7.1, 7.6.5).

### 7.6.1 Who runs it, and why only rank 0 (explicit.cu:1194-1196)

(quoted in Section 11.7; `is_cta0 = (rank == 0u)` at :1105, `lane = threadIdx.x & 31u` at :1102)

CUTLASS: `is_participant.sched = (warp_category == WarpCategory::Sched) && is_first_cta_in_cluster` with `is_first_cta_in_cluster = cta_rank_in_cluster == 0` (sm100_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:426, :451). Both reasons come from the hardware contract. First, one `try_cancel` per cluster, or you cancel several clusters (7.3 item 6). Second, the response is multicast to all four CTAs and completes all four full barriers (7.3 item 3), so the other three CTAs need no scheduler of their own: their warp 1 prefetches the A/B tensor maps in the prologue (explicit.cu:1113-1116), then falls through the dispatch chain and exits (note 7.3 step 7). Rank 0 is just a convention (`producer_blockid = 0`); any fixed rank would do, as long as every consumer releases to the same one.

### 7.6.2 Line 821: `griddep_wait()`

`griddepcontrol.wait` (W35, explicit.cu:599) mirrors `cutlass::arch::wait_on_dependent_grids()` at kernel `:716` in this tree (`:688` in the numbering explicit.cu's comment uses). It belongs to programmatic dependent launch (Chapter 11): it blocks until all prerequisite grids have completed and their memory operations are visible. Only two warp roles execute it in this kernel: warp 2 (before its first TMA load touches A and B) and rank 0's warp 1 (here); `ACQBULK` x2 in the explicit SASS (note G.3). The source does not say why the scheduler warp needs it. My hypothesis: a cluster of a dependent grid must not start cancelling (stealing) its own grid's clusters, and thereby committing itself to more work, before the dependency it was launched under has resolved. Mark that reasoning as (hypothesis); the observable fact is that CUTLASS puts the wait there and the explicit kernel keeps it.

### 7.6.3 Lines 822-824: three pipeline states

| State | Role of this warp | Stages | Start | Advanced at | Partner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `thc_idx, thc_phase` | throttle **consumer** | 2 | {0, 0} | :838 | rank-0 warp 2 (producer, `thr_idx, thr_phase = {0, 1}` at explicit.cu:766) |
| `clp_idx, clp_phase` | CLC **producer** | 2 | {0, 1} | :849 | the 800 consumers (release) and the hardware (fill) |
| `clc_idx, clc_phase` | CLC **consumer** | 2 | {0, 0} | inside `clc_consume` (:688) | the same as every other consumer warp |

All three advance exactly once per loop iteration, so after tile t they all point at slot (t + 1) % 2 with the parities of 7.2.1. The scheduler is the only warp that is a producer *and* a consumer of the same pipeline, which is why it carries two CLC states; CUTLASS gives it `ThreadCategory::ProducerConsumer` (kernel :503-505).

### 7.6.4 Lines 836-838: the throttle consumer

```
    EXPLICIT_WAIT(smem_base + OFF_THROTTLE_FULL + 8u * thc_idx, thc_phase, WAIT_THROTTLE_FULL, tile, 0u);
    mbar_arrive_remote(smem_base + OFF_THROTTLE_EMPTY + 8u * thc_idx, 0u);
    advance<kThrottleStages>(thc_idx, thc_phase);
```
(explicit.cu:836-838)

The producer side is in `producer_role`, rank 0 only, at the start of each tile, before any TMA of that tile (explicit.cu:783-787, quoted in Section 8.6.4).

- **Counts 32 / 32.** The explicit kernel initialises both throttle barriers with `kThrottleCount = 32` (explicit.cu:1159-1160, warp 3, as CUTLASS's `initializing_warp = 3`, kernel :549).
- **Why the consumer's release is the remote form to CTA 0, which is itself.** CUTLASS's `PipelineAsync::consumer_release` is `empty_barrier_ptr_[stage].arrive(params_.dst_blockid);` (cutlass/pipeline/sm90_pipeline.hpp:1236-1238) with `clc_throttle_pipeline_params.dst_blockid = 0` (kernel :548); `arrive(cta_id)` is the `mapa` + `mbarrier.arrive.shared::cluster` form (barrier.h:383-385 -> :486-499). The explicit kernel reproduces the form (W10) so that the PTX inventory matches (`mapa` 8 sites, note G.3). Nothing would break if it were a local arrive, but nothing is gained either.
- **Why the producer's acquire is a blocking wait with no peek.** `PipelineAsync::producer_acquire` has no `try` preceding it in the kernel (kernel :661 in this tree calls `producer_acquire` directly, then `producer_commit` at :662), and in practice it should never block (below; inferred, the wait was not timed), so a peek would be wasted.
- **Why the producer never blocks on the throttle.** The producer waits on `throttle_empty[i % 2]` before producing token i + 2, and in practice never has to wait: the scheduler spends nearly the whole tile blocked in its `throttle_full` wait (28.8-37.7 us per tile, 7.6.9), so token i is consumed, and slot i % 2 released, soon after its production and about two tile periods before token i + 2 is produced (8.6.4) [inferred from the scheduler-side timings; the producer-side wait itself was not timed].

### 7.6.5 Lines 840-842: acquire the slot and arm four full barriers

```
    uint32_t const full_addr = smem_base + OFF_CLC_FULL + 8u * clp_idx;
    EXPLICIT_WAIT(smem_base + OFF_CLC_EMPTY + 8u * clp_idx, clp_phase, WAIT_CLC_EMPTY, tile, 0u);   // wait own empty[idx]
    mbar_arrive_expect_tx_remote_pred(full_addr, lane, lane < 4u ? 1u : 0u, kClcTxBytes);   // lanes 0..3 arm CTAs 0..3's full[idx] with 16 bytes
```
(explicit.cu:840-842)

This is `advance_to_next_work`'s `producer_acquire`:

```
  CUTLASS_DEVICE
  void producer_acquire(uint32_t stage, uint32_t phase, ProducerToken barrier_token) {
    detail::pipeline_check_is_producer(params_.role);
    // 1. Wait for empty barrier to be ready
    // 2. Set the transaction bytes set to occur on the Full barrier for all blocks
    if (barrier_token == BarrierStatus::WaitAgain) {
      empty_barrier_ptr_[stage].wait(phase);
    }

    full_barrier_ptr_[stage].arrive_and_expect_tx(params_.transaction_bytes, lane_idx_, uint32_t(lane_idx_ < cluster_size_));
  }
```
`advance_to_next_work` calls `clc_pipeline.producer_acquire(clc_pipe_producer_state)` with no token (sm100_tile_scheduler.hpp:443), i.e. the `PipelineState` overload whose `barrier_token` defaults to `{BarrierStatus::WaitAgain}` (sm100_pipeline.hpp:1027). The `if` above is therefore always taken: the scheduler's empty-barrier wait is always the blocking form with no preceding peek.

- **Arming.** W13 (explicit.cu:393-405, quoted in Section 6.3.8).

  Every one of the 32 lanes executes the asm. Why `lane < 4`: the cluster has 4 CTAs (`lane_idx_ < cluster_size_` in the source; the explicit kernel hard-codes `lane < 4u` because its cluster is fixed at (2,2,1)). Why one lane per CTA rather than one lane doing four arrivals: the predicated form costs the same (one predicated instruction per lane, issued once per warp), needs no loop, and in SASS is one predicated arrive per lane, `@!P0 SYNCS.ARRIVE.TRANS64.RED RZ, [R11+URZ], R5` with `R5 = 0x10` (`0x1b70`, Section 12.2; the baseline's `@!P2 ..., [PRMT(lane)], R9`, note D.2).
- **The mbarrier count ranges.** PTX ISA 9.4 Table 43 for `.layout::v0` (the default, and the only layout this kernel uses) gives: expected arrival count 1 .. 2^20 - 1, pending arrival count 0 .. 2^20 - 1, tx-count -(2^20 - 1) .. 2^20 - 1. So `mbarrier.init` counts of 800 and 256 are legal, and a 16-byte (or 49152-byte) expectation cannot overflow. The Programming Guide states the two-sided completion rule (pending count and tx-count both zero, Chapter 4, Section 4.2.1) in its own words: "When a barrier uses a transaction count, it blocks threads at the wait operation until all the producer threads have performed an arrive and the sum of all the transaction counts reaches an expected value" (Asynchronous Barriers, 4.10.6).

### 7.6.6 Lines 843-849: the elected `try_cancel` and the producer advance

W33 `clc_try_cancel(result_addr, mbarrier_addr)` (explicit.cu:568-575, Sections 6.8.2 and 2.12.2) is the single instruction `clusterlaunchcontrol.try_cancel.async.shared::cta.mbarrier::complete_tx::bytes.multicast::cluster::all.b128 [%0], [%1];` with no `"memory"` clobber; the asm is `issue_clc_query`, cutlass/gemm/kernel/sm100_tile_scheduler.hpp:398-403.

- Operands: `result_addr = smem_base + 352 + 16 clp_idx` (this CTA's slot) and `mbarrier_addr = full_addr = smem_base + 208 + 8 clp_idx` (this CTA's full barrier), both `shared::cta` addresses of rank 0. With `.multicast::cluster::all` the hardware writes the same 16 bytes to offset 352 + 16 idx **in every CTA** and performs a complete-tx of 16 bytes on the barrier at offset 208 + 8 idx **in every CTA** (7.3 item 3). The addresses are rank-0 addresses, but the semantics are the ISA's "corresponding local shared memory addr of each CTA". This works because all four CTAs have the identical shared-memory layout (same `SharedStorage`; measured bases differ only in bits 24-25, note D.1 D5).
- `.async`: the instruction returns immediately; the response arrives later (consumed by the scheduler warp a median 1408 ns after issue, note D.3).
- Why `elect_one_sync()`: one request per cluster, submitted from a single thread as the Programming Guide recommends for this uniform instruction (7.3 item 6). The SASS confirms the "uniform": `UGETNEXTWORKID.BROADCAST [UR8], [UR9]` (`[UR4], [UR5]` in the baseline) is an unpredicated uniform-datapath instruction that issues once per warp, so the `ELECT` is folded away (note G.3, D.2). The PTX-level election is still required for correctness portability, and it is the contract the kernel writes (note E.6.6).
- No `"memory"` clobber on W33: the asm has none in the source either (`:398-403`). It does not read or write anything the compiler can see; its effects arrive through the mbarrier, which every subsequent wait observes with its own `"memory"` clobber.
- `advance<kClcStages>(clp_idx, clp_phase)` (:849): the next query uses the other slot, and every second query flips the parity the producer will wait for, in step with the consumers' releases.

### 7.6.7 Lines 853-856: consume your own response, then decide

```
    valid = clc_consume<K_CLC_SCHED_KIND>(smem_base, x, y, clc_idx, clc_phase, clc_count, tm_next, tn_next, tile);   // fetch_next_work (:702-706)
    tm = tm_next; tn = tn_next;
    ++tile;
  } while (valid);
```
(explicit.cu:853-856)

The scheduler warp is one of the 800 consumers (its 32 arrivals are counted in `NumSchedThreads`), so it runs the same `clc_consume` as every other consumer warp, on the response to the query it has *just* issued (same iteration: issue n at :847, consume n at :853). This is where the warp blocks for the query latency: its `EXPLICIT_WAIT` on `clc_full[idx]` returns when the hardware's bytes have landed (7.6.9 gives the numbers). The warp does not use `tm, tn` for anything but keeps them so the trace can report the mapped tile; in production the copy on :854 is dead and vanishes.

The loop ends on the first not-cancelled response (`valid == 0`), which answers the last query the warp ever issues. Issue query t (:847), then consume response t (:853), and enter iteration t + 1 only if response t succeeded: that order is what satisfies 7.3 item 7, no request after an observed failure.

### 7.6.8 Lines 857-867: the producer tail

The tail, quoted here because the state variables `clp_idx, clp_phase` and the query count T are defined in this chapter:

```
  // CLC producer_tail (sm100_pipeline.hpp:1041-1050): test_wait, then the blocking wait only if not done (Section 7.10 tail 2)
  #pragma unroll
  for (int i = 0; i < kClcStages; ++i) {
    uint32_t const done = mbar_test_wait(smem_base + OFF_CLC_EMPTY + 8u * clp_idx, clp_phase, 1u);
    if (!done) { EXPLICIT_WAIT(smem_base + OFF_CLC_EMPTY + 8u * clp_idx, clp_phase, TAIL_CLC, tile, uint32_t(i)); }
    advance<kClcStages>(clp_idx, clp_phase);

```
(explicit.cu:857-867)

Its source:

```
  // Prevents early exit of producer blocks in Cluster.
  // Does NOT reset transaction bytes.
  // This should be called once before kernel exits.
  CUTLASS_DEVICE
  void producer_tail(PipelineState state) {
    detail::pipeline_check_is_producer(params_.role);
    for (int count = 0; count < Stages; ++count) {
      bool done = empty_barrier_ptr_[state.index()].test_wait(state.phase());
      if (!done) {
        empty_barrier_ptr_[state.index()].wait(state.phase());
      }
      ++state;
    }
  }
```

**The parities for the measured tile counts** T = 32, 31 and 19 are worked in Chapter 4, Section 4.8.4 (note 7.4); the `K_TAIL` records of the explicit run verified them (note G.1: "CLC `((T+i) % 2, 1 ^ (((T+i) / 2) & 1))`").

Check one row of that table (Chapter 4, Section 4.8.4): for T = 32, response 30 used slot 0 and its 800 releases completed phase 15 of `clc_empty[0]` (phases are numbered by the responses that lived in the slot: 0, 2, 4, ..., 30 -> phase 15), parity 15 & 1 = 1.

**Why the tail exists.** Besides the remote-arrival rule (Chapter 4, Section 4.8), the exit discipline as a whole has an ISA-level reason: the `.multicast::cluster::all` exit rule of 7.3 item 3, which the kernel satisfies because the last `try_cancel` precedes every exit in the cluster (7.6.7).

**Why `test_wait` first.** If the phase has already completed, the blocking loop is skipped entirely; that holds for step 0 but not for step 1: warp 2 releases the final response only after issuing the last tile's 128 k-tiles of loads (7.8), about one tile time after this warp consumed it, so the second wait blocks in every cluster. Measured in the explicit kernel's trace run (a recount of the `K_TAIL` timestamps in `trace_out_v2/launch0.csv`): the step-0 record follows the scheduler's final K5b by only 0.7-1.2 us, while the step-1 record follows it by 33.7-34.6 us in all 32 unprobed clusters and by 58.0 us in cluster (0,0). Functionally the blocking wait alone would suffice (it returns immediately on a completed phase). CUTLASS chose the probe-then-wait form for this pipeline's `producer_tail` (the only `producer_tail` in sm90_pipeline.hpp and sm100_pipeline.hpp that probes first), and the explicit kernel mirrors it so that the two `test_wait.parity` sites of the baseline's PTX (note D.2) reappear in the explicit PTX (`mbarrier.test_wait.parity 2`, note G.3). The scheduler's two `EXIT` sites in SASS (code addresses, not timings) are `0x2f80`/`0x2fe0` in the baseline (note D.2) and `0x1e60`/`0x1ec0` in the explicit kernel (note G.3). The note itself reports no tail duration. What G.1 reports is the ordering of the `K_TAIL` records. The CLC tail records follow the pipeline formula `((T+i) % 2, 1 ^ (((T+i) / 2) & 1))` for every cluster's T. One step-0 record legitimately precedes its CTA's last K5c by 32 ns, because step 0 waits for the releases of response T - 2, not T - 1. The `1u` argument of `mbar_test_wait` is explained in 7.2.3.

### 7.6.9 Why one query per tile, why at most one outstanding, and what was measured

**One query per tile.** Every iteration of every role's loop consumes exactly one response, and the scheduler issues exactly one query per iteration. A cluster that processes T tiles (the launch tile plus T - 1 stolen ones) therefore issues exactly T queries: T - 1 answered "cancelled" and one answered "not cancelled" (note 7.4). Over the launch: 1024 queries, of which `N_native` fail, where `N_native` is the number of natively launched clusters. Measured: `N_native = 33` (= `cudaOccupancyMaxActiveClusters`), 991 cancelled + 33 not cancelled (note D.3, D9). 33 and not 148 / 4 = 37 because "a 2x2 cluster needs two whole TPCs in one GPC" and 8 leftover TPCs (16 SMs: 64, 65, 122-129, 142-147) cannot be paired (note D.3; on this B200's skyline the 8 are the one unpaired TPC of each odd-sized GPC, NVIDIA internal information; arithmetic in Section 2.1.1).

**At most one outstanding.** Chain the dependencies of one cluster:

```
producer warp 2 (rank 0):   begin tile t  --throttle_full[t%2]-->  scheduler: query t  --hw-->  response t (= tile t+1 or "none")
                            ... 128 k-tiles of loads for tile t ...                         ^
                            consume response t  <------------------------------------------+
                            begin tile t+1  --throttle_full[(t+1)%2]-->  scheduler: query t+1
```

Query t + 1 needs the producer to have begun tile t + 1. That needs the producer to have consumed response t (the end of its iteration t), which needs response t to have arrived. So query t + 1 is never in flight while query t is: **at most one query outstanding per cluster**, and query t (which fetches tile t + 1) is issued only after the loader has begun tile t (note D.7). Measured: "Never more than one query was outstanding per cluster (0 violations in 1024 queries); at most 25 were outstanding GPU-wide at any instant" (note D.3), and "a query is actually in flight only about 4% of the time" (note D.7).

**Why the throttle exists (CUTLASS's comment and my analysis).** The source comment reads "Throttle CLC query to mitigate workload imbalance caused by skews among persistent workers" (kernel :720 in this tree). Without it, only the CLC empty barriers (count 800) would gate the scheduler's loop, i.e. the slowest consumer of the response two queries back. Those releases happen *during* tile n (warps 0 and 4-7 consume response n at the start of their tile n, warp 2 after tile n's loads; 7.8), so query n + 2, which needs only `clc_empty[n % 2]`, could be issued while tile n is still running. During tile n the scheduler could then have issued queries n + 1 and n + 2. At the end of tile n the cluster would know tiles n + 1 (from response n), n + 2 and n + 3: up to three stolen-but-unstarted tile ids, against exactly one (tile n + 1) with the throttle. Meanwhile a faster cluster that has run out of work finds the queue empty. At the end of the grid that is pure tail imbalance: the last tiles would sit in the shared-memory slots of busy clusters while other SMs idle. Tying each query to the producer's *start* of a tile means a cluster never owns more than the tile it is loading plus one claimed id, so the hand-out tracks actual progress. The measured spread of tiles per cluster (32 for 13 clusters, 31 for 19, 19 for the probe-slowed cluster (0,0), note D.3) is the throttle working: the slow cluster simply took fewer tiles.

**Measured dynamics** (note D.3, CUTLASS trace build; the explicit kernel reproduced the same dynamics, note G.1; Chapter 12, Section 12.6.3 has the full tables). Query-to-consume latency: median 1408 ns, p90 1536, p99 1792; the explicit kernel's own trace build measured a 1024 ns median (note G.2), a probe-placement artefact irrelevant to the Release comparison. The scheduler's gap from consuming response n to issuing query n + 1, i.e. the throttle wait: 28.8-37.7 us, median 30.8 us, in the 32 unprobed clusters. Per-tile time: median 31.90 us in the trace build against 27.8 us in Release (0.889 ms / 32 tiles). Responses: 991 cancelled (ids 33..1023, each exactly once) plus 33 not cancelled, handed out in approximately increasing launch-linear order; the first, id 33, was consumed by cluster (0,0) 1.28 us after the first query. Outstanding queries: never more than one per cluster, at most 25 GPU-wide.

The latency is therefore completely hidden from the scheduler (it waits ~30 us for the throttle and ~1.4 us for the response). For the MMA warp the question is different, and it pays to separate the *warp* from the *tensor core*. The MMA warp consumes response t at the *start* of its tile t (explicit.cu:913 is the first statement of its loop body; Chapter 9), immediately after issuing k-tile 127 of tile t - 1. Its position in time is gated by `full[s]` (:923, the TMA data landing) and `acc_empty[st]` (:918), *not* by `empty[s]`. `tcgen05.mma` is asynchronous and its completion is observed only through `tcgen05.commit` (:942), so the warp's issue position can run ahead of tensor-core execution by up to the 8 stages the ring holds. It therefore reaches `clc_consume` roughly one TMA latency (~1 us, unmeasured; Section 3.5) after the producer issued load 127 of tile t - 1, which is also about when the producer began tile t and query t was issued. How far ahead of completion the warp really runs was not measured. The one measured datum is D.3's "K5c of rank 0 follows K5b by 96 ns median": the MMA warp's consume completes 96 ns after the scheduler warp's. That is what you would see if the MMA warp were already waiting on `clc_full` when the response lands, on most tiles rather than occasionally (my reading of D.3). This is harmless for throughput. The tensor core still holds the already-issued MMAs of up to 8 k-tiles (8 x 217 ns = 1.74 us of work at 27.8 us / 128 per k-tile, issued before the warp blocked). A tensor-core bubble can therefore appear only when the response latency exceeds that queue, i.e. above ~1.7 us, which is beyond p90 (1536 ns) and near p99 (1792 ns) (my analysis). The epilogue warps consume at the start of their tile, after the MMAs of the previous tile have completed, i.e. later still; how often they wait was not measured.

**What the kernel must not assume.** The hand-out order is a property of this hardware and this run; "the kernel must not depend on the order, D.7" (note 7.4). Nor on `N_native = 33`: "the kernel must work for any number of native clusters and any hand-out order" (note D.7). The explicit kernel satisfies this by construction: it uses only `valid` and the mapping, never the order, never a tile count, never a second `try_cancel` after a failure.

Why the order is *approximately* increasing (hypothesis): the CLC unit pops the next unlaunched cluster from the grid's launch queue, which is in launch-linear order. The swaps are not a timestamp-resolution artefact. D.3 broke same-tick ties by ascending id, so a same-tick pair is never counted as an inversion, and found that every one of the 25 inversions is a query issued in a *strictly later* 32 ns tick that received a *lower* id than an earlier one. That is, the CLC unit served two requests out of their issue order (hypothesis: arbitration between SMs or GPCs on the way to the unit). The count 25 holds only under that tie-breaking convention (other conventions give 32-62). None of this is relied upon.

---

## 7.7 One CLC round trip: the sequence

Response n uses slot `i = n % 2`; the parities are those of 7.2.1 with `k = n / 2`.

```
 rank-0 warp 2            rank-0 warp 1 (scheduler)              CLC hardware                 consumers, every CTA r (0..3)
 (throttle producer)                                                                            w0, w2, w4-7 (+ w1 of rank 0)
 ---------------------    ---------------------------------      ------------------           -------------------------------------
 begin tile n:
  wait  throttle_empty[i]
        (parity 1^(k&1))
  arrive throttle_full[i]
        x32 (local)   --------> wait throttle_full[i] (parity k&1)
                                 arrive throttle_empty[i] x32
                                   (mapa -> CTA 0 == self)
  issue 128 k-tiles of
  TMA for tile n ...             wait own clc_empty[i] (parity 1^(k&1))
                                   <== completed by the 800 releases of response n-2
                                 lanes 0..3: mapa(clc_full[i], lane)
                                   arrive.expect_tx 16  -------------------------------->  CTA r's clc_full[i]: pending arrivals 1 -> 0,
                                                                                            tx-count 0 -> +16
                                 elected lane:
                                   try_cancel [resp[i]], [clc_full[i]] --> cancel an unlaunched
                                                                           cluster (first CTA
                                                                           (x0,y0,z0)) or decline
                                                                           | 16 B async-proxy write to resp[i] of CTA 0,1,2,3
                                                                           | complete_tx 16 on clc_full[i] of CTA 0,1,2,3
                                                                           v                tx-count +16 -> 0  => phase k completes
                                 advance clp state
                                 consume (same code as ->)                                  each warp: wait own clc_full[i] (parity k&1)
                                   wait own clc_full[i]                                       ld.shared.b128 resp[i]
                                   decode, fence.proxy.async                                  is_canceled -> valid; @valid get_first_ctaid
                                   arrive CTA 0's clc_empty[i] x32 ----+                      fence.proxy.async.shared::cta
                                   advance clc state                   |                      arrive CTA 0's clc_empty[i] (x32 per warp,
                                   @valid: (tm,tn) <- map(x0,y0)       |                        x128 for w4-7)  ----------------------+
                                                                       |                      advance clc state                       |
                                                                       |                      @valid: (tm_next,tn_next) <- map(x0,y0) |
  ... last TMA of tile n                                               v                                                              v
  consume response n  (w2 of rank 0 is one of the consumers)       CTA 0's clc_empty[i]: 800 arrivals -> phase k completes
  tm,tn <- tm_next,tn_next                                          (this is what the scheduler's acquire for query n+2 waits for)
 begin tile n+1  ------------->  (next iteration: query n+1)
```

Arrival bookkeeping on the figure: each CTA r contributes w0 (32) + w2 (32) + w4-7 (128) = 192 arrivals to CTA 0's `clc_empty[i]`; rank 0 adds its w1 (32), so rank 0 contributes 224 and the total is 224 + 3 x 192 = 800 (7.4.5).

The MMA warp reaches its consume of response n at the start of its tile n, typically before the response has landed, and blocks on `clc_full[i]` while the tensor core drains the up-to-8 queued k-tiles (inferred in 7.6.9 from the one measured datum, note D.3 on the CUTLASS kernel's trace build: its consume follows the scheduler's by 96 ns median).

The slot and parity bookkeeping of the tail of the same round trips, for a cluster that processes T = 32 tiles (Chapter 4, Section 4.3.5 tabulates tiles 0..5; Section 4.8.4 tabulates these two tail waits):

| tile t | query / response n | slot | sched acquire: `clc_empty[slot]` parity |
|---|---|---|---|
| tail 0 | (32) | 0 | 1 (releases of resp. 30) |
| tail 1 | (33) | 1 | 1 (releases of resp. 31) |

---

## 7.8 Design notes: why the dispatcher has this shape, and how to reuse it

**Dynamic (CLC) instead of a static persistent stride.** A static persistent kernel would launch `N_native` clusters and have cluster c take tiles c, c + N_native, .... But `N_native` is not given by the SM count (33 here, not the arithmetic 37; `cudaOccupancyMaxActiveClusters` returned 33, note D.3, a co-residency maximum rather than a guarantee), and clusters do not run at equal speed (in the trace build 13 clusters did 32 tiles and 19 did 31; the probe-slowed cluster (0,0) did 19, note D.3). CLC lets the hardware be the queue: residency and speed differences are absorbed automatically, the hardware guarantees exactly-once coverage (7.3 item 2 and the scheduling model of Section 2.12.1), and the kernel needs no atomic counter in global memory. The cost is one 16-byte round trip per tile (1.4 us hidden behind 28 us) and, per CTA, 8 mbarriers (`clc_full[2]`, `clc_empty[2]`, `throttle_full[2]`, `throttle_empty[2]`: 8 x 8 B = 64 B at bytes 208..239 and 304..335) plus 2 x 16 B = 32 B of response slots (bytes 352..383). That is 96 B per CTA, 384 B cluster-wide, of which the throttle and `clc_empty` barriers are used only in rank 0 (ranks 1-3 initialise theirs too, explicit.cu:1135-1143 and 1155-1163, but never wait on or arrive at them; the constants are at :109-110, 144-145, 148-149, 151).

**Two slots, not one or eight.** With the throttle guaranteeing at most one query outstanding, two slots are the minimum that lets query n + 1 be issued while the slowest consumers of response n (the epilogue warps, which consume at the start of their tile n) are still to read it. One slot would force the scheduler to wait for all 800 releases of response n before issuing n + 1, serialising the round trip with the slowest warp's tile boundary. Where the 2 comes from: `kClcStages` mirrors `SchedulerPipelineStageCount`, a template parameter of the dispatch policy, not a hardware constant. The collective builder sets `SchedulerPipelineStageCount = cute::conditional_return<IsGroupGemm || IsRCGroupGemm>(8, 2)` (cutlass/gemm/collective/builders/sm100_umma_builder.inl:282), i.e. 2 for this dense GEMM, and passes it into `MainloopSm100TmaUmmaWarpSpecialized<PipelineStages, SchedulerPipelineStageCount, AccumulatorPipelineStageCount, ClusterShape_MNK, ArchTag>` (`:320-326`). The measured instantiations are `MainloopSm100TmaUmmaWarpSpecialized<8,2,4,(2,2,1),Sm100>` and `PersistentTileSchedulerSm100<(2,2,1),2>` (note D.1). The kernel reads it back as `DispatchPolicy::Schedule::SchedulerPipelineStageCount` (sm100_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:118) and sizes `CLCPipeline`, `CLCThrottlePipeline` and `clc_response[]` with it (`:172`, `:175`, `:200`). The CUTLASS documentation page says generically "The CLC pipeline has a depth of 3 to overlap the CLC operations of multiple waves for latency hiding"; that sentence describes a different configuration and does not apply to this build.

**The asymmetry of the barriers.** Both asymmetries (full barriers per CTA, empty barriers only in CTA 0; Chapter 4, Section 4.4.4) follow directly from the hardware contract and the single-requester rule; do not "symmetrise" them.

**Where each role consumes (Chapters 8-10 give the loops).** Warp 2 consumes response t after tile t's loads (Section 8.6.7); warps 0 and 4-7 consume it *before* computing/storing tile t; the MMA warp needs no coordinates at all (`(void)tm; (void)tn;`, explicit.cu:883), and the epilogue needs the *current* tile's coordinates, which it already has.

**Failure modes to design against (anticipated hazards, neither observed: the first is note E.6.4's warning, the second my analysis of the ISA; the first build and every run passed, note G.0):**

| Mistake | Symptom |
|---|---|
| A role skips one `clc_consume` (e.g. an early `continue`) | CTA 0's `clc_empty` never reaches 800: the scheduler's acquire two queries later deadlocks the whole cluster |
| A separate `mbarrier.arrive` issued *before* `expect_tx` | the arrival drops the pending count 1 -> 0 while the tx-count is still 0, so the phase completes immediately (ISA 9.7.15.16.8: completion when both counts are zero), before any response bytes exist, and the 800 consumers read a slot the hardware has not written yet; `expect_tx` then `arrive` would be safe, and the fused `arrive.expect_tx` removes the ordering question and matches the source |

**Generalising to other kernels.** The dispatcher is operator-agnostic: it hands out `(x0, y0, z0)` of a cancelled cluster and lets `swizzle_and_rasterize` turn it into work coordinates. To reuse it:

1. Arm `lane < cluster_size` CTAs.
2. Keep the throttle unless your producer has a different natural "begun a tile" point.
3. Replace the mapping with your own raster. For L > 1, bind `z0` to the batch coordinate as CUTLASS does: the baseline binds `word1 >> 16` to `L_idx` (note D.2); the explicit kernel drops it because L = 1 is fixed.
4. For a swizzled raster, implement the full `swizzle_and_rasterize` block (sm100_tile_scheduler.hpp:711-795; 742-826 in the working tree), which the fixed run skips.
5. For stream-K-style schedulers, honour `increment_pipe`: not every `fetch_next_work` consumes a response.

# Chapter 8. The Feeder: producer_role and load_ktiles (Warp 2)

Chapter 6 explains the PTX of W6, W7, W12, W21, W22 and W35 character by character; Chapter 4 explains parities and tokens in general. This chapter is about who calls those wrappers, on which addresses, with which numbers, and why.

---

## 8.1 Warp 2 in one picture

The producer warp is the only warp that moves A and B, and it never reads a byte of them. It hands coordinates to the TMA unit, which writes the bytes into the 8-stage shared-memory ring (and, for A, into a sibling CTA's ring as well), and it manages the ring with two mbarrier arrays. Everything downstream (UMMA, TMEM, epilogue) is somebody else's job.

```
 global A (fp16, K-major)            global B (fp16, K-major)
 rows 128 tm + 64 y .. +64           columns 128 tn + 64 x .. +64
 k = 64 q .. +64                     k = 64 q .. +64
        |                                   |
        | W21: cp.async.bulk.tensor.3d      | W22: cp.async.bulk.tensor.3d
        |      .cta_group::2 .multicast     |      .cta_group::2 (no multicast)
        |      mask 0x5 << x                |
        v                                   v
 +-------------------------------------------------------------+
 | this CTA's smem ring, stage s (and, for A, the ring of the  |
 | sibling CTA that shares tm)                                 |
 |   OFF_SMEM_A + 16384 s + 8192 y  <- 8192 B of A (my half)   |
 |   OFF_SMEM_B +  8192 s           <- 8192 B of B (my half)   |
 +-------------------------------------------------------------+
        |  complete_tx: every box credits the PAIR LEADER's full[s]
        v
 full[s] of the pair leader: count 1 (+49152 tx)   --->  warp 0 of the leader (Chapter 9)
 empty[s] of every CTA:      count 2                <---  tcgen05.commit, mask 0xF, from both leaders
```

Per CTA and per tile the warp issues 256 TMA instructions (2 per k-tile), performs 130 non-blocking peeks and at most 128 blocking waits on `empty[]`, and — on pair leaders only — 128 `mbarrier.arrive.expect_tx` of 49152 bytes. The same warp also takes part in the CLC protocol once per tile (Chapter 7), and on CTA 0 it drives the throttle that bounds the scheduler.

---

## 8.2 The section banner (explicit.cu:708-722), step by step

```
///////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
// 6. [PROD] TMA mbarrier  Mainloop producer: warp 2 of every CTA (Section 7.5, B.3.1; CollectiveMma::load, sm100_mma_warpspecialized.hpp:589-629)
//   Per k-tile q of the current tile (tm, tn), stage s = the producer's ring index (0..7, wraps; phase flips at each wrap):
//     1. wait empty[s] (parity prod_phase; count 2 = the two pair leaders' tcgen05.commit of the previous use of stage s)
//     2. leader lane of the pair leader only: mbarrier.arrive.expect_tx on its own full[s] with 49152 bytes
//     3. one elected lane issues two 2SM TMA loads, both completing on the PAIR LEADER's full[s] ((smem_base + 8 s) & ~(1 << 24)):
//        A  multicast to ranks x and x+2 (mask 0x5 << x), coordinates (64 q, 128 tm + 64 y, 0), destination OFF_SMEM_A + 16384 s + 8192 y
//           in both destination CTAs: this CTA supplies its 64-row half of the 128 x 64 A stage, the other cluster row supplies the other half
//        B  no multicast, coordinates (64 q, 128 tn + 64 x, 0), destination OFF_SMEM_B + 8192 s (this CTA's 64 N-columns)
//     4. advance {s, phase}; peek the next empty[] so that the blocking wait is skipped when the ring is free
//   Example: tile (tm, tn) = (5, 9), q = 7, rank 1 (x = 1, y = 0): A box (448, 640, 0) -> 0x01024800 (rank 1) and 0x03024800 (rank 3),
//   B box (448, 1216, 0) -> 0x01036800; rank 2 (x = 0, y = 1) writes its A half at 0x02026800 / 0x00026800 (offset + 8192).
//   Byte accounting per stage and pair: 2 CTAs x (2 A halves x 8192 + B 8192) = 49152 = the expect_tx of step 2.
//   After the last tile: 8 blocking waits (the tail) so that no stage is still being read when the CTA exits.
///////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
```

The header line names the role, the hardware families it touches (`TMA`, `mbarrier`), and the CUTLASS function it mirrors. The function is `CollectiveMma::load` in `include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm100_mma_warpspecialized.hpp:589-629`.

The four numbered steps are the body of one iteration of the k-tile loop (in the code the advance and peek of step 4 come before the TMA issues of step 3: lines 737-739, then 740-756):

1. **Wait `empty[s]`.** In CUTLASS's count formula `cluster_m / atom_m + cluster_n / atom_n - 1` (Section 4.4.2), the first term counts the MMA atoms along M that read this CTA's B: in CUTLASS's general form B is multicast along M, but here one 2SM atom spans the cluster's whole M extent, so the term is 1 (the own leader). The second term counts the atoms along N that read this CTA's A, which is multicast along N: 2 (the own leader and the other pair's leader). The `- 1` removes the own leader, which both terms counted [the formula is from source; this reading of its terms is my analysis].
2. **`arrive.expect_tx` 49152 on the leader's own `full[s]`.** Section 8.5.3 derives the number; Section 8.4.4 explains why only the leader lane arrives.
3. **Two TMA issues by one elected lane** (Section 8.4.6).
4. **Advance and peek** (Section 8.4.5).

The example line is recomputed in Section 8.7.1 (its arithmetic is correct, though its inputs are not a reachable state: rank 1's `tn` is always even), the byte accounting is derived in Section 8.5.3, and the tail in Section 8.6.8.

---

## 8.3 ProducerState (explicit.cu:723-726)

```
struct ProducerState {
  uint32_t prod_idx = 0, prod_phase = 1;   // mainloop producer state (8 stages), carried across tiles
  int q = 0;                                // k-tile index inside the current tile
};
```

Three integers, and each initial value is forced:

- `prod_idx = 0`: the ring is used from slot 0 (Section 4.3.1).
- `prod_phase = 1` (Section 4.2.3): a producer that started at phase 0 would wait for a release that never comes — a deadlock at `q = 0`, the symptom of the first row of the note's failure-mode table (E.7.2). That row lists the byte count, the arming lane, the barrier operand and the A mask as causes; a wrong start phase is not among them but produces the same symptom.
- `q = 0`: reset at the start of every tile (explicit.cu:779). It lives in the struct, not in a local of `load_ktiles`, because a tile's 128 k-tiles are issued by *two* calls (8 then 120, Section 8.6.5) and the second call must continue the k coordinate where the first stopped.

Inside one tile the producer's `empty[]` wait parity is: `q = 0..7` parity 1, `q = 8..15` parity 0, `q = 16..23` parity 1, ..., `q = 120..127` parity 0 (because `120 >> 3 = 15` is odd); the tail (Section 8.6.8) continues the sequence.

---

## 8.4 load_ktiles (explicit.cu:728-760), line by line

```
// One load() call: n k-tiles starting at state.q. Two calls per tile (8 then k_tiles - 8) give two rolled loops.
__device__ __forceinline__ void load_ktiles(ExplicitGemmParams const& params, ProducerState& st, int n, uint32_t smem_base,
                                            uint32_t a_dst_base, uint32_t b_dst_base, uint32_t full_masked_base, uint32_t empty_base,
                                            uint16_t a_mcast_mask, bool is_leader_lane, int a_row, int b_col, uint32_t tile) {
  uint32_t tok = mbar_try_wait(empty_base + 8u * st.prod_idx, st.prod_phase);            // producer_try_acquire before the loop (:604)
  #pragma unroll 1                                                                          // CUTLASS_PRAGMA_NO_UNROLL (:607)
  while (n > 0) {
    if (!tok) { EXPLICIT_WAIT(empty_base + 8u * st.prod_idx, st.prod_phase, WAIT_MAINLOOP_EMPTY, tile, uint32_t(st.q)); }   // producer_acquire (sm90_pipeline.hpp:531-536)
    if (is_leader_lane) { mbar_arrive_expect_tx_local(smem_base + OFF_MAIN_FULL + 8u * st.prod_idx, kMainloopTxBytes); }   // (:537-539), leader lane, 49152
    uint32_t const s = st.prod_idx;                                                          // write_stage
    advance<kStages>(st.prod_idx, st.prod_phase);
    tok = mbar_try_wait(empty_base + 8u * st.prod_idx, st.prod_phase);                     // peek the next stage, unconditional (:617)
    if (elect_one_sync()) {                                                                  // one election for the A+B pair (:619-622)
      int32_t const c0 = 64 * st.q;
      tma_load_2sm_mcast_3d(&params.tma_a, full_masked_base + 8u * s, a_mcast_mask, kCacheHintEvictNormal,
                            a_dst_base + kStageBytesA * s, c0, a_row, 0);                     // A: (64q, 128 tm + 64 y, 0), mask 0x5 << x
      tma_load_2sm_3d(&params.tma_b, full_masked_base + 8u * s, kCacheHintEvictNormal,
                      b_dst_base + kStageBytesB * s, c0, b_col, 0);                          // B: (64q, 128 tn + 64 x, 0)
    }
    --n;
    ++st.q;
  }
}
```

With the toggle off (the performance binary, note Part H.1) `EXPLICIT_WAIT(addr, parity, site, tile, q)` is `mbar_wait(addr, parity)` (explicit.cu:237), so the `tile` parameter and the `uint32_t(st.q)` argument vanish too; the two `[TRACE]` blocks at explicit.cu:742-746 and 749-753, compiled out in the same binary, are omitted from the listing above. What remains is a dozen statements.

The parameters. `params` is the `__grid_constant__` parameter block (Chapter 5), used only for `&params.tma_a` and `&params.tma_b`, the generic addresses of the two 128-byte `CUtensorMap`s in parameter space. `st` is the ring state and `n` the number of k-tiles to issue in this call. `smem_base` is this CTA's 32-bit `shared::cta` base. The five invariants `a_dst_base`, `b_dst_base`, `full_masked_base`, `empty_base`, `a_mcast_mask` are computed once per role (Section 8.6.2); the predicate `is_leader_lane` once at the role dispatch (explicit.cu:1192, Section 8.4.4); `a_row`/`b_col` once per tile (Section 8.6.3).

### 8.4.1 The pre-loop peek and the token (line 732)

```
  uint32_t tok = mbar_try_wait(empty_base + 8u * st.prod_idx, st.prod_phase);            // producer_try_acquire before the loop (:604)
```

The token is computed *before* the loop so that the first iteration, like every later one, decides with a single predicate whether it must block.

### 8.4.2 `#pragma unroll 1` (lines 733-734): why the k-tile loop stays rolled

```
  #pragma unroll 1                                                                          // CUTLASS_PRAGMA_NO_UNROLL (:607)
  while (n > 0) {
```

CUTLASS marks the same loop `CUTLASS_PRAGMA_NO_UNROLL` (`sm100_mma_warpspecialized.hpp:607`). Three reasons, in decreasing order of importance:

1. **Nothing to gain.** Each iteration is dominated by two asynchronous TMA issues whose cost the TMA unit pays, not this warp. The warp's own work is 37 instructions per k-tile (33 on the fast path), most of them uniform-datapath (measured, Section 12.5.2), and it spends most of its life blocked on `empty[]` (Section 8.9). Unrolling cannot shorten a wait.
2. **Uniform-register pressure.** Uniform registers (`URn`, with `URZ` the uniform zero) are the per-warp scalar register file of the SM's *uniform datapath*, 80 x 32-bit addressable `UR0`-`UR79` per warp on Blackwell, `URZ` not among them (NVIDIA internal), beside the per-lane vector registers (`Rn`); Chapter 12, Section 12.3.1 defines them, and the previous bullet and Section 8.9 use the term. A value ptxas can prove warp-uniform (an address, a mask, a descriptor, a coordinate) costs no per-lane register and is consumed by `U`-prefixed instructions issued once per warp. The baseline's tight resource is that uniform register file, not the vector file (note D.7, inferred from 44 uniform-to-vector spill/fill pairs in the CUTLASS kernel). An unrolled body would keep several stages' addresses and tokens live at once; rolled, the loop needs one slot address, one token, one coordinate and the invariants.
3. **Code size and the performance contract.** The baseline's SASS has exactly two rolled producer loops of 8 and 120 iterations with one `UTMALDG.3D.MULTICAST.2CTA` and one `UTMALDG.3D.2CTA` each (note D.2, measured: "loop 1 counter runs -7..1 (8 iterations), loop 2 8..k_tiles (120); loop 2 body = 31 instructions"). The explicit kernel reproduces that shape (note G.3, measured; Section 12.5.2 sets the instruction counts against the baseline's). Section 12 of the note makes the instruction-stream shape part of the performance-equivalence contract ("the instruction-stream shape should match").

### 8.4.3 The blocking wait only when the token says "not done" (line 735)

```
    if (!tok) { EXPLICIT_WAIT(empty_base + 8u * st.prod_idx, st.prod_phase, WAIT_MAINLOOP_EMPTY, tile, uint32_t(st.q)); }   // producer_acquire (sm90_pipeline.hpp:531-536)
```

W6 (`mbar_wait`, explicit.cu:296-311) is `LAB_WAIT: mbarrier.try_wait.parity.shared::cta.b64 P1, [addr], phase, ticks; @P1 bra DONE; bra LAB_WAIT;` with `ticks = 0x989680` = 10,000,000 ns = 10 ms, the ISA's `timeHint` (Chapter 2, Section 2.8.4). The hint *may* be used and the suspended thread may resume early, so the outer `bra LAB_WAIT` is what makes the wait correct, not a fallback for a rare case. In practice a large hint lets the thread sleep until released instead of busy polling (my analysis of the purpose, as in Section 4.5.2: the ISA says only that the thread "may be suspended"; the measured retry loop sleeps in `NANOSLEEP.SYNCS 0x989680` between re-tests, note D.2; how the sleeping warp is woken: Chapter 12, Section 12.2.2). The `if (!tok)` is `if (barrier_token != BarrierStatus::WaitDone)` of `sm90_pipeline.hpp:533`.

### 8.4.4 The leader lane's `arrive.expect_tx` of 49152 bytes (line 736)

```
    if (is_leader_lane) { mbar_arrive_expect_tx_local(smem_base + OFF_MAIN_FULL + 8u * st.prod_idx, kMainloopTxBytes); }   // (:537-539), leader lane, 49152
```

Three "why"s:

- **Why `arrive.expect_tx` as one instruction, and why count 1.** Warp 0's elected lane initialises `full[s]` (count 1; Sections 4.2.2, 4.4.1): `if (warp_idx == 0) { if (elect_one_sync()) {` at explicit.cu:1124-1125, the loop at :1126-1130. The tx-count is **signed**, with range `-(2^20 - 1) .. 2^20 - 1` (PTX ISA 9.7.15.16.3, "Contents of the mbarrier object", the same range for both mbarrier layouts), and the ISA's complete-tx operation simply says "tx-count is decremented by completeCount". The leader's one `arrive.expect_tx` both raises the tx-count by 49152 and drops the arrival count to 0; 49152 sits far inside the range (`2^20 - 1 = 1048575`). [the kernel's value-equal runs would deadlock at `q = 0` if the ISA rules of Section 4.2.2 were otherwise — the symptom in the first row of note E.7.2's failure-mode table.] One arrival by one lane is the minimum that keeps the completion gated; 32 arrivals (all lanes) would need count 32 and would buy nothing.
- **Why only the pair leader's lane.** `is_leader_lane` is `lane_pred != 0u && is_leader` at the call site (explicit.cu:1192): `lane_pred` is the result of the prologue's `elect_one_sync()` (explicit.cu:1103, one lane of each warp, fixed for the kernel's lifetime) and `is_leader` is `(rank & 1) == 0` (explicit.cu:1106).
- **Why the peer's `full[]` barriers exist but are never used.** Both CTAs run the same code with the same `SharedStorage` layout (the 2SM MMA requires identical smem layouts in the pair, note B.6), so the peer initialises its eight `full[]` barriers like everyone else (count 1) and leaves them in phase 0 forever. They are 64 bytes of smem that keep the two CTAs' address maps identical. In SASS the arrive and the `MOV` that feeds its byte count are, apart from the two `@P1`/`@!P1` branches on the `try_wait` result, the loop's only two lane-predicated *vector* instructions: `@!P0 MOV R5, 0xc000` and `@!P0 SYNCS.ARRIVE.TRANS64 RZ, [UR10], R5` (note G.3, measured). Mind the predicate sense: `P0` is the *complement* of `is_leader_lane`, so the `@!P0` guard executes both instructions in the one lane where `P0` is false, and in no lane of the peer. They cannot be uniform instructions because only one lane may execute them. A third instruction completes the picture. `VOTEU.ALL UP1, P0` votes the lane predicate into a uniform predicate: `UP1` is true when every lane has `P0` set, i.e. when nobody arrives. It gates the arrive-address computation `@!UP1 ULEA UR10`, so the peer, where no lane arrives, skips the `ULEA` uniformly while the leader executes it (note G.3 for the instructions; the reading of the vote is mine).

### 8.4.5 Capture `s`, advance, peek the next stage — and the discarded peek (lines 737-739)

```
    uint32_t const s = st.prod_idx;                                                          // write_stage
    advance<kStages>(st.prod_idx, st.prod_phase);
    tok = mbar_try_wait(empty_base + 8u * st.prod_idx, st.prod_phase);                     // peek the next stage, unconditional (:617)
```

`s` is the slot this k-tile writes (`write_stage`, `sm100_mma_warpspecialized.hpp:615`).

The **last** iteration of every call peeks one slot past what the call will use and throws that token away: `tok` is a local of `load_ktiles`, and the next call (or the next tile's first call) starts with its own pre-loop peek (line 732). A `try_wait` has no side effect on the barrier, so the two wasted peeks per tile (one per call) cost two `SYNCS.PHASECHK.TRANS64.TRYWAIT` per tile and nothing else.

### 8.4.6 One election, two TMA issues (lines 740-756)

```
    if (elect_one_sync()) {                                                                  // one election for the A+B pair (:619-622)
      int32_t const c0 = 64 * st.q;
```

W2 (`elect_one_sync`, explicit.cu:263-278) is `elect.sync`: exactly one lane of the converged warp gets the predicate. One election covers *both* TMA issues, the granularity CUTLASS uses (`sm100_mma_warpspecialized.hpp:619-622`) and the note fixes as the contract (E.6.6: "one `elect_one_sync()` per TMA A+B pair"). It is a *fresh* election, not `is_leader_lane`: the arriving lane and the issuing lane may differ, and the issuing lane exists in every CTA (the peer issues its loads too), whereas `is_leader_lane` is false in the peer. In SASS no `ELECT` survives here. `UTMALDG` is a uniform-datapath instruction that issues once per warp whatever the number of active lanes, so ptxas folds the election away (note D.2, D.6 item 6): the PTX form is what you write, the hardware form is what you get.

`c0 = 64 * st.q` is the innermost TMA coordinate: the k index of the first element of the box, in elements. A TMA coordinate tuple is `(innermost, outer, batch)` in **elements**, and each coordinate is a *signed* 32-bit integer (PTX ISA, `cp.async.bulk.tensor`: "The individual tensor coordinates in tensorCoords are of type .s32"). That is why `c0`, `a_row` and `b_col` are `int32_t`/`int` and W21/W22 bind them with the `"r"` constraint on `int32_t`. For the A and B maps the tuple is `(k, row, l)` (Chapter 5: the maps are encoded with mode order `(K, M, L)` / `(K, N, L)`, note Section 5.3). Elements of a box that fall outside the tensor are zero-filled: the maps are encoded with `CU_TENSOR_MAP_FLOAT_OOB_FILL_NONE` (note Section 5.3), the ISA's "Zero fill mode" ("Elements in the Bounding Box which fall outside of the tensor boundary are set to 0"). Nothing in this run is out of bounds (K = 128 x 64 exactly, note Section 10). But this is why a K that is not a multiple of 64 would still give the right D with this very loop: `k_tiles = (params.k + 63) >> 6` (explicit.cu:1112) rounds up, the last k-tile's tail columns of A and B read as zeros, and zeros add nothing to the accumulator [derived from source; the residue path is not exercised by the fixed run].

The A issue is W21 (explicit.cu:449-460, quoted in Section 6.6.3).

It is called as `tma_load_2sm_mcast_3d(&params.tma_a, full_masked_base + 8u * s, a_mcast_mask, kCacheHintEvictNormal, a_dst_base + kStageBytesA * s, c0, a_row, 0)`. Operand by operand:

| PTX operand | C++ argument | Value for this CTA | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `[%0]` destination (`shared::cluster`) | `a_dst_base + 16384 s` | `smem_base + 33792 + 16384 s + 8192 y` | This CTA's 64-row half goes to the upper (`y = 1`) or lower (`y = 0`) 8192 bytes of stage `s`. The multicast writes the *same CTA-relative offset* in every destination CTA (note B.6; Colfax: the operation "places the loaded data into the SMEMs of all CTAs specified by the bitmask"; gau-nernst, tcgen05 post ("tcgen05 for dummies"): smem layouts "must be identical across cluster ranks" for exactly this reason), so both receivers get the half in the right place. Rank bits [24,26) of this address name the issuing CTA; the TMA uses the offset part for the other receiver. |
| `[%1, {%4,%5,%6}]` tensor map + coordinates | `&params.tma_a`, `(c0, a_row, 0)` | `(64 q, 128 tm + 64 y, 0)` | 64 k values (one 128-byte row of the box), 64 rows starting at this CTA's half, batch 0. The box is `(64, 64, 1)` fp16 = 8192 B (Chapter 5, note Section 5.3: the per-CTA A box is the 128-row tile *divided by the multicast count 2*, `copy_traits_sm90_tma.hpp:996-1002`). |
| `[%2]` mbarrier | `full_masked_base + 8 s` | `(smem_base & 0xFEFFFFFF) + 8 s` = the **pair leader's** `full[s]` | `.cta_group::2` lets the barrier operand name either CTA of the pair — PTX ISA, `cp.async.bulk.tensor`: "When .cta_group::2 is specified, the mbarrier object mbar can be in shared memory of either the same CTA as the shared memory destination dstMem or in its peer-CTA"; clearing address bit 24 selects the even rank (`Sm100MmaPeerBitMask = 0xFEFFFFFF`, `include/cute/arch/copy_sm100_tma.hpp:45`). CUTLASS applies the mask at `:63/:89/:115` and, in `SM100_TMA_2SM_LOAD_MULTICAST_3D` (`:281-305`, whose `copy` member is the `:283-305` of the W21 comment), at `:292`. With multicast, each destination CTA's signal goes to the barrier at that offset in *its* pair leader — ISA: "for each destination CTA specified in the ctaMask, the mbarrier signal is sent either to the destination CTA or its peer-CTA based on the %cluster_ctarank parity of the shared memory where the mbarrier object mbar resides" (note B.6; Colfax: "a CTA can find the address of its leader CTA's mbarrier by taking its own mbarrier address and setting the 24th bit to 0"). |
| `%3` ctaMask (`.b16`, `"h"`) | `a_mcast_mask` | `0x5 << x`: `0x5` (ranks 0, 2) for `x = 0`, `0xA` (ranks 1, 3) for `x = 1` | The two CTAs with the same `x` share `tm` (Section 8.5.4) and therefore need the same 128 A rows. Bit `i` of the mask = rank `i` receives the box. CUTLASS derives the mask with `create_tma_multicast_mask<2>` (`include/cute/atom/copy_traits_sm90_tma.hpp:1468-1501`, reached through the projection overload at `:1504-1511`, which slices the `(v, m, n, k)` cluster layout at every mode but N); the explicit kernel writes the result (explicit.cu:772). |
| `%7` cache policy (`.b64`, `"l"`) | `kCacheHintEvictNormal` | `0x1000000000000000` | `TMA::CacheHintSm100::EVICT_NORMAL` (`include/cute/arch/copy_sm90_desc.hpp:194`), the default of CUTLASS's `with()` (`include/cute/atom/copy_traits_sm100_tma.hpp:182, 193`). The `.L2::cache_hint` qualifier is part of the copied string, so an operand must be supplied; EVICT_NORMAL is the neutral policy. In SASS it is the 64-bit `desc[UR32] = {0x0, 0x10000000}` (note G.3). |

The B issue (W22, explicit.cu:462-473, quoted in Section 6.6.4) is the same instruction without `.multicast::cluster` and without the mask operand.

It is called as `tma_load_2sm_3d(&params.tma_b, full_masked_base + 8u * s, kCacheHintEvictNormal, b_dst_base + kStageBytesB * s, c0, b_col, 0)`: destination `smem_base + 164864 + 8192 s` (this CTA's whole 64 x 64 B stage, no `y` term), coordinates `(64 q, 128 tn + 64 x, 0)` (64 k values, this CTA's 64 of the 128 N columns of tile `tn`), the same pair-leader barrier, no multicast. B still carries `.cta_group::2`: that is what allows the barrier operand to be the leader's even though the data is purely local.

Why does the *peer* issue loads at all, if only the leader computes? Because the 2SM MMA reads the peer's smem directly (Chapter 9, note B.6: "A rows [0,128) and B columns [0,64) of the 256x128 instruction come from the leader's smem and the remaining halves from the peer's smem at the same CTA-relative addresses"). The peer must therefore fill its own ring, slot for slot in lockstep with the leader. Both producers do that automatically because they wait on `empty[]` barriers released by the same commits.

Why the elected lane and not all 32 lanes? The PTX instruction is per-thread; 32 lanes would issue 32 copies of each box. (The epilogue's TMA *store* is deliberately issued by all 32 lanes of warp 4 because the baseline does so; ptxas turns it into one uniform `UTMASTG` anyway, Chapter 10. A different history, the same hardware outcome.)

### 8.4.7 `--n; ++st.q;` (lines 757-758)

`n` counts down the k-tiles of this call; `st.q` counts up the k index for the coordinate. In CUTLASS these are `--k_tile_count; ++k_tile_iter;` where the iterator is a plain integer for a rank-1 K mode (note B.3.1 step 11). Keeping both is what makes two calls per tile trivial: the second call starts at `st.q = 8` with `n = 120`.

---

## 8.5 Assembling a stage across the cluster

### 8.5.1 Who loads which rows and columns

Let the cluster's 256 x 256 tile start at CTA tile `(Tm, Tn)` with `Tm`, `Tn` even. Rank `r = x + 2y` works on CTA tile `(tm, tn) = (Tm + x, Tn + y)` (Section 8.5.4). Its loads:

| rank | `(x, y)` | tile `(tm, tn)` | A box rows (`a_row .. +64`) | A lands in (mask) | A offset in stage | B box columns (`b_col .. +64`) | B lands in |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | (0, 0) | `(Tm, Tn)` | `128 Tm + 0` | ranks 0, 2 (`0x5`) | `+0` | `128 Tn + 0` | rank 0 |
| 1 | (1, 0) | `(Tm+1, Tn)` | `128 (Tm+1) + 0` | ranks 1, 3 (`0xA`) | `+0` | `128 Tn + 64` | rank 1 |
| 2 | (0, 1) | `(Tm, Tn+1)` | `128 Tm + 64` | ranks 0, 2 (`0x5`) | `+8192` | `128 (Tn+1) + 0` | rank 2 |
| 3 | (1, 1) | `(Tm+1, Tn+1)` | `128 (Tm+1) + 64` | ranks 1, 3 (`0xA`) | `+8192` | `128 (Tn+1) + 64` | rank 3 |

### 8.5.2 The A-stage assembly diagram

```
 cluster tile (Tm, Tn): 256 rows of A (two tm) x 256 columns of B/D (two tn)

                 y = 0  (tn = Tn)                       y = 1  (tn = Tn + 1)
            +----------------------------+        +----------------------------+
  x = 0     | rank 0                     |        | rank 2                     |
  tm = Tm   | A stage s (16384 B):       |        | A stage s (16384 B):       |
            |  [+0    ] rows 128Tm+0..   | --+--> |  [+0    ] rows 128Tm+0..   |  <- loaded by rank 0, multicast 0x5: lands in ranks 0 and 2
            |  [+8192 ] rows 128Tm+64..  | <--+-- |  [+8192 ] rows 128Tm+64..  |  <- loaded by rank 2, multicast 0x5: lands in ranks 0 and 2
            | B stage s (8192 B):        |        | B stage s (8192 B):        |
            |  cols 128Tn + 0..63        |        |  cols 128(Tn+1) + 0..63    |  <- each CTA loads its own, no multicast
            +----------------------------+        +----------------------------+
  x = 1     | rank 1                     |        | rank 3                     |
  tm = Tm+1 |  [+0    ] rows 128(Tm+1)+0 | --+--> |  [+0    ] rows 128(Tm+1)+0 |  <- loaded by rank 1, multicast 0xA: lands in ranks 1 and 3
            |  [+8192 ] rows 128(Tm+1)+64| <--+-- |  [+8192 ] rows 128(Tm+1)+64|  <- loaded by rank 3, multicast 0xA: lands in ranks 1 and 3
            |  B cols 128Tn + 64..127    |        |  B cols 128(Tn+1)+64..127  |
            +----------------------------+        +----------------------------+
             \________ MMA pair {0,1} _______/     \________ MMA pair {2,3} _______/
              A: 256 rows [128Tm, 128Tm+256)        A: the same 256 rows
              B: 128 cols [128Tn, 128Tn+128)        B: 128 cols [128(Tn+1), +128)

 arrows = the direction of the multicast copy, from the issuing CTA into its sibling (same x, other y):
   the [+0] half is issued by the y = 0 CTA and flows left -> right into rank 2 / rank 3;
   the [+8192] half is issued by the y = 1 CTA and flows right -> left into rank 0 / rank 1
```

After the cluster's four A issues and four B issues of a stage have landed, each CTA holds the *entire* 128 x 64 A stage of its own `tm` (its own half plus the half multicast by the sibling with the same `x`) and its own 64 x 64 B half. The pair leader's `tcgen05.mma.cta_group::2` then sees A as 256 rows (leader's 128 + peer's 128) and B as 128 columns (leader's 64 + peer's 64); each CTA's TMEM receives the 128 x 128 accumulator of its own `(tm, tn)` (Chapter 9).

[derived from source + measured] This is precisely what the K4a records of the first cluster show for `q = 0` (note D.1 D8; recomputed in Section 8.7.2).

### 8.5.3 The 49152-byte ledger of one leader barrier

Take the pair `{0, 1}` and its leader's `full[s]` (rank 0's, at `0x00000400 + 8 s`). Which boxes credit it? Every box whose destination CTA has rank 0 as pair leader, i.e. every box landing in rank 0 **or** rank 1:

| box | issued by | lands in | credits rank 0's `full[s]`? | credits rank 2's `full[s]`? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A rows `128Tm + 0..63` | rank 0 | ranks 0, 2 | yes (via rank 0) | yes (via rank 2) |
| A rows `128Tm + 64..127` | rank 2 | ranks 0, 2 | yes (via rank 0) | yes (via rank 2) |
| A rows `128(Tm+1) + 0..63` | rank 1 | ranks 1, 3 | yes (via rank 1, peer-bit) | yes (via rank 3, peer-bit) |
| A rows `128(Tm+1) + 64..127` | rank 3 | ranks 1, 3 | yes (via rank 1, peer-bit) | yes (via rank 3, peer-bit) |
| B cols `128Tn + 0..63` | rank 0 | rank 0 | yes | no |
| B cols `128Tn + 64..127` | rank 1 | rank 1 | yes (peer-bit) | no |
| B cols `128(Tn+1) + 0..63` | rank 2 | rank 2 | no | yes |
| B cols `128(Tn+1) + 64..127` | rank 3 | rank 3 | no | yes (peer-bit) |
| **total** | | | **6 x 8192 = 49152** | **6 x 8192 = 49152** |

Every A box credits *both* leaders because both pairs need all 256 A rows; each B box credits one leader because B is split, not shared. Per cluster and per k-tile the TMA unit moves 8 boxes = 65536 bytes from L2 and writes 4 x 24576 = 98304 bytes of shared memory (the A halves are written twice). Without 2SM and multicast, four independent 128 x 128 CTA tiles would read 4 x (16384 + 16384) = 131072 bytes per k-tile from L2 — twice as much [my analysis].

The right-hand columns hold only because every box's barrier operand is the leader's masked address (`full_masked_base`, explicit.cu:770). With an unmasked operand the peer's three boxes would credit the peer's never-armed barrier, the leader's `full[s]` would stall at 24576 of 49152 bytes, and every run would deadlock at `q = 0`, the first row of the note's E.7.2 failure-mode table ("unmasked TMA barrier operand (peer's boxes credit the peer)"). Instead, every run completed value-equal (G.1), and the SASS shows the masked operand being issued: the baseline masks the barrier register inside each producer loop (`ULOP3 ..., 0xfefffff8` at `0x1b90`/`0x1e80` of `sass_gemm.txt`; note Section 7.5), while the explicit kernel folds the mask once onto the hoisted base before both loops (`ULOP3 ..., 0xfefffff0` at `0x0c00`) and forms `full[s]` from it per k-tile with `ULEA` (G.3; Section 2.9.3).

### 8.5.4 Why `tm % 2 == x`, hence `a_row = 128 tm + 64 y`

The comment on explicit.cu:777 says "tm % 2 == x for every tile this CTA receives (B.3.1 step 13)". Proof from the two mapping formulas:

- **Launch tile** (explicit.cu:1175-1176): `tm = 2 (blockIdx.y >> 1) + (blockIdx.x & 1)`, `tn = 2 (blockIdx.x >> 1) + (blockIdx.y & 1)`. The cluster is `(2, 2, 1)` and clusters tile the grid in `blockIdx` order, so `%cluster_ctaid.x = blockIdx.x & 1 = x` and `%cluster_ctaid.y = blockIdx.y & 1 = y` (explicit.cu:1173-1174 comments: `x == rank & 1`, `y == rank >> 1`). The mapping is the `AlongN` transpose of `possibly_transpose_work_tile` (`include/cutlass/gemm/kernel/sm100_tile_scheduler.hpp:668-677`): the cluster index of the grid's x (`blockIdx.x >> 1`) indexes N and that of y (`blockIdx.y >> 1`) indexes M, while the in-cluster offsets `blockIdx.x & 1` and `blockIdx.y & 1` stay with M and N. Hence `tm % 2 = blockIdx.x & 1 = x`.
- **CLC tile** (explicit.cu:692-693, Chapter 7): `tm = 2 (y0 >> 1) + (x0 & 1) + x`, `tn = 2 (x0 >> 1) + (y0 & 1) + y`, where `(x0, y0)` is the launch-grid id of the cancelled cluster's *first* CTA. A cluster's first CTA is cluster-aligned, so `x0` and `y0` are even (measured for all 991 cancelled responses, note D.3: "every valid first-CTA id is even"), the `& 1` terms vanish and `tm = y0 + x`, `tn = x0 + y`. Hence `tm % 2 = x` again.

So every tile the CTA processes has `tm = Tm + x` with `Tm` even and `tn = Tn + y` with `Tn` even. The two CTAs with the same `x` (ranks `x` and `x + 2`, `y = 0` and `1`) share `tm` and need the same 128 A rows `[128 tm, 128 tm + 128)`. They split the work by `y`: rank `(x, y)` loads rows `[128 tm + 64 y, +64)` and multicasts them to both. That is `a_row = 128 tm + 64 y` (explicit.cu:777), with destination `a_dst_base = smem_base + OFF_SMEM_A + 8192 y` (explicit.cu:768) so that the `y = 1` half lands in the upper 8192 bytes of the stage in both receivers. Symmetrically, the two CTAs of a pair (same `y`) share `tn` and split B by `x`: `b_col = 128 tn + 64 x` (explicit.cu:778), destination `OFF_SMEM_B + 8192 s`. There is no `x` term: each CTA keeps only its own half, and the MMA reads the other half from the peer.

CUTLASS does not select the B half by `%cluster_ctaid.x`. Its B coordinate is `128 tn + 64 V` with `V = blockIdx.x % 2`, the slice index of `TiledMma{}.get_slice(blockIdx.x % size(AtomThrID))` (`sm100_mma_warpspecialized.hpp:516`, note B.3.1 step 3; equal in value to the kernel's `cta_coord_v = rank % 2`, kernel :427), the CTA's position inside the MMA pair (note B.3.1 step 13: `tBgB = tBgB_nkl(_, tn, _, 0)`, coordinate `(0, 128*tn + 64V, 0)`; note B.4: `(64q, 128*tn + 64*(tm%2), 0)`). Its A coordinate is `256 (tm/2) + 128 V + 64 y`. The explicit kernel writes `64 x` and `128 tm + 64 y` because `V = rank % 2 = x = tm % 2` is an invariant of both tile mappings (proved above; `r = x + 2y` gives `rank % 2 = x`).

Note Section 7.5 gives the same formulas with the cluster's launch coordinate: for the launch cluster at `(CX, CY)`, rank `r` loads A rows from `256 CY + 128 x + 64 y` and B columns from `256 CX + 128 y + 64 x`.

### 8.5.5 Why A is multicast across `y` and B is not multicast at all

Two CTAs that need the same operand tile can either each load it (two L2 reads) or have one load and multicast (one L2 read, two smem writes). Inside this cluster:

- The same **A** rows are needed by the two CTAs with equal `x` (different pairs). Nothing else connects those two CTAs, so the only way to share the load without a second copy is TMA multicast. The 128-row tile is split into two 64-row halves so that both CTAs issue work and the L2 traffic is halved (note Section 5.3: `make_tma_atom_A_sm100` passes `num_multicast = 2` and the box is truncated from `(64, 128, 1)` to `(64, 64, 1)`).
- The same **B** columns are needed by the two CTAs of a pair. But the pair is already joined by the 2SM MMA, which reads both CTAs' smem; so B is *split*, each CTA loading its 64 columns, and no byte of B is written twice. Multicasting B across `x` would double the smem writes for nothing. (Colfax's cluster tutorial describes the general 1SM pattern — A multicast along cluster rows, B along cluster columns; with 2SM MMA the B sharing is absorbed by the instruction itself.) [derived from source; the design rationale is my analysis]

Options the design does *not* take: multicasting A across the pair (the two `tm` differ, so there is nothing to share) or a 4-CTA multicast (no two CTAs beyond the `x`-pairs share A). The `(2,2,1)` cluster is exactly the shape in which every operand is loaded once per cluster.
