## 8.6 producer_role (explicit.cu:762-807), line by line

```
__device__ __forceinline__ void producer_role(ExplicitGemmParams const& params, uint32_t smem_base, uint32_t x, uint32_t y,
                                              bool is_cta0, bool is_leader_lane, int k_tiles, int tm, int tn) {
  griddep_wait();                                                                              // wait_on_dependent_grids (kernel :620)
  ProducerState st;
  uint32_t thr_idx = 0, thr_phase = 1;      // CLC throttle producer (rank 0 only), 2 stages
  uint32_t clc_idx = 0, clc_phase = 0, clc_count = 0;   // CLC consumer, 2 stages
  uint32_t const a_dst_base       = smem_base + OFF_SMEM_A + kStageBytesAHalf * y;   // + 8192 * y: this CTA's 64-row half of the 128x64 A stage (B.4)
  uint32_t const b_dst_base       = smem_base + OFF_SMEM_B;
  uint32_t const full_masked_base = smem_base & kPeerBitMask;                    // (smem + 8 s) & 0xFEFFFFFF names the pair leader's full[s]
  uint32_t const empty_base       = smem_base + OFF_MAIN_EMPTY;
  uint16_t const a_mcast_mask     = static_cast<uint16_t>(0x5u << x);            // ranks x and x + 2 (create_tma_multicast_mask<2>)
  int tm_next = tm, tn_next = tn;
  uint32_t tile = 0;
  bool valid;
  do {
    int const a_row = 128 * tm + 64 * static_cast<int>(y);   // A rows of this CTA's half; tm % 2 == x for every tile this CTA receives (B.3.1 step 13)
    int const b_col = 128 * tn + 64 * static_cast<int>(x);   // B columns of this CTA's half
    st.q = 0;
    if (is_cta0) {                                                                             // throttle producer_acquire + producer_commit (kernel :632-636)
      EXPLICIT_WAIT(smem_base + OFF_THROTTLE_EMPTY + 8u * thr_idx, thr_phase, WAIT_THROTTLE_EMPTY, tile, 0u);   // blocking, no peek (PipelineAsync)
      mbar_arrive_local(smem_base + OFF_THROTTLE_FULL + 8u * thr_idx);                        // all 32 lanes (count 32)
      advance<kThrottleStages>(thr_idx, thr_phase);
    }
    int const k_tile_prologue = k_tiles < kPrologueKTiles ? k_tiles : kPrologueKTiles;        // min(Stages, k_tile_count) (kernel :629)
    load_ktiles(params, st, k_tile_prologue, smem_base, a_dst_base, b_dst_base, full_masked_base, empty_base, a_mcast_mask, is_leader_lane, a_row, b_col, tile);
    // (load_order_barrier.arrive() between the two load() calls is skipped: is_epi_load_needed is false for beta = 0)
    load_ktiles(params, st, k_tiles - k_tile_prologue, smem_base, a_dst_base, b_dst_base, full_masked_base, empty_base, a_mcast_mask, is_leader_lane, a_row, b_col, tile);
    __syncwarp();                                                                              // (kernel :664)
    valid = clc_consume<0u>(smem_base, x, y, clc_idx, clc_phase, clc_count, tm_next, tn_next, tile);   // consume response t AFTER this tile's loads (:665-670)
    tm = tm_next; tn = tn_next;                                                                // the fetched tile becomes current only here
    ++tile;
  } while (valid);
  // load_tail = producer_tail (sm90_pipeline.hpp:445-454): 8 blocking waits continuing the producer state (Section 7.10 tail 1)
  #pragma unroll
  for (int i = 0; i < kStages; ++i) {
    EXPLICIT_WAIT(empty_base + 8u * st.prod_idx, st.prod_phase, TAIL_MAINLOOP, tile, uint32_t(i));
    advance<kStages>(st.prod_idx, st.prod_phase);
  }
}
```

The call site is explicit.cu:1192, inside the `if (warp_idx == 2) {` ... `}` of :1191-1193: `producer_role(params, smem_base, x, y, is_cta0, lane_pred != 0u && is_leader, k_tiles, tm, tn);`.

### 8.6.1 `griddep_wait()`: what PDL does here (line 764)

This launch carries **no** PDL attribute (`launch_with_pdl == false`, note Section 5.4), so there are no prerequisite grids and `griddepcontrol.wait` completes at once [derived: PTX semantics + the launch configuration]. It is kept for semantics preservation: the CUTLASS kernel executes it, and if a user later launched this kernel with PDL after a producer of A/B, the wait is what makes the TMA loads read the finished data. Warps 4-7 wait in neither kernel: their only global-memory traffic is the TMA store of D, whose data derives from A and B loaded after warp 2's wait in both kernels (explicit.cu:764; kernel :620) [my analysis].

### 8.6.2 The invariants (lines 765-775)

| local | value | why it is hoisted / why this value |
|---|---|---|
| `st` | `{0, 1, 0}` | Section 8.3. |
| `thr_idx, thr_phase` | `{0, 1}` | Throttle *producer* state (2 slots); producers start at phase 1, as in Section 8.3, so CTA 0's first two tiles pass the throttle wait (Section 8.6.4). |
| `clc_idx, clc_phase, clc_count` | `{0, 0, 0}` | CLC *consumer* state (2 slots): consumers start at phase 0 and block until the first response lands (Chapter 7). |
| `a_dst_base` | `smem_base + 33792 + 8192 y` | `OFF_SMEM_A = 33792` (explicit.cu:154) plus this CTA's half offset; `kStageBytesAHalf = 8192` (explicit.cu:117, "equal to kStageBytesB by coincidence of the tile shape" — the half of a 128 x 64 fp16 tile happens to equal a 64 x 64 fp16 tile). |
| `b_dst_base` | `smem_base + 164864` | `OFF_SMEM_B` (explicit.cu:155). |
| `full_masked_base` | `smem_base & 0xFEFFFFFF` | `kPeerBitMask` (explicit.cu:187). Because `OFF_MAIN_FULL = 0`, `full[s]` is `smem_base + 8 s`, and masking the base once equals masking every `(smem_base + 8 s)`: the mask touches only bit 24, and `8 s <= 56` cannot carry into it from a base whose low 24 bits are `0x400`. Measured values: `0x00000400` for ranks 0 and 1, `0x02000400` for ranks 2 and 3 (note D.1 D5: `base & 0xFEFFFFFF` is the even partner's base). nvcc folds known-zero low bits into the constant: `0xFEFFFFF8` in the CUTLASS kernel (three alignment bits of an 8-byte barrier, note D.6 item 2) and `0xFEFFFFF0` here (`and.b32 ..., -16777232`, since the base itself is masked; note G.3); the results are identical for these addresses. The source comment at explicit.cu:187 ("nvcc folds it to 0xFEFFFFF8") holds only for the epilogue's accumulator-release site (`0x44c0`, note G.3), not for the producer's SASS, whose fold is the `0xFEFFFFF0` above. |
| `empty_base` | `smem_base + 64` | `OFF_MAIN_EMPTY` (explicit.cu:140). |
| `a_mcast_mask` | `0x5 << x` (16-bit) | Section 8.4.6. The `"h"` constraint needs a `uint16_t`. |
| `tm_next, tn_next, tile, valid` | `tm, tn, 0, -` | The CLC consume writes the *next* tile into `tm_next/tn_next`; the current tile stays in `tm/tn` until the end of the loop body (Section 8.6.7). `tile` is the tile counter, used only by the trace. |

Hoisting these is not an optimisation nvcc needed help with. It is the discipline of note D.7 ("the explicit kernel should keep loop-invariant operands few (descriptor bases, masks, barrier bases) and let ptxas keep them uniform"), restated as a rule in note E.6.6. In the measured SASS, four loop invariants (only one of them, the mask, from this table) are nevertheless re-materialised per k-tile, in five instructions (the B tensor-map address, the mask insert `UPRMT ..., 0x5410`, the z coordinate, `0xc000`). They are the largest part of the *net* +6 instructions over the baseline's loop (note G.3). Section 8.9 lists all eight and argues that they cost nothing; Section 12.5.2 gives the full ledger against the baseline's loop.

### 8.6.3 Per-tile setup (lines 777-779)

`a_row` and `b_col` are recomputed from the current `(tm, tn)` (Section 8.5.4) and `st.q` is reset to 0 — but `st.prod_idx/prod_phase` are not touched: the ring continues.

### 8.6.4 The throttle producer on CTA 0 (lines 783-787)

```
    if (is_cta0) {                                                                             // throttle producer_acquire + producer_commit (kernel :632-636)
      EXPLICIT_WAIT(smem_base + OFF_THROTTLE_EMPTY + 8u * thr_idx, thr_phase, WAIT_THROTTLE_EMPTY, tile, 0u);   // blocking, no peek (PipelineAsync)
      mbar_arrive_local(smem_base + OFF_THROTTLE_FULL + 8u * thr_idx);                        // all 32 lanes (count 32)
      advance<kThrottleStages>(thr_idx, thr_phase);
    }
```

Barriers: `throttle_full[2]` at `OFF_THROTTLE_FULL = 304`, `throttle_empty[2]` at `OFF_THROTTLE_EMPTY = 320`, both count 32 (explicit.cu:148-149, 185; initialised by warp 3, explicit.cu:1155-1162). The arrive is `producer_commit`, one `mbarrier.arrive.shared::cta.b64` per thread (`sm90_pipeline.hpp:1193-1196`); hence "all 32 lanes (count 32)" and W9 at explicit.cu:345-354.

**Why warp 2 rather than warp 0, and why a blocking wait.** Tying the query to warp 2's progress issues it as early as the "one ahead" rule (Section 4.4.5) allows, which gives the response (median latency 1.4 us, note D.3) the most time to arrive before anyone needs it [my analysis]. The wait is blocking, without a peek, because it almost always passes immediately and happens once per tile; a peek and its token test would add instructions for a wait that almost never blocks [my analysis; CUTLASS just calls `PipelineAsync::producer_acquire` with its default `WaitAgain` token, `sm90_pipeline.hpp:1110`].

**How far ahead the release is.** For every tile `t >= 2`, the release warp 2 depends on (the scheduler's release of slot `t % 2` after tile `t - 2`, Section 4.3.5) is about two tile periods old: about 2 x 27.8 us = 55.6 us in the Release run (0.889354 ms over 32 tiles), 2 x 31.9 us in the trace build (note D.3's per-tile time) [the `t - 2` relation is derived from the code; the per-tile times are measured; the product is my inference]. Note D.3's 28.8-37.7 us (median 30.8 us) is a *different* number: the scheduler's gap from consuming response `n` to issuing query `n + 1`, i.e. how long the scheduler sits in its `throttle_full` wait per tile. That measurement shows that the scheduler, not warp 2, is the one that waits.

**Why two slots rather than one.** With one slot, warp 2 at tile `t + 1` would block until the scheduler had woken up and consumed tile `t`'s arrive. With two, warp 2 can arrive for tile `t + 1` before the scheduler has consumed tile `t`'s, so the producer is never gated on the scheduler's wake-up latency while the scheduler is still held to one query ahead [my analysis; the 2 is the baseline's stage count, note Section 7.2, `kThrottleStages = 2` at explicit.cu:110].

### 8.6.5 `k_tile_prologue` and the two `load_ktiles` calls (lines 788-791)

```
    int const k_tile_prologue = k_tiles < kPrologueKTiles ? k_tiles : kPrologueKTiles;        // min(Stages, k_tile_count) (kernel :629)
```

`kPrologueKTiles = kStages = 8` (explicit.cu:107, 115); `k_tiles = (params.k + 63) >> 6 = 128` (explicit.cu:1112). The first call issues `min(8, k_tiles)` k-tiles — one full pass over the ring, which never blocks on a fresh ring (Section 8.3) — and the second issues the remaining `k_tiles - 8 = 120`. Why two calls? In CUTLASS, between them sits

```
        if (do_load_order_arrive) {
          load_order_barrier.arrive();
          do_load_order_arrive = false;
        }
```

When `beta != 0`, the epilogue's C-load warp (warp 3) may start its TMA loads of C only after the mainloop producer has issued its first pass of loads over the ring, so that the mainloop gets a head start on the TMA unit and L2 [my analysis; CUTLASS states no rationale]. For `beta = 0` the arrive is skipped (`is_epi_load_needed` is false; the explicit kernel does not even initialise the load-order barrier, explicit.cu:141-143, "reserved, not initialised"). But the two `load` calls remain in the baseline, and each becomes its own rolled loop in SASS: "two rolled k-tile loops (8 and 120 iterations)" (note D.2, measured). The explicit kernel keeps two calls for the same reason it keeps `#pragma unroll 1`: the instruction-stream shape is part of the contract, and the semantics are identical either way (the state lives in `st`, and the second call re-peeks before its loop, Section 8.4.5). For `k_tiles <= 8` the second call runs zero iterations (its pre-loop peek still executes once, harmlessly); for `k_tiles == 0` both do.

### 8.6.6 `__syncwarp()` (line 792)

W37, `bar.warp.sync -1`. CUTLASS: "Sync warp to prevent non-participating threads entering next wave early" (`sm100_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:663-664`). In the PTX model only the elected lane executed the TMA issues; the other 31 lanes could run ahead into the CLC consume while the elected lane was still issuing its TMA loads. The `__syncwarp` reconverges the warp first. In SASS it produces no instruction (note D.2: "warp 2's per-tile `__syncwarp()` (`ptx.txt:1026`) produced no instruction") because ptxas folded the election into uniform instructions, leaving no divergence to repair. You write it for the PTX contract.

### 8.6.7 `clc_consume` after the loads (lines 793-795)

```
    valid = clc_consume<0u>(smem_base, x, y, clc_idx, clc_phase, clc_count, tm_next, tn_next, tile);   // consume response t AFTER this tile's loads (:665-670)
    tm = tm_next; tn = tn_next;                                                                // the fetched tile becomes current only here
    ++tile;
```

`clc_consume` (Chapter 7) waits on this CTA's `clc_full[idx]`, decodes the 16-byte response, fences, arrives remotely on CTA 0's `clc_empty[idx]` (this warp's 32 arrivals are part of the 800), advances the 2-slot state and, if the response is a cancelled cluster, writes the next tile into `tm_next/tn_next`. The template argument `0u` means "no record" (explicit.cu:675; with the toggle off, `K_CLC_SCHED_KIND` and `K_CLC_MMA_KIND` are `0u` as well, :238-239).

**Why after the loads?** If warp 2 consumed response `t` *before* issuing tile `t`'s loads, it would stall ~1.4 us at every tile start while the ring drains, a bubble the MMA warp would feel eight k-tiles later. Consuming *after* the 128 k-tiles of loads (roughly 28 us, because the ring paces the producer) finds the response long since landed, so the consume is free. The baseline's comment and code order (`fetch_next_work` at `:665` after the loads; `:742` before `mma()`; `:878` before `store()`) is preserved exactly. [derived from source; the latency reasoning is my analysis supported by note D.3's measurements]

**Why `tm = tm_next` only here.** `a_row`/`b_col` for the current tile were computed from `tm/tn` at the top of the body and must not change under the loads; the fetched tile becomes current at the end of the body, as in CUTLASS (`work_tile_info = next_work_tile_info` at `:670`). The loop ends when a response is *not cancelled* (`valid == false`): no unstarted clusters remain anywhere in the grid (Chapter 7).

### 8.6.8 The tail: eight blocking waits, parity 1 (lines 797-806)

```
  #pragma unroll
  for (int i = 0; i < kStages; ++i) {
    EXPLICIT_WAIT(empty_base + 8u * st.prod_idx, st.prod_phase, TAIL_MAINLOOP, tile, uint32_t(i));
    ...
    advance<kStages>(st.prod_idx, st.prod_phase);
  }
```

This is `load_tail` -> `PipelineTmaAsync::producer_tail` (`sm100_mma_warpspecialized.hpp:633-640`, `sm90_pipeline.hpp:448-454`: `for (count < Stages) { empty_barrier_ptr_[state.index()].wait(state.phase()); ++state; }`). It **continues the producer state** where the loop left it (note Section 7.2 warns against applying one parity to all eight barriers).

**Proof that every tail step waits parity 1 for any tile count.** Let `n_tiles` be the number of tiles this CTA processed (32 or 31, and 19 for the probed cluster, in the traced run, note D.3; it is spelled out because the lecture's `T` is the TMEM base of Chapters 9-10). After `n_tiles` tiles the producer has made `N = 128 n_tiles` steps. Step `i` of the tail (`i = 0..7`) is step `N + i` of the state and waits on `empty[(N + i) % 8]` with parity `1 ^ (((N + i) / 8) & 1)`. Since `128 n_tiles % 8 = 0`, `(N + i) % 8 = i` and `(N + i) / 8 = 16 n_tiles` for `i < 8`; `16 n_tiles` is even for every `n_tiles`, so the parity is `1 ^ 0 = 1` and the slot is `i`: the tail waits on `empty[0..7]` in order, each with parity 1. [derived] Measured: 1518 `K_TAIL` records in the traced run, 8 `TAIL_MAINLOOP` per CTA with `idx 0..7` and parity 1 in every one of the 132 CTAs ("every mainloop tail step waited parity 1 (`k_tail_mainloop_parity` PASS)", note G.1).

**What parity 1 means at that moment.** Stage `i` was used `16 n_tiles` times (16 times per tile: 128 k-tiles over 8 slots), each use completing one phase of `empty[i]` (two commit arrivals). The barrier is in phase `16 n_tiles`; the most recently completed phase is `16 n_tiles - 1`, odd, parity 1. `try_wait.parity(1)` therefore returns true exactly when the *last* use of stage `i` has been released by both pair leaders — the commits for k-tiles `120 + i` of the final tile. In a hypothetical shape where some stage is never used, its barrier is still in phase 0 and parity 1 passes immediately; CUTLASS's own comment: "if the stage was never used then would just be acquired since the phase was still inverted" (`sm100_mma_warpspecialized.hpp:634-639`). Hard-coding parity 1 would be correct for this shape and wrong in general: 72 k-tiles per tile, for example, gives `9 n_tiles` passes, odd after an odd number of tiles, so the tail would then have to wait parity 0. Continuing the state is always correct.

**Why the tail exists.** There is no cluster-wide barrier at kernel exit (note Section 7.10). Two things would go wrong without it:

1. The last `tcgen05.commit` of each pair leader multicasts arrivals (mask `0xF`) into *this* CTA's `empty[]`; if this CTA had exited, a remote `mbarrier.arrive` would target freed shared memory (undefined; note B.6, `mbarrier.*.shared::cluster` rule).
2. Worse, the 2SM MMA of this CTA's pair leader reads this CTA's smem stages directly. (The leader of the *other* pair reads nothing from our smem; what it reads of ours is the A half our producer wrote into its sibling's slots.) Waiting on `empty[0..7]`, released only after *both* leaders' MMAs have finished reading every stage, guarantees that nobody is still reading shared memory this CTA is about to give up. The peer's warp 0 has no tail of its own on this ring (it never consumed it), so warp 2's eight waits are the only guard on this ring, though not the only one holding a peer past its leader's last MMA (the peer's epilogue waits on the last tile's `acc_full`, explicit.cu:1030-1034, and the dealloc handshake, guard (4), follows). [derived from source; note Section 7.10 "guard (1)"]

**Why `#pragma unroll` here (explicit.cu:798), when both k-tile loops are `#pragma unroll 1`.** The tail mirrors `producer_tail`'s `for (count < Stages)` over a compile-time bound, which nvcc unrolls in the baseline as well ("`producer_tail` = 8 unrolled waits", note D.2), and note E.6.6 makes the shape part of the contract ("tails as unrolled `for` over compile-time `Stages`"). The tail runs once per kernel, so its code size is irrelevant, and unrolling removes the counter and the back-branch. What remains is eight waits, each followed by `advance`'s state update. In SASS that is eight waits with the `UIADD3 +1; UISETP.NE.U32 ..., 8; USEL; LOP3 ... 0x3c` sequence between them, and the warp's `EXIT` follows the last. Baseline: tail `0x2660-0x2a60`, the last wait with an inline retry loop, `EXIT` at `0x2a90` (note D.2). Explicit kernel: warp 2's `EXIT` at `0x1980` (note G.3); the note records no start address for the explicit tail.

## 8.7 Worked examples and counts

Addresses are 32-bit `shared::cta` values with `smem_base = 0x400 + (r << 24)`; `OFF_SMEM_A = 33792 = 0x8400`, `OFF_SMEM_B = 164864 = 0x28400`, stage strides `0x4000` (A) and `0x2000` (B), A half offset `0x2000 y`.

### 8.7.1 Example A: the banner's example, recomputed, and the whole cluster around it

**The formula check.** Feed the banner's inputs — rank 1 (`smem_base = 0x01000400`, `x = 1`, `y = 0`), tile `(5, 9)`, `q = 7` — into the code: `s = 7`, `c0 = 448`, `a_row = 128 x 5 + 0 = 640`, `b_col = 128 x 9 + 64 = 1216`; `a_dst_base = 0x01000400 + 0x8400 + 0 = 0x01008800`, A destination `0x01008800 + 7 x 0x4000 = 0x01024800`, multicast `0xA` -> the same offset in rank 3, `0x03024800`; `b_dst_base = 0x01028800`, B destination `0x01028800 + 7 x 0x2000 = 0x01036800`; barrier `(0x01000400 & 0xFEFFFFFF) + 56 = 0x00000438` = rank 0's `full[7]`. Rank 2's A half (`a_dst_base = 0x0200A800`) goes to `0x0200A800 + 0x1C000 = 0x02026800` in itself and `0x00026800` in rank 0. All five numbers of the banner (explicit.cu:718-719) are reproduced.

**One caveat about the inputs.** By Section 8.5.4, a `y = 0` CTA receives only even `tn` (`tn = Tn + y` with `Tn` even), so tile `(5, 9)` can never be rank 1's in this run; it is rank 3's tile of cluster tile `(Tm, Tn) = (4, 8)` (for which `a_row` would be `704`, not `640`). The banner's line is a correct exercise of the *address formulas* on arbitrary inputs, not a reachable state; the measured records of Section 8.7.2 are. [derived from the mapping formulas]

**The reachable cluster containing (5, 9):** `(Tm, Tn) = (4, 8)`, tiles rank 0 `(4, 8)`, rank 1 `(5, 8)`, rank 2 `(4, 9)`, rank 3 `(5, 9)`; `q = 7`: `s = 7`, within-tile parity `1 ^ ((7 >> 3) & 1) = 1`, `c0 = 448`. Destinations and barriers do not depend on the tile:

| rank | `(tm, tn)` | `a_row` | A destination (`a_dst_base + 7 x 0x4000`) | A lands in | `b_col` | B destination (`b_dst_base + 7 x 0x2000`) | barrier operand (`full_masked_base + 56`) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | (4, 8) | 512 | `0x00008800 + 0x1C000 = 0x00024800` | ranks 0, 2 | 1024 | `0x00028800 + 0xE000 = 0x00036800` | `0x00000438` (rank 0's `full[7]`) |
| 1 | (5, 8) | 640 | `0x01008800 + 0x1C000 = 0x01024800` | ranks 1, 3 | 1088 | `0x01028800 + 0xE000 = 0x01036800` | `0x00000438` (rank 0's `full[7]`) |
| 2 | (4, 9) | 576 | `0x0200A800 + 0x1C000 = 0x02026800` | ranks 0, 2 | 1152 | `0x02028800 + 0xE000 = 0x02036800` | `0x02000438` (rank 2's `full[7]`) |
| 3 | (5, 9) | 704 | `0x0300A800 + 0x1C000 = 0x03026800` | ranks 1, 3 | 1216 | `0x03028800 + 0xE000 = 0x03036800` | `0x02000438` (rank 2's `full[7]`) |

After the stage lands, rank 0's stage 7 holds A rows `[512, 576)` at `0x24800` (its own box) and `[576, 640)` at `0x26800` (rank 2's box) = the 128 rows of `tm = 4`; rank 1 holds rows `[640, 768)` = `tm = 5`. Pair `{0, 1}`'s MMA reads A rows `[512, 768)` and B columns `[1024, 1152)` (rank 0's `[1024, 1088)` + rank 1's `[1088, 1152)`) — the two CTA tiles `(4, 8)` and `(5, 8)`; pair `{2, 3}` reads the same A rows and B columns `[1152, 1280)` — tiles `(4, 9)` and `(5, 9)`.

## 8.8 What the TMA unit does on write: SWIZZLE_128B

The producer passes *linear* destination addresses (`a_dst_base + 16384 s`, `b_dst_base + 8192 s`) and never computes a swizzled offset, yet the bytes do not land linearly: both tensor maps are encoded with `CU_TENSOR_MAP_SWIZZLE_128B` (Chapter 5; note Section 5.3, measured D3), and the UMMA descriptors declare `layout_type = 2` = SWIZZLE_128B (`include/cute/arch/mma_sm100_desc.hpp:114`; explicit.cu:171 `kSmemDescHi`). Writer and reader agree on the same permutation, so the kernel can be oblivious to it (explicit.cu:203: "applied by the TMA unit on write and by the UMMA unit on read (SWIZZLE_128B); the kernel never computes it").

### 8.8.1 `Swizzle<3,4,3>`

CuTe's `Swizzle<BBits, MBase, SShift>` (`include/cute/swizzle.hpp:54-68`) XORs `BBits` bits of an offset, located `MBase` bits up (`zzz_msk`), with the `BBits` bits `SShift` further up (`yyy_msk`): `apply(o) = o ^ ((o & yyy_msk) >> SShift)`. For `<3,4,3>`: `zzz_msk = 0b111 << 4 = 0x70` (bits [4,7)), `yyy_msk = 0b111 << 7 = 0x380` (bits [7,10)); explicit.cu:204 asserts exactly `yyy_msk == 0x380` and `num_shft == 3`. On a byte address:

```
 physical = pre ^ (((pre >> 7) & 7) << 4)
```

Bits [4,7) are the index of the 16-byte chunk inside a 128-byte row; bits [7,10) are the row index modulo 8. So: **inside each 1024-byte atom (8 rows x 128 B), chunk `c` of row `r` is stored at chunk position `c ^ (r % 8)`.** The CUDA Programming Guide states the same rule for the 128B mode as `smem[y][((y + offset) % 8) ^ x]` with `x` the 16-byte unit, `y` the row, and `offset = (smem_ptr / 128) % 8` (its Table 24, "Swizzle Pattern Pointer Offset Formula and Index Relation"). `offset` is the row-within-atom position of the buffer's *start address*; it is added to the row index because the hardware swizzles on absolute address bits, not on offsets from the buffer's start. For a 1024-byte-aligned base, `offset = 0`, and the Guide's formula collapses to the `chunk ^ (row % 8)` above; every base in this kernel is such a base (Section 8.8.3). The pattern repeats after 8 rows = 1024 bytes.

### 8.8.2 One stage, drawn

Plain (pre-swizzle) byte offset of A element `(m, k)` in stage `s`: `16384 s + 128 m + 2 k` (K-major: 64 fp16 = 128 B per row `m`; the CuTe layout at explicit.cu:124-125, `((_128,_16),_1,_4,(_1,_8)) : ((_64,_1),_0,_16,(_0,_8192))` in elements, says the same: row stride 64 elements, k-block stride 16 elements = 32 B, stage stride 8192 elements). For B element `(n, k)`: `8192 s + 128 n + 2 k`. Since `2 k < 128`, bits [7,10) of the plain offset are `m % 8`, so the physical byte is `16384 s + 128 m + ((2 k) ^ ((m % 8) << 4))`; the 16-byte chunk `k >> 3` of row `m` sits at chunk `(k >> 3) ^ (m % 8)`.

```
 one 1024-byte atom = rows m..m+7 of a stage (128 B each); entries = logical chunk (8 fp16 = 16 B) stored at that physical position

 physical chunk ->    0   1   2   3   4   5   6   7        <- the 8 x 16 B = 128 B of one row
 row m%8 = 0        [ 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 ]      k 0-7, 8-15, ..., 56-63 in order
 row m%8 = 1        [ 1 | 0 | 3 | 2 | 5 | 4 | 7 | 6 ]
 row m%8 = 2        [ 2 | 3 | 0 | 1 | 6 | 7 | 4 | 5 ]
 row m%8 = 3        [ 3 | 2 | 1 | 0 | 7 | 6 | 5 | 4 ]
 row m%8 = 4        [ 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 ]
 row m%8 = 5        [ 5 | 4 | 7 | 6 | 1 | 0 | 3 | 2 ]
 row m%8 = 6        [ 6 | 7 | 4 | 5 | 2 | 3 | 0 | 1 ]
 row m%8 = 7        [ 7 | 6 | 5 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 1 | 0 ]

 A stage s = 16 such atoms (rows 0-7, 8-15, ..., 120-127), 16384 B, at smem_base + 0x8400 + 0x4000 s
   the y = 0 half (rows 0-63) = atoms 0-7 at +0, the y = 1 half (rows 64-127) = atoms 8-15 at +8192: each multicast box is 8 whole atoms
 B stage s = 8 atoms (rows 0-63), 8192 B, at smem_base + 0x28400 + 0x2000 s
 k-block kb of a k-tile = logical chunks 2 kb and 2 kb + 1 of every row (32 B = 16 fp16): the UMMA descriptor's start address advances by 32 B per kb
```

Why this pattern? Shared memory is banked 32 x 4 B = 128 B wide, so one row covers all banks and a *column* of chunks (the same `k` range in 8 consecutive rows) would hit the same four banks eight times. XORing the chunk index with the row index spreads those eight accesses over all eight chunk positions, i.e. all 32 banks — the CUDA Programming Guide's "each matrix element is from a different bank for both the rows and columns, and so without any bank conflicts". The UMMA reads core matrices of 8 rows x 16 B at a time; with the swizzle it reads them conflict-free [derived; the UMMA's internal access pattern is the hardware's business].

### 8.8.3 Why 1024-byte alignment, and why the kernel never computes the swizzle

Both units apply the XOR to **absolute shared-memory address bits**, not to offsets within a box or a tile. The row index they use is address bits [7,10). For that to equal `m % 8`, the stage base must contribute zeros in bits [7,10): `base % 1024 == 0`. The kernel guarantees it three times over. `OFF_SMEM_A = 33792 = 33 x 1024` and `OFF_SMEM_B = 164864 = 161 x 1024` (explicit.cu:162, `static_assert(OFF_SMEM_A % 1024 == 0 && OFF_SMEM_B % 1024 == 0, "SW128 stage bases need 1 KiB alignment (Section 7.5)")`). The stage strides 16384 and 8192 and the half offset 8192 are multiples of 1024. The dynamic base's low 24 bits are `0x400 = 1 x 1024` (measured, note D.1 D5). The kernel declares no static `__shared__` (explicit.cu Section 10 banner), so the dynamic buffer starts right after the 1 KiB of system-reserved shared memory. Which of these is hardware-mandatory and which is a design choice? The CUDA Programming Guide's hard requirement for a swizzled TMA destination is **128-byte** alignment ("When using TMA, the shared memory is required to be aligned to 128 bytes"; its Table 25, stated for Compute Capability 9, lists "Shared memory alignment" 128 bytes for every swizzle mode); 1024 is only a recommendation ("For simplicity shared memory should be aligned according to the number of bytes after which the swizzle pattern repeats"). A destination that is 128-byte but not 1024-byte aligned is legal for the TMA: the pattern is simply shifted by `offset = (addr / 128) % 8` rows (Section 8.8.1). The reader is what makes 1024 a *hard* requirement for this kernel. The UMMA descriptor carries a 3-bit `base_offset` field (`mma_sm100_desc.hpp:112-113`) precisely for a swizzle pattern whose start address has non-zero bits [7,10) (PTX ISA 9.7.18.4.1: the base offset is 0 when the pattern starts on a 1024-byte boundary, otherwise `(pattern start addr >> 0x7) & 0x7`). CUTLASS leaves it at 0 (`constexpr uint8_t base_offset = 0; desc.base_offset_ = base_offset;`, `mma_sm100_desc.hpp:757-758`), and the explicit kernel's `kSmemDescHi = 0x40004040` (explicit.cu:171) has zeros in those bits too (Chapter 9). With `base_offset = 0` the UMMA assumes the stage has `offset = 0`, so the TMA side must be handed a base with `offset = 0` as well: 1024-byte aligned. The dependency chain: the TMA requires 128 B; the UMMA with `base_offset = 0` requires 1024 B; the kernel chooses `base_offset = 0`, as CUTLASS does, and therefore pays 1024-byte alignment on `OFF_SMEM_A`, `OFF_SMEM_B`, the stage strides and the dynamic base [derived from source; the Guide's two statements are quoted from its async-copies page].

Because the permutation is a function of the address, the UMMA can start a k-block *inside* an atom: the descriptor's start address `+ 32 kb` has bits [4,7) = `2 kb`, which the hardware XORs with the row bits of each row it fetches, landing on the right chunks. This is why the producer can write 64-wide k-tiles with one box while the MMA consumes them in four 16-wide k-blocks without anybody shuffling data. The kernel's only swizzle arithmetic is the epilogue's `Swizzle<2,5,2>` on *its own* `st.shared` stores (Chapter 10), where the writer is software; here both writer and reader are hardware.

### 8.8.4 Why the k-tile is 64

For `CU_TENSOR_MAP_SWIZZLE_128B` the inner box dimension may be at most 128 bytes. The CUDA Programming Guide's Table 25 gives "Shared box's inner dimension <= 128 bytes" for the 128B mode, and the driver enforces it: the CUDA Driver API reference for `cuTensorMapEncodeTiled` states "CU_TENSOR_MAP_SWIZZLE_128B* require the bounding box inner dimension to be <= 128" and lists `CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_VALUE` among its returns. CuTe performs *no* check of this rule: its encoder (`copy_traits_sm90_tma.hpp:1004-1013`) asserts only the generic box limits, `1 <= boxDim[i] <= 256` (the Driver API's "must be non-zero and less than or equal to 256"), and `:1015-1024` the `1..8` element-stride limits. 128 bytes of fp16 is `128 / 2 = 64` elements, so one TMA box covers at most 64 k values, and the UMMA's SW128 K-major canonical layout is exactly 8 rows x 64 fp16. The name to follow is `UMMA::Layout_K_SW128_Atom<ElementType>`, which `sm100_smem_selector` (`include/cutlass/gemm/collective/builders/sm100_common.inl:82`, the branch at `:116-117`) picks because `BLK_K = 64` is a multiple of the atom's K extent. That name is an alias (`using cute::GMMA::Layout_K_SW128_Atom;`, `include/cute/atom/mma_traits_sm100.hpp:71`) of the definition in namespace `SM90::GMMA`, so a reader searching for the UMMA name must hop through the alias. The definition is `ComposedLayout<Swizzle<3,4,3>, smem_ptr_flag, Layout<Shape<_8,_1024>,Stride<_1024,_1>>>` in bits (`include/cute/atom/mma_traits_sm90_gmma.hpp:84`) and typed at `:104`. A k-tile of 64 is therefore the widest unit that one swizzled TMA box and one SW128 UMMA atom both span in K, and the unit one `mbarrier` phase accounts for; four `tcgen05.mma` of K = 16 consume it (Chapter 3 for the design arithmetic, Chapter 9 for the descriptor increments). The 64 x 64 boxes respect the 256-element limit with room to spare.

---

## 8.9 The footprint of warp 2, and why its loop length does not matter

What the loop keeps live per k-tile: the slot index and phase (`st.prod_idx`, `st.prod_phase`), the token, `n`, `st.q`, the five hoisted invariants of Section 8.6.2 (two destination bases, the masked barrier base, the empty base, the mask), the cache hint (64-bit), two tensor-map addresses (constant-bank addresses, `&params.tma_a/b`), `a_row`, `b_col`, and the two predicates (`is_leader_lane`, the fresh election). Nothing is indexed at run time and nothing lives in local memory: the whole kernel reports `REG 26, LOCAL 0, STACK 0` (note G.3, measured). [my analysis: the 26 is set by the epilogue warps, which hold 16 `tcgen05.ld` results plus store addresses live at once (`alpha` and `beta` sit in uniform registers, Section 11.4.1), the largest per-thread working set in the kernel, not by this warp, whose state is almost entirely uniform.]

The explicit-only instructions in the producer loop, relative to the baseline (eight by note G.3's count; the matching of Section 12.5.2 counts nine, adding the wait-block `ULEA UR4`), are five re-materialisations of four loop invariants (the 49152 immediate, the `tma_b` parameter address pair, the multicast-mask insert and the z coordinate), the warp vote `VOTEU.ALL UP1, P0`, the predicated arrive-address `@!UP1 ULEA UR10` and the masked-`full[s]` `ULEA UR17`; all but the lane-predicated `MOV R5` and the `VOTEU.ALL` are uniform-datapath instructions (Section 8.4.2 for the term). The issue order wait -> `expect_tx` -> peek -> TMA A -> TMA B is identical in the explicit and baseline loops.

The k-tile budget is about 426 cycles (from the CUTLASS baseline's 0.888 ms, the working number of Chapter 3, Section 3.9.2; the explicit kernel's own median gives 427, Chapter 9, Section 9.8). Within it the tensor core executes four 256 x 128 x 16 MMAs (256 cycles at peak, Section 3.9.2) and the TMA/L2 delivers 24576 bytes per CTA; which resource sets the 426 is the open question of Chapter 3, Section 3.9 (shared-memory bandwidth is the leading hypothesis). The producer warp may run eight k-tiles (about 1.7 us) ahead of the MMA, and after the first ring pass it is mostly waiting for a slot rather than working (my analysis: 37 loop instructions per k-tile against that budget; the wait fraction was not measured). What hides the TMA round trip is the ring depth, not the loop length: 8 stages, all the shared memory left after the epilogue and the barrier carve-out (Chapter 3, Section 3.4.1).

---

## 8.10 Carrying this to other kernels

- **One barrier per shared resource, owned by the consumer that needs the whole resource.** The pair leader's `full[s]` sums the pair's bytes because the leader's MMA is the single consumer of the pair's stage. When you design a multi-CTA operand, ask "who issues the instruction that needs all of it?" and route every `complete_tx` there; then `expect_tx = sum of everything that lands in the consumer's domain`, and the arrival count is the number of distinct *arrivers*, not of boxes.
- **Multicast where CTAs share data and nothing else joins them; split where an instruction already spans the CTAs.** A across `y` (shared `tm`, no other link), B across the pair (joined by `cta_group::2`).
- **Peek-then-wait, and continue the state across tiles and into the tail.** The parity bookkeeping is the entire correctness of a ring; compute it from a running counter, never from the tile shape.
- **Keep producers oblivious to layout transforms that hardware applies symmetrically.** The TMA writes swizzled, the UMMA reads swizzled; your job is alignment (1024 B) and box shape (inner dim <= 128 B), not XORs.
- **Order the slow consume after the fast issue.** Any per-tile handshake whose latency is comparable to a pipeline refill (the CLC response here) belongs after the work that keeps the pipeline busy.
- **Tails are not optional in cluster kernels.** Every barrier that a remote CTA can still arrive on, and every smem region a remote instruction can still read, needs a wait before `EXIT`.

---

# Chapter 9. The Engine: mma_role (Warp 0)

## 9.1 Where the engine sits

Chapter 8 left the mainloop producer (warp 2) filling an 8-stage ring of A and B tiles in shared memory and signalling the pair leader's `full[s]` barrier with 49152 transaction bytes per stage. Chapter 10 will take the finished accumulator out of TMEM. Between them sits warp 0: the only warp that issues MMAs to the tensor core. Its job is simple to state and exacting to get right:

1. once per CTA: allocate the whole TMEM of the pair, publish the base address to the epilogue warps, build the two descriptor bases;
2. once per tile, leader only: wait until an accumulator stage is free, then for each of the 128 k-tiles wait for the stage to be full, issue four 2SM MMAs, release the stage to all four producers; finally hand the accumulator stage to both CTAs' epilogues;
3. once per tile, both CTAs: consume one CLC response and advance the accumulator state;
4. at the end: release the allocation permit, drain the accumulator pipeline, shake hands with the peer, deallocate.

The whole role is explicit.cu:871-975. We read it in that order.

---

## 9.2 The banner, sentence by sentence (explicit.cu:871-880)

872://   Both CTAs of the pair: tcgen05.alloc 512 TMEM columns (cta_group::2: one allocation for the pair, the result written to smem + 384 of
873://   both CTAs), bar.arrive 6,160 to release the epilogue warps, and the accumulator producer state; at the end relinquish + dealloc.
874://   The PAIR LEADER only, per tile: wait acc_empty[st] (count 256 = 2 x 128 epilogue threads released stage st), then per k-tile:
875://     wait full[s] (count 1 + 49152 tx bytes, section 6) -> 4 x tcgen05.mma.cta_group::2 (one per 16-k block; the first of the tile with
876://     scale_c = 0 overwrites the accumulator, the rest accumulate) -> tcgen05.commit to empty[s] of all four CTAs (mask 0xF, count 2 per CTA)
877://   then tcgen05.commit to acc_full[st] of the pair (mask 0x3 << 2y) and advance the accumulator stage (both CTAs advance the state).
878://   TMEM address = (lane << 16) | column; tmem_c = T + 128 st with T = 0 measured: stage st is columns [128 st, 128 st + 128) of all 128 lanes.
879://   The MMA tile is 256 (M) x 128 (N): rows [0,128) come from the leader's A stage, [128,256) from the peer's; N from both B halves.
